title: Trump Wants “Model Cities” With High-Tech Police. New Orleans Just Said “No.” | Truthout
authors: Zack Kligler, Mike Ludwig, Earle J. Fisher, Nick Fulton, Aura Bogado, Brian Dolinar, Shireen Akram-Boshar, Mathew Witecki, Ryan Brennan, Lee Hedgepeth
description:
After taking a “serious look” at applying for federal funding under the Trump administration’s Model Cities Initiative, the city leaders of cash-strapped New Orleans announced on August 31 that they will not apply for the controversial grant program.
New Orleans joined Charlotte, North Carolina, and Billings, Montana, in publicly announcing that an application for Model Cities would not be submitted before the deadline passed on September 1.
Unlike traditional grants, the Model Cities Initiative requires cities to enter into a “cooperative agreement” with the Trump administration, which would have “substantial involvement” in the planning and implementation of projects funded with the grant.
The New Orleans City Council recently voted to increase oversight of the city’s controversial surveillance drone program.
Romero said activists are now urging leaders in East Baton Rouge to abandon the Model Cities Initiative as well.
text:
After taking a “serious look” at applying for federal funding under the Trump administration’s Model Cities Initiative, the city leaders of cash-strapped New Orleans announced on August 31 that they will not apply for the controversial grant program.

The $300 million grant program for cities and local governments of more than 100,000 people offers to pay for high-tech policing and public safety infrastructure in exchange for local officials complying with federal mass deportation efforts, among other priorities. Critics say the initiative is the tip of the spear for deploying mass surveillance tech and indulging the authoritarian impulses of President Donald Trump, who has filled the streets of multiple cities with violent federal immigration agents and, in several cases, armed federal troops.

New Orleans is a majority-Black city steeped in civil rights history, and activists have been ringing alarm bells for weeks as Mayor Helena Moreno and other city leaders mulled over whether to apply for the grant amid pressure from the state’s GOP-controlled government to address an ongoing budget crisis.

Edith Romero, an organizer in New Orleans with the privacy group Eye on Surveillance, is grateful that local advocates and residents voiced their opposition and pushed the city away from applying for the grant.

“The Model Cities Initiative is a Justice Department grant program that comes with serious strings attached, including the sharing of immigration information between state, federal and local agencies,” Romero told Truthout in an email. “This means surveillance for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to separate families and terrorize our communities.”

According to the Justice Department, one of the policy “blueprints” for the Model Cities Initiative is President Donald Trump’s law enforcement surge in Memphis, Tennessee — another Democratic-led, majority-Black city in a GOP-controlled state. Launched about a year ago and involving 13 federal agencies as well as state and local law enforcement, the surge of what the White House calls “hypervigilant policing” in Memphis is still in effect. Residents and civil rights groups describe the surge as a racist and militarized federal “assault” and “occupation” and a new form of colonialism.

While the administration claims the Memphis task force is focused on “arresting violent criminals … seizing firearms, and locating missing children,” the operation, in actuality, was part of an aggressive immigration sweep. Officers have made large numbers of traffic stops to check for immigration status and have engaged in clearly documented racial profiling, according to local officials.

In Memphis, the Trump administration’s multi-agency Memphis Safe Task Force has been accused of terrorizing Black and Brown neighborhoods and retaliating against locals who attempt to record interactions with law enforcement on their phones in violation of their First Amendment rights, according to a lawsuit filed in May on behalf of four Memphis residents by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Federal troops and officers with the task force shot and killed at least four Black men in Memphis over a two-month period this summer. In at least two of the cases, autopsies and surveillance video footage cast doubt on initial claims by law enforcement that the victims pointed firearms at officers.

A National Guard team on the task force fatally shot 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson in the back as he was running away in July. Johnson’s family is calling for the guardsmen responsible to be criminally charged. Meanwhile, in New Orleans, the National Guard just finished its latest deployment to the historic French Quarter, where federal troops have mingled among tourists for the past eight months.

In a statement on August 31, New Orleans Deputy Mayor of Public Safety Michael Harrison cited unspecified questions about “legal issues” as he said that the city had decided against applying for the Model Cities Initiative. New Orleans joined Charlotte, North Carolina, and Billings, Montana, in publicly announcing that an application for Model Cities would not be submitted before the deadline passed on September 1.

“New Orleans has historically low crime, and it has been on a downward trend for years,” said Sarah Whittington, advocacy director at ACLU of Louisiana, in an interview. “So, there is a complete disconnection between reality and what the Trump administration is claiming that this funding will be used for.”

Just upriver from New Orleans, the parish government in notoriously segregated Baton Rouge recently applied for the Model Cities grant, though civil rights organizers in that city are pushing back, Romero says. The $300 million in grant funding will be split between two to four cities chosen by the Trump administration. The Justice Department is now reviewing applications, and it remains unclear whether other cities applied besides Baton Rouge.

In a collective statement, members of the Baton Rouge-based immigrant advocacy group Mision Migrante said the city’s current law enforcement system is already well-known for serious racial disparities in use the of police force without the Model Cities Initiative. Shouldn’t the city reform its historically white supremacist justice system, they ask, before bringing in AI surveillance?

“We are already concerned of the current law enforcement system we have as of today — as it has shown us serious racial disparities in the use of police force against our Black communities,” the group said.

Like the rest of Louisiana, New Orleans has a history of fiscal struggles. However, the budget crisis currently facing city leaders is profound, and voters in 2025 elected Moreno, a centrist Democrat viewed as a pragmatist, to deal with it. Harrison said the city did consider applying for the Model Cities Initiative because of the “significant investments” it could bring but ultimately decided against applying due to legal concerns around federal oversight.

Unlike traditional grants, the Model Cities Initiative requires cities to enter into a “cooperative agreement” with the Trump administration, which would have “substantial involvement” in the planning and implementation of projects funded with the grant. While cities could receive funding for prisoner reentry support programs and drug courts, they would also have to comply with Trump’s push to incarcerate and deport millions of people. The Justice Department also calls for the forced confinement of houseless people under the program, which is also known as involuntary commitment.

“Involuntary commitment is scary because it allows the government to decide who can and cannot handle their own affairs and be on streets, and it flies in the face of community-based care for reentry and success,” Whittington said. “This administration and the folks who would be in place and overseeing those programs do not necessarily have the community or those individuals’ best interests in mind, if all they are trying to do is fill beds.”

The grant also promotes the purchase of high-tech drones, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and other mass surveillance technology that has faced intense public backlash in New Orleans and across the country. Additionally, New Orleans taxpayers could be on the hook for reimbursing the federal government for the cost of deploying federal law enforcement in the event of a vaguely defined “surge in violent crime or public disorder,” according to the Justice Department.

Local ordinances regulating the capture and storage of surveillance and personal data by law enforcement do not apply to the federal government, and Whittington said allowing the Trump administration to direct local police surveillance would expose the residents of New Orleans to federal data collection efforts without legal guardrails.

The New Orleans City Council recently voted to increase oversight of the city’s controversial surveillance drone program. That the Moreno administration even considered applying for the Model Cities grant was controversial given Louisiana’s history of white supremacy and the lingering trauma among Black residents from federal troop deployments during the fatal devastation following Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

In December, ICE and Border Patrol rampaged through suburban cities outside of New Orleans that, unlike the city itself, maintain cooperation agreements with the Department of Homeland Security. The operation was widely seen by ICE critics and anti-racist locals as an abusive stunt by Gregory Bovino, the disgraced former Border Patrol commander. At the time, Moreno came under significant pressure from the White House to cooperate with the raids on one side, and frustrated constituents demanding an end to the federal invasion on the other.

Romero said activists are now urging leaders in East Baton Rouge to abandon the Model Cities Initiative as well. “We hope that New Orleans and the rest of Louisiana will continue to closely examine and reject these programs that promote surveillance as a false solution and put the safety of our communities in danger,” Romero said.

Updated with a statement from Mision Migrante on September 11.

text:
PHOENIX — The state Court of Appeals has rejected efforts to void a 2024 voter-approved immigration measure.

In a new ruling Thursday, the judges upheld Proposition 314, which allows police to arrest those who cross the border at other than a port of entry and charge them with committing a state crime.

In 2025, Living United for Change in Arizona sued, charging that the law has provisions that violate federal and state constitutional protections, ranging from possible discriminatory enforcement to whether the measure failed to provide for a new source of revenues for enforcement.

But Judge David Weinzweig, writing for the unanimous three-judge panel, said that, in the end, all that is irrelevant. He said that the challenge fails if for no other reason than LUCHA lacks standing to sue in the first place.

The ruling drew an angry reaction from Alejandra Gomez, the executive director of the community organizing group.

“We are appalled that the Court of Appeals has allowed Proposition 314 to stand at a moment when immigrant communities are already being terrorized by an increasingly aggressive federal immigration enforcement apparatus,” she said.

Gomez said no decision has been made whether to seek Arizona Supreme Court review.

Prop. 314 is crafted in a way designed not so much to incarcerate the border crossers but instead convince them to agree to be deported. That, in turn, means all charges against them would be dropped.

LUCHA argued that the provision is worded in a way that it is more likely to affect its members who share the “race, ethnicity or national origin of the immigrants who enter Arizona from the southern border” and they are more “vulnerable to misapplication” than the public at large.

Weinzweig, however, said the possibility that the law may be misapplied in the future — and to someone who shares the same ethnic background as LUCHA members — doesn’t allow them to try to ask courts to halt enforcement of the law.

“Declaratory relief should be based on an existing set of facts, not those which may or may not arise in the future,” he wrote.

That conclusion parallels a similar ruling in July by U.S. District Court Judge Michael Liburdi. He tossed a challenge to Prop. 314 brought by the Florence Immigrant Rights and Refugee Project noting that the organization had failed to show anyone had actually been affected by the new law.

In Thursday’s state appellate court ruling, Weinzweig also rejected the claim that the standards that allow police to arrest border crossers ignore constitutional requirements.

The law provides three options: the officer’s own observation, a recording, or “any other constitutionally sufficient indicia of probable cause.” While that last provision is not defined in Prop. 314, Weinzweig said those are the same standards already required for arrest under the Fourth Amendment, which protects against illegal search and seizure.

LUCHA fared no better with a parallel attack on how Prop. 314 would be funded.

The challengers pointed out that the Arizona Constitution says any ballot measure that proposes the mandatory spending of state revenues must also provide a new source for those dollars.

Put another way, a ballot measure is invalid if it simply says that any required costs will be picked up from already existing taxes or other sources. And it applies regardless of whether the proposal was referred to voters by lawmakers themselves — as is the case here — or was put on the ballot through an initiative petition of Arizona voters.

In this case, the challengers noted, Prop. 314 requires the state Department of Corrections to transport those who agree to leave the country to the border. And that, the challengers said, is an obligation to spend state resources without a commensurate increase in new dollars.

Weinzweig wasn’t buying it.

He said the measure is crafted so the mandatory obligation to transport people to the border actually falls on local law enforcement agencies whose anticipated new expenses are not covered by the state constitutional requirement. Weinzweig said the only time costs are borne by the state is if the local agency does not have the capacity to hold someone.

“This is a contingency, not a mandate,” the judge wrote.

Gomez, in her statement, said the ruling comes as the Trump administration “continues expanding the reach of immigration enforcement into more parts of everyday life.”

“Proposition 314 threatens to pour gasoline on that fire,” she said.

“It gives Arizona another vehicle to target immigrant communities, drag state and local institutions deeper into immigration enforcement, and force taxpayers to bankroll a reckless law with no clear way to pay for it,” Gomez said.

title: Policing built on human rights, accountability and trust, beyond enforcement | OHCHR
description:
Nationally, UN Human Rights is helping States analyse the root causes of violations and abuses and supporting building strong security institutions able to uphold human rights obligations.
In 2025, this partnership included organizing a hybrid Masterclass on Building Trust with Communities for human rights officers and law enforcement officials.
The masterclass was recorded and is available through UN Human Rights’ Security Forces Knowledge Hub as a training resource.
That same year, UN Human Rights published the revised Guidance and Training Package on Human Rights and Law Enforcement.
Türk called for deeper cross-border police cooperation anchored in legality, accountability and respect for human rights.
text:
“Public safety and human rights go hand in hand. Policing that respects human dignity is not only a legal obligation, it is one of the strongest foundations for public trust and lasting security,” said UN Human Rights Chief, Volker Türk, on the International Day of Police Cooperation, observed each year on 7 September.

This year's theme, "Protecting against Vulnerability – Building Trust and Legitimacy in Policing," underscores that effective policing depends on the cooperation of the communities it serves. That cooperation, UN Human Rights argues, cannot be sustained “without nurturing a mutually respectful relationship exemplifying a consistent commitment to human rights and putting words into action.”

The High Commissioner’s message builds on UN Human Rights’ 2025 office-wide strategy for engaging with security forces, adopted in recognition of the growing global involvement of security actors to manage complex phenomena, such as migration, terrorism, climate change and violent extremism.

The strategy is built on the premise that human rights-compliant security forces are integral to good governance and underpin “the stability of States, the social contract, and the pursuit of the Sustainable Development Goals," while warning that violations by security forces corrode public trust and are "often considered a major factor in radicalisation and participation in violence.”

To implement its strategy, UN Human Rights has been engaging with a broad range of security actors, including military forces, law enforcement and intelligence agencies, border and immigration authorities, prison administration, wildlife ranger authorities, accountability mechanisms, and, where relevant, non-State armed groups.

Structured around national, regional and global engagement, the strategy guides action at multiple levels with global, regional and national partners.

Nationally, UN Human Rights is helping States analyse the root causes of violations and abuses and supporting building strong security institutions able to uphold human rights obligations. as The Office also plays a role in addressing the growing role of non-State armed groups and private security actors, and building safeguards around emerging technologies like AI, drones, facial recognition and surveillance databases.

Regionally, it is deepening partnership with the African Union's peace and security architecture and with regional economic communities, alongside continued efforts to keep human rights and international humanitarian law at the centre of Security Council-authorized operations.

Globally, the Office is supporting law enforcement institutions to address systemic racism and prevent discriminatory practices. It is expanding its role in screening and training uniformed personnel in UN-mandated and authorized peace operations, advancing adherence to human rights not only as an obligation but a force enabler that strengthens mission’s effectiveness, legitimacy and public trust, including under recent Security Council resolutions on financing African Union operations and the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti.

The results are already visible. In Belize, UN Human Rights supports institutional capacity-building and leadership development to sustain rights-based policing; in Chile, it backs the integration of human rights into law enforcement protocols and trainings; and in Kenya, capacity building, accountability, legal and policy reform, fostering community-policing relationships, and gender integration are its main areas of intervention

In Mozambique, support for human rights considerations have been woven into the national police's strategic planning, covering doctrine, training and oversight. In Thailand, the Office has worked with security forces on institutionalising capacity around the use of force and facilitation of peaceful protests.

“Human rights must not be an afterthought in policing. They must be embedded through transparent processes in policies, recruitment, training, leadership, oversight, and daily operations. This is how trust is built, legitimacy is strengthened, and communities are better protected,” Türk said.

Building trust between police and communities

Community trust-building also features prominently. Between 2023 and 2026, the Office strengthened its collaboration with the Netherlands Police, particularly on initiatives aimed at building trust and cooperation between law enforcement agencies and the communities they serve.

In 2025, this partnership included organizing a hybrid Masterclass on Building Trust with Communities for human rights officers and law enforcement officials. The event brought together participants from more than 40 countries, both in person and online. The masterclass was recorded and is available through UN Human Rights’ Security Forces Knowledge Hub as a training resource.

That same year, UN Human Rights published the revised Guidance and Training Package on Human Rights and Law Enforcement. Mozambique, the Philippines and Somalia are using the package to update their guidance materials, training curricula and operational tools.

The Office is also collaborating with the International Ranger Federation on the global rollout of a Ranger Code of Conduct for Wildlife Ranger Institutions, which places strong emphasis on human rights standards and accountability.

UN Human Rights also supports the implementation of the Model Protocol for Law Enforcement Officials to Promote and Protect Human Rights in the context of Peaceful Protests, in collaboration with the Special Rapporteur on freedom of peaceful assembly and of association and the UNODC. The overall aim is at supporting g law enforcement agencies to shifting from “enforcement” to “facilitation” of peaceful protests in line with international human rights standards; an approach which will contribute to enhancing further the trust of the population.

Türk called for deeper cross-border police cooperation anchored in legality, accountability and respect for human rights.

“Open communication and genuine dialogue with communities can help identify risks, understand vulnerabilities and develop more effective responses,” Türk said. “Transparency regarding policies, practices and decision-making processes is essential for strengthening public confidence. Independent oversight and effective complaints mechanisms likewise play a critical role in ensuring accountability and reinforcing trust.”

text:
NEW YORK — Once a week, in a Queens office building, a group of immigrants in their 50s and 60s gathers. They've all known each other for some 25 years: they met when they were cleaning up ground zero together. They are among the thousands of cleanup crews who rushed to the destruction in lower Manhattan following the attacks of 9/11. Many of those workers were immigrants and as many as 6,000 of them were undocumented. They were all exposed to toxic debris, and psychological trauma. And as the Trump administration pursues its aggressive immigration agenda, many are living in enhanced fear of immigration enforcement.

"We would have lunch in the rubble, in the dust"

"Every morning I would stand on Roosevelt Avenue and 82nd," says a woman in the group named Lucelly. She asked NPR to withhold her last name — like many here, she's undocumented. She came to the U.S. from Colombia in 2000, and would wait on the avenue to get picked up for cleaning gigs.

On the morning of September 12th, 2001, the day after the attacks, a van pulled up. "Come on, let's go!" she recalls the driver yelling. They offered her $8.50 an hour to clean the wreckage.

"If the driver had told us: 'We're going to a danger zone,' people would not have rushed in," she says.

But she says it felt like just another job, and a duty to the city that had welcomed her. Like a lot of people who went to clean up at ground zero, she went armed only with her house-cleaning gear: a paper mask and rubber gloves.

The hours were long. "We would have lunch in the rubble, in the dust," she recalls. "Then we'd go home wearing the same clothing we'd been working in."

Since then, Lucelly has battled breast cancer and respiratory disease. She is among the tens of thousands whose health was severely compromised by exposure to the hundreds of tons of toxic debris the tower's collapse released into the air. According to the World Trade Center health program, there have been over 57,000 cancer cases, and a myriad other health conditions. Officials knew within weeks but called it safe.

What we know about the undocumented workers at ground zero

It's not known how many undocumented workers were involved in the 9/11 cleanup, but advocates say it's somewhere between 2,000 and 6,000 people.

"There was this rush to clean everything up quickly," says social worker Rosa Bramble Caballero, who runs the clean up crew support group in Queens. "The city hired multiple contractors for the clean up. In turn these contractors subcontracted, and those subcontractors subcontracted, and hired day laborers who were standing in street corners in Queens. Mind you, these were companies who had received millions of dollars from the city. Many women who did housekeeping were taken there. And then they got there and realized they were actually at ground zero, which, by the way, sometimes they were not told that that's where they were going."

A nearly decade-old legislative push to give undocumented ground zero workers a path to citizenship has failed to gain traction. The 9/11 Immigrant Worker Freedom Act was first introduced in 2017, then again in 2021. It was reintroduced in 2025 by Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. No Republicans have signed on to the bill, each version of which has remained stalled in the House Judiciary Committee. On the eve of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Representative Ocasio-Cortez told NPR she believes "this legislation genuinely should be bipartisan and non-controversial. These heroes, many of whom sacrificed their lives, are people who are absolutely deserving of citizenship." But with immigration reform remaining a highly divisive topic, it is unlikely the bill would advance.

NPR reached out to the White House for comment, and received no response.

"I was blindfolded": the psychological toll of 9/11 cleanup

A woman named Rosa, from Guatemala, says she arrived at the site the days after the attack. She asked that NPR withhold her last name: although she is legally in the U.S., she is nervous about increased immigration enforcement operations here in Queens.

Back then she worked in demolition, and unlike most in the group, she arrived at ground zero with union training on how to handle asbestos and other toxic materials, and the proper equipment. She says when she got to the scene, she was shocked. "It was mostly Ecuadorians, Colombians, Peruvians, Mexicans. There were so many people doing the same work as me … but wearing little paper masks."

Rosa has acid reflux related to exposure, for which she has received worker's compensation. But she is one of the only people in the group who did not go on to develop a debilitating disease.

The emotional scarring, however, runs deep.

"You might not have noticed this," she says, "but I'm sitting in this chair because I need to see the exit. If I don't see a door at all times, I get a panic attack."

Soon after starting at the site, she made a gruesome discovery. "An arm. I… I can't forget it. I will never get over it. I touched it. We had been trained to lift a little yellow flag when we found a body part, and I did. The police came, and we put it in a bin, we covered it, and we took it to the Trinity Church."

A few days after arriving, she says she was blindfolded with a sleeping mask by her supervisors, and escorted to another area. "When we got there, they were sifting in the dirt. They were sifting for body parts. They assigned me to go through found objects. Jewelry. Wallets. ID's. Those little name plates people put on their offices. I would put them in separate bags."

She believes she was blindfolded because of the amount of looting and attempted stealing. She says there were five people doing that job- herself and immigrants from Mexico, Paraguay and Poland. She says they worked in silence, and were closely monitored. Eventually, she was moved to an underground area with a vault. She and her coworkers worked alongside law enforcement. She believes it was the massive vault system underneath The World Trade Center, where hundreds of thousands of tons of precious metals were recovered.

In those days, Rosa also says she joined as a Red Cross volunteer, tasked with helping any of the cleanup and first responders who got injured. She beams, "they gave me a certificate of honor, responsibility and honesty. It makes me proud. I've told some people back home, but I almost never talk about it, because I consider it something personal. It is mine to remember."

9/11: For immigrant workers, a different kind of legacy

These days, Rosa is more concerned about the reality of immigration raids in Queens. Although she has legal status, she says she is afraid of being targeted, and is hypervigilant for her friends in the retiree cleanup group who are undocumented.

Undocumented workers are entitled to worker's compensation, and many have received it for their work in 9/11, as well as assistance through the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act. But Bramble Caballero says to this day she meets people who are too scared to apply.

For those who have received compensation, she says, it's typically around $80,000. Bramble Caballero says that money only goes so far. "Because they are undocumented and their health has been compromised, they really can no longer work. So although they may have received awards, those awards dry out," she says.

The fear of being picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement as operations spike in Queens and nationwide, has added to the PTSD which most in the group suffer.

"I am scared. We are all scared", says Lucelly, the woman who took her lunch breaks in the rubble of ground zero. "My daughter lives in New Jersey, and I don't even go visit her, because I am scared of immigration. It is a new pain on top of an old one."

She says returning home to Colombia is not an option: she worries she would not have access to the same quality care for her health problems. It's a sense of limbo shared by many in this group: to return to their towns and villages might mean not being able to access quality care. The alternative is to live in the U.S., with the constant fear of being picked up, but access to medical treatment.

Lucelly says her bitterness grows as the anniversary of the attacks approaches.

text:
Thousands of Salvadoran immigrants nationwide faced uncertainty after the federal government failed to decide by a Wednesday deadline whether to extend or terminate their longtime temporary protections against deportation.

Those protections, known as Temporary Protected Status or TPS, allow immigrants to obtain work permits and by Thursday some Salvadorans had already been fired from their jobs. Others who had been let go were reinstated after the Trump administration clarified that an announcement on TPS for Salvadorans would come “at the appropriate time” and that they would retain work authorization in the meantime.

Employers also expressed uncertainty about whether the statement was enough to legally keep Salvadoran employees on their payroll. Those who lost their jobs worked across the U.S. in construction, at hotels and as janitors.

Some took the announcement that work authorizations remained in place — made late Wednesday by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — as a cause for hope, while others saw it as prolonged mental torture. There are 170,000 Salvadoran TPS holders, including 36,000 living in California.

Asked for further guidance on Thursday, Homeland Security sent a link to the USCIS website.

Advocates with the National TPS Alliance distributed a letter including the administration’s announcement for TPS holders to share with their employers and stating that “any decision to terminate could not take effect for a minimum of 60 days.” The letter seemed to help, as advocates reported that some fired employees had been able to return to work.

Not everyone was reinstated. Jose Ramirez reported to his construction job in Santa Monica for the last time on Wednesday.

The 63-year-old had been legally working in the U.S. since 2001, when TPS was first extended to Salvadoran immigrants.

He had been in the country for six years before that, and constantly struggled to find stable work. The work permit was a lifeline. He’d dedicated the last 25 years to construction, during which he fathered three daughters and set roots in Compton.

Still, his boss said Ramirez could no longer present for work Thursday.

“I’ve worked on buildings that reach the skies of Los Angeles,” Ramirez said. “I’ve contributed economically and lent my labor to this great country.”

Ramirez’s boss said his job would be available to him, but he’d need to show proof of an active work permit. A notice or a letter is not enough, Ramirez said.

The USCIS announcement was “a ray of hope that they will give us an extension,” Ramirez said. “But, it’s just not certain. Anything can happen. We’re just praying to God that the government will make it official.”

Others were luckier. Karina, 42, who has been a custodian at a university in Houston for 18 years, said she panicked when a human resources representative called to say she wouldn’t be able to return to work. Karina asked The Times not to include her last name or the name of the university where she works out of concern for her employment.

She said her job pays for half of her daughter’s college tuition and the health insurance of both of her children. She also pays for her mother’s kidney disease medication in El Salvador.

Given the uncertainty, the university gave Karina one month of unpaid leave, she said. But after the USCIS announcement, the representative called her back Thursday and said she could return to work the next day.

Karina said she owns a house, has always paid taxes and never relied on government assistance. She said she was grateful for the reprieve, albeit momentary.

“I have my whole life here,” she said of the U.S. “Over there, I have nothing.”

Ending TPS would be a shock to El Salvador’s economy, where remittances from Salvadorans in the U.S. make up nearly a quarter of the nation’s GDP — nearly $10 billion last year. In 2019, President Nayib Bukele, an ally of President Trump, publicly called on the U.S. to extend TPS for Salvadoran immigrants.

More recently, Bukele has embraced Trump’s deportation agenda, including by accepting controversial deals to house foreign detainees in the country’s mega-prison. The number of people deported to El Salvador nearly doubled in the first three months of 2026.

The decision by the Department of Homeland Security to extend or terminate TPS typically has been made at least 60 days before the designation was set to expire. DHS can extend the program for a six, 12 or 18-month period or decide to cancel the designation.

But the Trump administration has delayed announcements, including some made days after the designation expired. A Supreme Court ruling in June determined that the Homeland Security secretary has final authority over the program and cut down the ability for advocates to sue.

Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition, said she spoke on Wednesday with Trump administration and Homeland Security officials. The group represents companies that employ immigrants, including TPS holders.

She said there has been an internal debate within the administration around the economic impact of eliminating work authorization for Salvadorans, who have lived in the U.S. for decades, perform skilled jobs and can’t easily be replaced. That debate escalated last week, she said.

In initial statements to reporters on Wednesday, Homeland Security had said only that until an announcement about TPS, Salvadorans would “retain protection.” Shi said the clarification that evening that Salvadorans would also retain work authorization was a good sign.

“We’re cautiously optimistic,” she said. “DHS yesterday could have said nothing. The fact that they made that change — that had to be a decision because of the pressure.”

For now, though, some employers are stuck waiting for answers.

Lauren Truslow, CEO of 3D Enviro, a Virginia company that does identification and abatement of hazardous materials, said the lack of a decision on TPS has been stressful and costly. Three of her 30 employees are TPS holders from El Salvador. Another, who is married to a Salvadoran TPS holder, told her his family plans to leave the country if the program is canceled.

3D Enviro is a federal contractor, and Truslow said that her employees’ driver’s licenses and federal badges expired on Wednesday.

“How do they continue to work for me?” she said. “No one seems to know the answer to that. They can’t get into federal facilities without valid ID. Them showing a memo from USCIS is not going to cut it.”

During a news conference organized on Thursday by the Central American Resource Center of Los Angeles, other immigrant rights groups and local elected officials, speakers urged TPS holders to form a plan for their families and schedule a legal consultation with a trusted lawyer. They also called on the administration to issue a decision on TPS for El Salvador and a pathway to permanent legal status.

“Salvadoran families deserve clear, timely and trustworthy information from the government,” said Martha Arévalo, CARECEN’s executive director. “As we gather this morning, we don’t have an extension for TPS. … What we have is another waiting game and a renewed limbo for families.”

“We are going to fight this,” vowed Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass.

In a statement, Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) called the USCIS announcement “clear as mud.”

“Once again, the Trump Administration is punishing immigrants who have followed the rules with chaos, uncertainty, and cruelty,” he wrote.

Also in attendance at the news conference was Carmen Sanchez, 49, who works the night janitorial shift cleaning offices in Los Angeles. She said many of her co-workers who were also protected under TPS were told not to return to work after Wednesday.

Sanchez planned to report to work Thursday evening, but was sure she’d suffer the same fate. She said she has three adult children in El Salvador and is helping two of them pay for college.

“If we lose our work permit, we lose our job. We lose our stability. We lose everything,” Sanchez said. “We’re being kept on this thread of extensions, and we don’t know when that thread is going to break.”

text:
BALTIMORE —

Immigrant rights groups and Maryland residents have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, alleging that Immigration and Customs Enforcement has conducted more than 5,000 illegal arrests in Maryland since January 2025 through racial profiling, aggression, and without probable cause.

"It is illegal and unacceptable," said Shana Khader, legal director of We Are CASA.

The plaintiffs, including the organization We Are CASA and several individual Marylanders, announced the lawsuit in an effort to end what they describe as illegal ICE arrests across the state.

"That fear doesn't leave when the detention ends," said Guillermo, a member of We Are CASA, speaking under a pseudonym.

Francisco, another member of We Are CASA using a pseudonym, shared his experience.

"The worst part is when I see a car that resembles an ICE vehicle. My whole body starts shaking. I'm afraid they might detain me again, and I just don't know what would happen," he said through a translator.

The lawsuit seeks class-action status, a temporary injunction, and an eventual end to the practice.

"We want to hold them accountable and reduce the number of arrests that are going on," Austin Rose of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights said.

Sonia Kumar of the ACLU of Maryland added, "The surging we're seeing across Maryland — including in Frederick —has just added sort of fuel to the fire we feel in our bellies to sort of get the case out. It all feels relevant and connected."

In a statement to WBAL-TV 11 News, the Department of Homeland Security denied the allegations.

"Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in 'racial profiling' are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S.—NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity. ICE has authority for lawful arrests under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices.

The statement did not address claims in the lawsuit made by a U.S. citizen.

title: Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs
description:
Hundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said.
Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France.
The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time.
However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown.
Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK.
text:
Hundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said.

The pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, announced it in July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France.

The deal is due to expire on 1 October and at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, and the French government has indicated it wants the scheme to be expanded Europe-wide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone.

One French politician told the Guardian that so far France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response.

About 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed. These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time.

At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Mike German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground.

Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in, one out treaty.

The Home Office disputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute.

“Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.”

However, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred children had been identified as unlawfully detained as adults for the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”.

French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe.

The Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys.

Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances.

Harris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.”

Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown.

“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said.

Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said.

text:
The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission), through the Country Rapporteur on Human Rights in the Republic of Kenya, Honourable Commissioner Solomon Ayele Dersso, expresses grave concern over a recent public statement and government directives made regarding the closure of small businesses operated by foreign nationals.

Reports reaching the Commission indicate that, following the statement made by H.E. President William Ruto on 2 September 2026 suggesting the immediate closure of small businesses, incidents of physical attacks, intimidation and harassment targeting establishments of foreign nationals, particularly from Burundi, with some experiencing looting and destruction of their businesses, costing them their livelihoods, have occurred. The situation has triggered heightened anxiety and uncertainty particularly on the part of Burundians living in Kenya, prompting hundreds of them descending on the Burundi Embassy in Nairobi.

The African Commission affirms that the authority of the Government of Kenya, for enforcing laws that regulate migration and the establishment and operation of businesses, should be executed both with full compliance with due process of the law and fundamental human rights and without triggering incitement of hate and violence against foreign nationals.

The Commission in this respect reminds Kenya, and all States Parties to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter), that the rights enshrined in the African Charter, notably the rights of everyone to non-discrimination, equality, dignity and the security of their person, lives and property, are guaranteed to all individuals in their territory, including foreign nationals and migrants irrespective of their legal status.

In view of the foregoing, the Commission respectfully invites the Government of Kenya to:

i. Conduct prompt investigations into all reported incidents of violence and intimidation against foreign nationals, in accordance with international human rights standards;

ii. Initiate measures that ensures that members of the public cease acts of violence and intimidation purporting to enforce directives on the closure of foreign national run small businesses;

iii. Take all necessary measures to ensure protection the foreign nationals and migrants residing in Kenya, particularly those operating small businesses with particular focus to Burundian nationals at risk of intimidation and violence; and

iv. Ensure that enforcement of laws on immigration and operation of small businesses complies with standards of legality, due process of the law, equality and non-discrimination.

The African Commission will continue to monitor the situation closely and remains ready to engage with and support the Government of Kenya in upholding its human and peoples’ rights obligations and ensuring justice, accountability, and the protection of human and peoples’ rights in Kenya.

Banjul, 09 September 2026

title: Mass. judge accused of enabling immigrant to escape ICE gets a rare public reprimand
description:
The highest court in Massachusetts on Thursday issued a public reprimand against a district court judge who was accused of allowing an immigrant to escape U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.
The decision by the Supreme Judicial Court follows a recommendation for the reprimand by a hearing officer for the Commission on Judicial Conduct.
It concluded that Joseph created the appearance of impropriety and failed to comply with the law.
The case has escalated a clash between the Trump administration and local authorities over the Republican president’s sweeping immigration crackdown.
That agency, the Commission on Judicial Conduct, concluded that Joseph “engaged in willful judicial misconduct that brought the judicial office into disrepute, as well as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice and unbecoming a judicial officer.”
text:
The highest court in Massachusetts on Thursday issued a public reprimand against a district court judge who was accused of allowing an immigrant to escape U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

The case dates back to 2018 when Judge Shelley Joseph was accused of colluding with the immigrant’s attorney and a court officer to allow him escape out a back door of the courthouse after a hearing on charges that included drug possession.

The decision by the Supreme Judicial Court follows a recommendation for the reprimand by a hearing officer for the Commission on Judicial Conduct. It concluded that Joseph created the appearance of impropriety and failed to comply with the law.

“The respondent’s statements during that conversation, including her proposal to detain (the immigrant) overnight in State custody, and her conduct in instructing the clerk to turn off the court room audio recording system, created an appearance of impropriety in violation of her duties,” according to the Supreme Judicial Court ruling.

Joseph's attorney, Elizabeth Mulvey, argued at the commission hearing last year that the case had been distorted over time and that everyone had come to believe that her client “let an illegal immigrant out of the door” with half the public believing she should be jailed and the other half calling her a “folk hero.”

Mulvey also argued that Joseph had been vilified in the media and people were giving the impression that “dozens of people” had seen Joseph “get off the bench, escort the defendant to the door, give him a hug and wish him God speed.”

On Thursday, Mulvey acknowledged that it had been an “incredibly long and difficult eight years for Judge Joseph.”

“We are grateful to the hearing officer who undertook this monumental task and pleased that his efforts have shown that this was a baseless federal prosecution from the beginning and solely the work of the defense lawyer involved,” Mulvey said in a statement. "Judge Joseph is thankful for everyone who stood by her and looks forward to rejoining her colleagues.”

The case is similar to that of a former Wisconsin judge who was convicted in December of felony obstruction for helping a man evade immigration authorities. The case has escalated a clash between the Trump administration and local authorities over the Republican president’s sweeping immigration crackdown.

Last year, Hannah Dugan escorted a man and his lawyer out of her courtroom through the jury door after learning that immigration authorities were seeking his arrest. The man was taken into custody outside the courthouse after agents chased him on foot.

Dugan resigned the Milwaukee County circuit judgeship she had held for nine years in January amid threats of impeachment from Republican state lawmakers who labeled her an activist judge. In her resignation letter, she said her prosecution threatened “the independence of our judiciary.” Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, a fierce Trump loyalist running for Wisconsin governor, had urged authorities to “lock her up.”

Then in July, U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman fined Dugan $5,000, describing the case as a situation where an otherwise good person, upset by immigration policies in this country, made a bad decision in the moment. She was spared prison time.

In the Massachusetts case, federal obstruction of justice charges against Joseph were dropped in 2022 after she agreed to refer herself to a state agency that investigates allegations of misconduct by members of the bench.

That agency, the Commission on Judicial Conduct, concluded that Joseph “engaged in willful judicial misconduct that brought the judicial office into disrepute, as well as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice and unbecoming a judicial officer.”

title: Denver Sues to Block Armed ICE Agents at Voting Sites - GV Wire
description:
The City of Denver, Latino civil rights organizations and government watch groups asked a federal judge on Thursday to block the Trump administration from allowing armed federal immigration agents to serve warrants at polling sites.
The possibility of federal agents at the ballot box has intensified concerns of Election Day chaos in an already volatile campaign season.
Fears that the Trump administration might send armed federal agents or troops to polling places or election offices have simmered among Democrats, voting rights groups and immigrant rights networks for months.
Trump administration officials have said there is no plan to deploy armed agents or troops in the upcoming elections.
But they have also not ruled out the possibility that armed agents could be present at polling locations or involved in elections.
text:
The City of Denver, Latino civil rights organizations and government watch groups asked a federal judge on Thursday to block the Trump administration from allowing armed federal immigration agents to serve warrants at polling sites.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., asserts that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and David Venturella, the acting head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are allowing federal agents to enforce civil immigration laws at polling locations as a matter of policy. The plaintiffs argue that the practice violates federal laws protecting free and fair elections.

“The presence of federal force at the polls interferes with the smooth administration of elections at the local level,” the lawsuit states. “It disrupts voting and makes it more difficult for state and local election officials and law enforcement to do their jobs by making polling places spaces of confrontation.”

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Speaking to reporters last week in New York, Mullin said that Democrats were fearmongering and that ICE was not patrolling polling places. “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place,” he said, “or we’re serving a warrant.”

The groups that brought the suit argue such actions violate federal law, which bans military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Their case is the first lawsuit against the administration over such actions.

Civil rights and government watch groups say they have chronicled several encounters at polling sites nationwide since the spring that they said failed to meet that bar. In May, they allege, armed agents “swarmed” the parking lot of an active polling site in San Antonio to detain a person in plain view of voters until the county sheriff ordered them leave.

In June, ICE agents entered a polling site in Syracuse, New York, to interrogate an election volunteer over a social media post that she made five months earlier regarding the fatal ICE shooting of a woman in Minneapolis, according to the lawsuit.

The possibility of federal agents at the ballot box has intensified concerns of Election Day chaos in an already volatile campaign season. Ahead of the 2026 midterms in November, the Trump administration has sought to impose restrictions on mail voting, prompted a congressional redistricting race and escalated efforts to identify and deport noncitizens who registered to vote, even with no evidence of widespread voter fraud.

Fears that the Trump administration might send armed federal agents or troops to polling places or election offices have simmered among Democrats, voting rights groups and immigrant rights networks for months. Trump has long repeated unfounded assertions of electoral fraud and has called for Republican officials to “take over” elections in parts of the country.

Trump administration officials have said there is no plan to deploy armed agents or troops in the upcoming elections. But they have also not ruled out the possibility that armed agents could be present at polling locations or involved in elections.

In the lawsuit filed Thursday, city and county officials in Denver said the area is home to a large immigrant population, making it a likely target for ICE operations during the midterm election.

The presence of armed officers could deter residents from casting votes or dropping off mail-in ballots and could fuel anxiety among election workers and volunteers, they said in the lawsuit. Election officials in Denver have already scheduled training for election workers on how to identify federal agents in plain clothes, document their presence and de-escalate interactions, according to the lawsuit.

In a statement, Mayor Mike Johnston of Denver, a Democrat who has sparred with the Trump administration over its mass deportation efforts, said his city would “fight tooth and nail” to prevent the stationing of ICE agents near polling sites.

“Our right to vote is powerful and enshrined in the U.S. Constitution and U.S. Code,” Paul López, the Denver clerk and recorder, said in a statement.

The groups involved in the lawsuit — Common Cause; the League of United Latin American Citizens, or LULAC; and UnidosUS — said recent ICE activity at polling locations was already chilling voter registration drives, canvassing efforts and civic participation in the electoral process. The organizations have also diverted funding, staff time and ad space away from standard voter mobilization efforts toward establishing rapid-response safety networks, “Vote Safe from ICE” educational materials and de-escalation training.

In a statement, Janet Murguía, the president and CEO of UnidosUS, said sending officers into polling locations was “not immigration enforcement” but “voter suppression, plain and simple.”

Juan Proaño, the CEO of LULAC, called the actions part of the administration’s “attempts to weaken the very institutions it is entrusted to protect.”

—

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

title: It's Been 25 Years Since 9/11. What Has DHS Become? - POLITICO
description:
He hoped to build a homeland security structure akin to the National Security Council, which coordinates interagency work among cabinet departments, and saw a presidential-level office with strong budget responsibilities as the best way to focus disparate agencies and functions.
Yet as evidence mounted about the myriad warning signs that U.S. law enforcement and intelligence had missed leading up to the attacks, congressional pressure for a major reorganization became politically inescapable by 2002.
At the time, there was a widespread push to split the bureau into a British-style domestic law enforcement agency, like Scotland Yard, and a domestic intelligence agency, like MI5.
But in a careful, quiet personal lobbying campaign, Mueller made the case that having the bureau’s intelligence and law enforcement capabilities under one roof made the nation safer.
Instead, DHS possessed very narrow domestic criminal investigative authorities, mostly focused on customs smuggling and human trafficking (Homeland Security Investigations) and counterfeiting and financial crimes (Secret Service).
text:
The Sept. 11 attacks, though, raised terrorism from background noise to an existential dread. It was clear to the officials leading government at the time that living up to Bush’s mantra would require a new approach. “I don’t think that anybody of my generation — and even older generations — had ever experienced anything like this kind of successful attack, killing over 3,000 Americans. It was worse than Pearl Harbor in numbers and in terms of the fact that the victims were civilians and not even military,” Michael Chertoff, who at the time was head of the criminal division at the Department of Justice and who later became the second secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, told me this summer, when we spoke as part of my podcast, Long Shadow. “It was a real revolution in what the threats were. We needed to re-orchestrate how we secure our people and our property against this kind of attack.”

Bush resisted the push for the new Cabinet department for months, believing that he could best coordinate existing departments from a newly created White House Office of Homeland Security, which was created 11 days after 9/11 and first headed by former Pennsylvania governor Tom Ridge. He hoped to build a homeland security structure akin to the National Security Council, which coordinates interagency work among cabinet departments, and saw a presidential-level office with strong budget responsibilities as the best way to focus disparate agencies and functions.

Yet as evidence mounted about the myriad warning signs that U.S. law enforcement and intelligence had missed leading up to the attacks, congressional pressure for a major reorganization became politically inescapable by 2002.

“There was a recognition that we were too fragmented and that there were a lot of silos and that we needed to find a way to bring together all of the sources of information and all of the expertise to build a capability to prevent acts of terrorism,” Chertoff said.

Exactly what that new structure would look like, though, was very much an open debate. Amid fierce turf battles and lobbying by Cabinet officials and congressional leaders, the very agencies that failed to “connect the dots” ahead of 9/11 — the FBI and the CIA — remained apart from the new Cabinet department. Instead of a sweeping “homeland security” mandate, the new department that emerged from legislative and presidential wrangling and horse-trading in late 2002 might have been better termed the “Department of Border and Transportation Security.”

Jeh Johnson, who served as DHS secretary in the second term of the Obama administration, says the focus at the time the department was founded was more about securing borders than the more nuanced work of preventing terrorism.

“The thinking was that terrorism was an extraterritorial threat, so let’s consolidate the regulation of all the different ways somebody can enter the country into one Cabinet-level department — land, border patrol, courts, customs, aviation security, air and water, Coast Guard — and throw in a few additional ones in there with it, like the Secret Service and FEMA,” Johnson told me in an interview.

Nevertheless, at the time of its creation, DHS was the largest reorganization of government since the creation of the Department of Defense after World War II and brought together all or parts of 22 separate government agencies, from the U.S. Coast Guard, housed in the Transportation Department, and Treasury’s Secret Service to the Immigration and Naturalization Service at the Justice Department to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service and Plum Island Animal Disease Center, as well as FEMA, which had been an independent agency reporting to directly to the president.

The result became the nation’s third-largest Cabinet department, with an amalgamation of organizational cultures that ranged from the U.S. Customs Service and Coast Guard, which date to the first years of the U.S. government in the late 1700s, to the fiercely independent Border Patrol — whose leaders lobbied to keep its traditional green uniform rather than unite under a common CBP blue uniform — to then-entirely new creations like the Transportation Security Administration.

Given that complexity, it’s perhaps not surprising that DHS has struggled ever since to coalesce into one organization with a shared mission and culture — and it shows. DHS’s own workforce has borne the brunt of the mission mismatch; it has consistently ranked at or near the bottom of federal government morale surveys. In the 18 surveys of the U.S. government’s “Best Places to Work” conducted by the non-partisan Partnership for Public Service between 2005 and 2024, DHS ranked last or second-to-last an astounding 13 times among the roughly 20 large government departments.

Many of the agencies reflect deeply troubled internal cultures: Using CBP’s own discipline reports, I calculated earlier this year that 4,913 CBP officers and Border Patrol agents have been arrested for crime, corruption and misconduct from 2005 to 2024 — a total that works out to be one agent or officer arrested every 36 hours for more than two decades, and a number that itself would represent the nation’s fourth-largest civilian police department, equal roughly to the entire size of the Philadelphia police force. While exact statistics are difficult to calculate, it appears that CBP has a misconduct rate five times greater than other federal law enforcement agencies — and that perhaps CBP officers and Border Patrol agents even are arrested at a higher rate per capita than that of the unauthorized immigrant population.

While DHS leadership under previous presidents has been largely steady, it has proven a damaging revolving door in both Trump presidencies; the department lacked a Senate-confirmed leader through nearly the entire final two years of Trump’s first term and the administration even struggled to prove in court who was legally in charge of the department. In his second term, DHS secretary Kristi Noem lasted just 14 months before being forced out.

But if DHS has proven itself ill-suited to focus on foreign terrorism, it has become a useful catch-all presidential “Praetorian Guard” across both of Trump’s presidential terms. In his first term, amid the nationwide protests that followed the murder of George Floyd, Trump turned to a dubious legal interpretation to deploy Border Patrol agents and other DHS officers to do battle with protesters in cities like Portland, Oregon. “I don’t need invitations by the state, state mayors or state governors to do our job,” then-acting DHS secretary Chad Wolf told reporters amid the 2020 unrest. “We’re going to do that whether they like us there or not.” In recent days, Trump has launched a nationwide “surge” of ICE agents to investigate voter fraud, a vanishingly rare crime with no clear nexus to ICE’s normal investigative responsibilities.

Altogether the ranks of DHS have swelled greatly since its creation and fundamentally altered the balance of federal law enforcement; recent government figures show that roughly half of all federal law enforcement officers are now housed inside DHS, while just a third of federal agents and officers are housed in the Department of Justice, which includes the FBI, DEA, and ATF. Today, again, while it’s hard to calculate exact figures given the recent hiring surge by ICE and CBP, DHS may in fact employ as much as 55% to 60% of all federal law enforcement personnel. Last summer’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act funneled billions of fresh dollars into DHS, ICE and CBP, turbocharging their budgets even further. As I calculated earlier this year, the $53 billion procurement and construction budget for CBP alone is equal to the entire 2024 defense expenditures of 10 European countries — Hungary, Austria, the Czech Republic, Switzerland, Finland, Greece, Belgium, Romania, Denmark and Norway.

Today, 25 years after 9/11, DHS’s core original mission of combating and responding to terrorism seems all-but forgotten in the public eye — and it seems particularly ill-poised to respond to the modern terrorism or national security threats as they currently exist.

While al Qaeda certainly remained dangerous for years after 9/11 — including executing the 2004 Madrid train bombings and the 2005 bus and train bombings in London, remembered as the 7/7 attacks — Osama bin Laden never successfully directed another attack at the U.S. homeland before he was killed in 2011 by a SEAL Team Six raid after intelligence located his secret hideout in Pakistan. (The only al Qaeda-directed attack to hit the U.S. homeland since 2001 was a December 2019 shooting by a Royal Saudi Air Force aviation student at Naval Air Station Pensacola that investigators later determined was directed by al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, an affiliate group known as AQAP; the shooter killed three U.S. sailors before being killed by responding sheriff deputies.)

The U.S. did weather a wave of attacks across the mid-2010s by individuals inspired by ISIS, an Islamic extremist group that grew out of the chaos caused by the U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, but in the last decade, the primary terrorism threat has become domestic actors — especially far-right white supremacists and mass shooters. DHS has specifically struggled to even name that threat: Then-DHS secretary Janet Napolitano backpedaled after a 2009 intelligence report cited the rising threat of far-right actors and former military veterans.

Elizabeth Neumann, then-DHS assistant secretary for counterterrorism, told me that in Trump’s first term she was startled to realize that there was no one paying attention to the rise of domestic extremists and white supremacists. As she said, “In the analysis field, it takes years for you to gain an understanding of an enemy and their tactics, their techniques, so that you can look at an event and say, this matters or this doesn’t matter. It just turns out there had been nobody working the domestic terrorism beat…. We really felt like we were in the dark.”

It’s a threat that has grown even more serious in the years since — and yet still remains largely off the radar of DHS. “Most acts of terrorism now — by any objective measure — in this country are from within,” Johnson told me. “There are not a whole lot of DHS cops running around the interior looking for terrorists. That task has always been with the FBI.”

Looking back, there were three decisions that hobbled DHS’s mission and responsibilities from the start.

The first was FBI director Robert Mueller’s successful argument that the FBI should remain intact. At the time, there was a widespread push to split the bureau into a British-style domestic law enforcement agency, like Scotland Yard, and a domestic intelligence agency, like MI5. The U.S., in fact, is one of the few Western countries that unites its domestic intelligence capabilities along with its equivalent of a national police force. (Canada, for instance, has both the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.) Immediately after the 9/11 attacks, and as evidence mounted of the failures of the FBI and the CIA to communicate successfully and “connect the dots,” many on Capitol Hill called to break the bureau apart. But in a careful, quiet personal lobbying campaign, Mueller made the case that having the bureau’s intelligence and law enforcement capabilities under one roof made the nation safer. Ultimately, congressional leaders acquiesced — largely as a personal endorsement of Mueller, who had taken over the bureau just a week before 9/11 and who had committed to a top-to-bottom reorganization of the bureau.

Second, despite its new labeling as “homeland security” — a phrase all-but born into official Washington lingo in the wake of the 9/11 attacks — the newly formed DHS actually had shockingly little responsibility for combatting terrorism, which mostly remained firmly the purview domestically of the Department of Justice, with its FBI and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Instead, DHS possessed very narrow domestic criminal investigative authorities, mostly focused on customs smuggling and human trafficking (Homeland Security Investigations) and counterfeiting and financial crimes (Secret Service). In fact, despite its name, many of HSI’s most legendary and important investigations and prosecutions have come in cases overseas, focused on cybercrime, transnational organized crime and the smuggling of weapons of mass destruction. As early as 2005, a Washington Post investigation concluded, “To some extent, the department was set up to fail. It was assigned the awesome responsibility of defending the homeland without the investigative, intelligence and military powers of the FBI, CIA and the Pentagon; it was also repeatedly undermined by the White House that initially opposed its creation.”

Third, there was a challenge more visible in retrospect: The new department inherited what would become one of the nation’s most divisive issues — immigration and border security — alongside a whole host of what were traditionally more nonpartisan responsibilities, from FEMA’s disaster relief to the search-and-rescue efforts and navigation aid maintenance of the Coast Guard to the airport security checkpoints of the newly-created TSA, as well as the protection of the nation’s critical civilian infrastructure, from water utilities to government IT networks, of what is now called the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. In many countries, these functions are housed in something more like a national civil defense agency. The shortcomings of this model became evident in multiple subsequent crises, including famously during Hurricane Katrina in 2005 when FEMA — which traditionally had reported directly to the White House — struggled to mobilize relief efforts across the government.

The result of this organizational mismatch has become an all-too-obvious mission creep — as a department ill-poised to do the thing it was created to do instead became a politically useful and opportunistic cudgel for a president with authoritarian impulses. Across his two terms, Trump has seized political openings and turbocharged DHS’s funding to target not foreign terrorists like al Qaeda or ISIS, but political dissidents and protesters here at home — people Trump himself has repeatedly labeled “terrorists.”

“I have seen firsthand how law enforcement agencies compete for space,” Johnson says. “Their jurisdiction does tend to overlap in ways the public does not understand — one agency is always nipping at the heels of the other, and very often who has the case depends on who got there first. A consolidation is in order.”

Johnson’s proposed model suggests also separating the government’s investigators from the prosecutors at the Justice Department — in the same way many states separate district attorneys from police departments at the local level. To him, that split would also limit the possibility of the weaponization of federal prosecution, requiring the assent of not just the attorney general but a second Cabinet leader before cases could be pursued against perceived political enemies.

Calls to undo the mistake of DHS’s creation aren’t exactly new — a one-time DHS official at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute think tank was calling for the department’s end even before its 10th birthday, as did the libertarian CATO Institute. Ahead of the 20th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the ACLU joined in the call for its dismantling, and that was well before Trump sent ICE and CBP en masse into U.S. cities. Yet there are few examples in modern history of a former Cabinet official like Johnson calling for his own former department’s dissolution. Indeed, across Washington, most one-time Cabinet leaders spend the rest of their careers dining out on their prestigious presidential appointments; Johnson, however, tries his hardest now to avoid being publicly recognized as a former DHS official.

“The immigration mission has overwhelmed the department,” Johnson said. “If I have a DHS gym bag or a DHS hat, I don’t wear it in public anymore because the immigration mission has become so politically volatile.”

But DHS isn’t shying away from controversy or its combative stance domestically — in fact, this week, as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approached, current Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced that he was redoing the department’s official seal to reflect that DHS was “at war every single day.”

It’s a striking admission that with the wind-down of the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, the longest-running of the “9/11 forever wars” appears to be the one we launched here at home, against ourselves.
