text:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.

Ohio officials and candidates alike have reacted to the death of a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant who died by apparent suicide after being bullied because of his immigration status and the ankle monitor he was required to have.

Pierre Damas Bel was a Springfield High School graduate and Wright State University student at the time of his death, when he walked into Interstate 70 traffic on Aug. 31. Social media posts from Damas Bel’s account talked about his desire to pursue his education in the U.S., to build a future and play college-level soccer while working toward medical school.

“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” Damas Bel wrote.

His father said Damas Bel had told him earlier in the day on Aug. 31 that he hadn’t been “feeling okay mentally because of the bullying” he was receiving due to the ankle monitor.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement required the tracking anklet after the Trump administration eliminated Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants living in Springfield and across the country.

At a vigil for Damas Bel on Sept. 2 at Columbus City Hall, state Rep. Munira Abdullahi, D-Columbus, related to Damas Bel’s story of hoping to better the country with his presence. She decried the process that brought with it an ankle monitor and discouragement for the young student.

“We can not accept an immigration system that loses sight of people over paperwork and political dogma,” Abdullahi said. “Pierre deserved better. His family deserves better.”

She demanded the end of “cruelties,” the release of those in ICE detention, and “for my colleagues across the aisle and our Congress members to stand up and do something about this and end it.”

More than 40 Haitians living in Springfield had already been detained by ICE at the time of Damas Bel’s death.

Abdullahi’s fellow state Rep. Latyna Humphrey, also a Democrat representing Columbus, released a statement honoring Damas Bel and talking about the “devastating toll” the immigration process had had on him.

“There are real human beings behind every immigration policy and every government action,” Humphrey said. “…Whatever our political disagreements about immigration may be, our government should never lose sight of the dignity and humanity of the people affected by its decisions.”

The Ohio Senate Democratic Caucus released a joint statement calling Damas Bel’s death “a direct result of this administration’s inhumane and racist immigration policies.”

Democratic Ohio U.S. Rep. Greg Landsman said his office has “reached out directly to the Department of Homeland Security to end the use of ankle monitors on our Haitian neighbors who have done nothing wrong.”

According to the letter dated Sept. 3, Landsman mentioned Damas Bel by name in pushing for the Department of Homeland Security to “reconsider the policy of requiring former TPS holders with no criminal history to wear ankle monitors while going through the legal immigration process.”

“Our country needs border security and immigration enforcement, but the manner in which we prioritize deportations and allocate resources is skewed,” the letter read. “We are wasting time, money, and lives targeting good, law-abiding people rather than clearly prioritizing threats to public safety.”

In a separate statement, Landsman said the U.S. House has passed legislation to extend temporary protections for Haitians for three years, but the U.S. Senate has not taken up the measure.

Federal immigration officials have encouraged Haitians to “self-deport,” despite the fact that the U.S. Department of State still lists Haiti at a Level Four “Do Not Travel” advisory because of the risk of “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare.”

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has made previous comments disagreeing with the decision to end the Temporary Protected Status for Haitians in Springfield, believing that “it will hurt us in the long run.”

“You’ve heard me talk a lot about what I consider to be a very misguided and wrong policy in regard to mass deporting people from this country,” DeWine said in comments on Sept. 1.

He said there are consequences to mass deportation, just as there are for other things done by the government. In defending the work of immigrant populations, he said one-third of caregivers in nursing homes and home healthcare workers are immigrants.

“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is it really good, is it what we want done, to see people like this being picked up and facing deportation,” DeWine said. “Do we want that done in our name? And my position has been that it’s a mistake.”

DeWine also said, however, that he felt the Trump administration “has done a very good job with regard to the Southern border, and I think that’s what people wanted.”

Former congressman and Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Sherrod Brown said in a Substack post about Damas Bel that he agreed with DeWine on the issue of immigrants in Springfield, adding that the decision to suspend TPS for the Haitian community “was wrong and has done nothing to make our communities safer.”

The incumbent in the Senate seat for which Brown is campaigning, Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, did not release a statement about Damas Bel. In a Sept. 3 press conference, he said his office plans to help those who have had their Temporary Protected Status taken away “to find out if there are any other methods for them to stay here legally,” but his office plans to maintain “the rule of law,” according to the Springfield News-Sun.

The Democratic candidate for governor, Dr. Amy Acton, released a statement saying she was “devastated by the tragic passing” of Damas Bel.

“Everyone in Ohio deserves to feel safe and to be treated with dignity, and we can uphold the rule of law without creating chaos and fear in our communities,” Acton said in a statement. “Ohio, this is a moment where we are all being asked to stand up for our common humanity. We must build a better way forward.”

In terms of immigration enforcement, Acton has made comments that conflict with Ohio Democratic Party stances, saying she wouldn’t prevent local law enforcement from working with federal law enforcement.

Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy didn’t release comments on Damas Bel, but has previously made comments that the Trump administration’s general mass deportation policy was “pragmatic.”

Back in 2024, Ramaswamy attended a town hall in Springfield, in which residents expressed concerns about the number of Haitians in the community. Ramaswamy said he didn’t blame the Haitian migrants who were brought here “by unconscionable means,” instead blaming “federal policies,” according to coverage of the meeting by WSYX.

At the time, Ramaswamy also said he supported mass deportation, but “if you’re going to pick a limited number, you may as well pick the ones who are most likely able to assimilate, most likely to participate in economic action, and those who are able to actually integrate their kids into the schools.”

text:
San Diego, CA — Today, Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) released the following statement after San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) and San Diego City College both informed the Congressman's office of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest activity outside their schools within the past week:

"I am deeply troubled by reports that students and parents were detained without warning while trying to attend classes or bring kids to school. Schools are supposed to be a safe place for young people to learn. Yet this Administration exploits the places we trust most—schools, childcare facilities, hospitals, courthouses, and places of worship. President Trump has turned these places into hunting grounds.

“ICE isn’t going after the 'worst of the worst,' as President Trump promised. We saw this at Buona Forchetta, when ICE agents threw the owner against a wall, handcuffed employees, and used flash-bang grenades on bystanders. These people weren't drug lords or violent criminals; they were workers trying to make a living.

“Parents and children should not have to worry about ICE agents waiting outside a classroom or a doctor's office. That's why I led introduction of the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would bar immigration enforcement within 1,000 feet of schools, hospitals, and churches except in true emergencies. I will also continue working with SDUSD and City College to make sure San Diegans have the resources they need to stay informed and protected.

"Until ICE operates responsibly and reasonably to target dangerous criminals instead of hardworking families, I will push for real reforms from ICE and hold them accountable for the fear they have inflicted on my constituents and communities across the country. I urge all state and local elected officials to express their support for the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act and my Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act so we can deliver commonsense reforms that keep our communities safe."

Background:

Last year, Rep. Peters led the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, a bill to make our communities safer by establishing a stronger standard for Federal immigration agents' use of force. The bill would also restrict use of crowd munitions like tear gas and create greater transparency in enforcement by requiring the use of body cameras and strictly limiting the use of masks. Rep. Peters has pushed Congress to pass these common sense reforms, but they have been blocked by the Republican majority.

text:
A former San Francisco immigration judge fired by the Trump administration last year filed a federal whistleblower lawsuit Thursday accusing the Department of Justice of terminating her for raising due process concerns over new policy directives and ICE enforcement tactics.

Judge Chloe Dillon is among 14 San Francisco judges fired since President Trump’s return to office and is the first of the group to sue over her removal.

Her lawsuit opens with a quote from George Orwell: “If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.”

Dillon, like dozens of other immigration judges fired since last year, was originally appointed by the Biden administration. She first took the bench in 2022 after serving for nearly a decade as a federal public defender in San Diego.

“I was really excited,” Dillon told NBC Bay Area. “I felt like it was an excellent fit for me. I felt it was something that I cared about – ensuring justice in immigration court.”

Over the next three years working as a judge at one of the country’s busiest immigration courts, Dillon said she resolved thousands of cases, earning excellent performance reviews along the way. According to Dillon’s lawsuit, her “decisions were almost never appealed.”

“It was really interesting work,” Dillon said. “I felt like it was really important that people were heard and that their cases were decided carefully and based on all the evidence.”

But Dillon said the job began to change almost immediately following President Trump’s inauguration, as new appointees took over the senior levels of the country’s immigration court system.

In the spring of 2025, Dillon’s suit alleges that San Francisco Assistant Chief Immigration Judge Loi McCleskey directed the court’s judges “to grant any and all motions to change venue” filed by ICE attorneys. That meant immigrants’ cases would be transferred out of San Francisco to another court – potentially far away from their attorneys and witnesses.

“I think my first reaction was confusion because I felt that the policy was not in accordance with what the law was,” Dillon said. “It was certainly part of a larger project to detain people and bring their cases to conclusion, likely resulting in deportation, as quickly as possible. Because these cases were being moved to detained courts and being moved to locations that were more remote.”

Dillon’s suit alleges she expressed concern over the new directive in an email to McCleskey and later met with her supervisor in person.

“ACIJ McCleskey expressed empathy with Plaintiff’s point of view but warned her that the 'White House’ was paying attention to this and to be careful about pushing the issue further,” the lawsuit alleges.

McCleskey did not immediately respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment.

In one case, according to the suit, Dillon denied an ICE motion to change venue, but learned the case was transferred anyway.

Later that summer, Dillon described being alarmed by another new ICE tactic as the agency filed thousands of boilerplate motions to re-calendar cases in immigration court that had previously been administratively closed. Many of the cases had been administratively closed – essentially pausing removal proceedings – because USCIS, rather than the Immigration Court, had initial jurisdiction over the pending asylum applications.

Some of those cases involved unaccompanied minors, according to the lawsuit, and Dillon denied two government motions to reopen such cases.

“For unaccompanied minors, they have a statutory right under the law to have their asylum case decided in the first instance by the asylum office,” Dillon said.

The situation came to a head in August of last year. According to the lawsuit, ICE agents arrested a young man who came to the U.S. as an unaccompanied minor after a hearing in Dillon’s courtroom, telling the judge he would be placed in expedited removal.

“I had concerns because, first of all, people who are in that position cannot be put into expedited removal,” Dillon said.

Protestors clashed with federal agents as they took the young man from the courthouse and Dillon said she could hear the commotion from her chambers.

That afternoon, Dillon’s lawsuit alleges she emailed her supervisor warning of possible legal and due process violations, adding that courthouse ICE arrests – which had become common by then – were disrupting “the orderly administration of justice.”

Dillon said she was fired by email two days later by the acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

Dillon described being terminated as “really scary” – especially since it would leave her family of four without health insurance. But she said she has no regrets about sending the email.

“I don’t,” Dillon said. “Like, not at all. I felt that it was my duty to bring forward something that I felt was a violation of the law.”

Nearly a year after her firing, Dillon sued the DOJ, EOIR and Attorney General Todd Blanche, alleging a host of civil violations, including retaliation and violations of the Whistleblower Protection Act.

“I felt it was important for people like Judge Dillon to know that they had legal recourse and they had support,” said Melanie Proctor, Dillon’s attorney. “Federal employees have a right and a responsibility to raise suspected violations of the law to the appropriate authorities within their agencies.”

In an emailed statement, a DOJ spokesperson said the agency doesn't usually comment on pending litigation or personnel matters but described the allegations in the lawsuit as "patently false."

"After four years of the Biden Administration forcing Immigration Courts to implement a de facto amnesty for hundreds of thousands of aliens, this Department of Justice is restoring integrity to our immigration system," the agency added.

San Francisco’s immigration court was officially closed earlier this month following a wave of firings and retirements involving the court’s judges. Most of the court’s cases were reassigned to the immigration court in Concord.

“I think if you go back and you look at Project 2025, that’s essentially a plan that you can see happening in real time right now,” Dillon said. “They consider the immigration courts to be sort of an obstruction to a project to detain and deport as many people as possible.”

For the immigrants with pending cases in immigration court, Dillon said the stakes are high.

“For people who are seeking asylum, it's about making a decision as to whether they should be returned to a country that they're saying that they face persecution and potentially even death in that country,” Dillon said. “I think that we all have an interest in seeing that those cases are heard and decided fairly because these are people that we know and that we interact with on a daily basis.”

text:
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Elected officials and Haitian community leaders are demanding answers after ICE arrested two parents near John Marshall Elementary School in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood Wednesday morning.

On Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed the arrests of James Mervil and Josselene Polidor were part of a targeted enforcement operation. The agency said the couple entered the country lawfully in 2022 but overstayed their welcome, though officials did not specify how.

DHS said the pair ran when agents initiated a traffic stop, and that Polidor ignored commands to stop and bit an officer while resisting arrest.

People who know the couple said they had Temporary Protected Status until late July, when the Trump administration ended TPS for all Haitians in the country. They also said the couple has a pending asylum case.

DHS said the children's father was released late Wednesday night with an ankle monitor. Polidor will remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.

Witnesses say the couple's 2- and 5-year-old children had just been dropped off at John Marshall Elementary when the arrests took place. With no one immediately available to care for them, the school stepped in.

"So terrible, there was nobody else to pick up the kids; it was the school who organized to drop the kids to a stand-in guardian," Wister Gaetan said.

text:
One private company is benefiting financially from ICE increasingly using GPS ankle monitors to track immigrants awaiting legal proceedings instead of a less expensive smartphone app.

B.I. Incorporated won a contract in September 2025 initially valued at $1.02 billion to provide ankle monitors and other non-detention supervision services for ICE. The agency has so far obligated $228.5 million to the company under the contract.

B.I. Incorporated is part of the GEO Group, a business already profiting from immigration enforcement as the nation’s largest private operator of ICE detention centers.

RELATED STORY | DHS is placing ankle monitors on Haitians who were in the US under Temporary Protected Status

The ankle monitors have become a significant source of revenue, GEO Group Chairman and CEO George Zoley told investors during an August 2026 earnings conference call.

“The app is far less expensive than the ankle monitors,” Zoley said.

On the call, the GEO chief also said the number of immigrants on ankle tracking devices had more than tripled from 17,000 in 2025 to 54,000 so far this year. He predicted more monitors and money from the ICE contract yet to come, particularly from scores of Haitians who recently lost Temporary Protected Status under the Trump administration.

"Most of them we believe would be placed under the ankle monitoring supervision technique,” Zoley said.

Pierre Damas Bel, 20, was one of the Haitian immigrants required by ICE to wear a GPS ankle monitor.

He posted a photo on Instagram saying the device caused "a feeling of shame and humiliation.”

Weeks later, he died after stepping out into traffic in what his family says was suicide, blaming the ankle monitor for some of his despair.

A class action lawsuit challenging the use of ankle monitors says they can cause “pain, swelling and scarring.” A declaration in the lawsuit says the stigma makes it difficult to keep a job.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Corporate owners of ICE detention centers report another revenue surge

The electronic clasps are both intrusive and expensive, said Sarah Decker, senior staff attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.

“These devices come at enormous taxpayer expense," Decker said. “It drives up profits directly into the hands of the private prison company that is manufacturing these devices. It's not an unintended side effect. It's really the reason why this rule is implemented in our view.”

DHS disputes that money has anything to do with the increasing reliance on ankle monitors, saying they allow officers to more accurately track immigrants in supervision compared to the app.

“Illegal aliens--just like U.S. citizens--are subject to the legal system and may be subject to release conditions that include ankle or wrist-worn GPS technology,” an unnamed DHS spokesman said in an email responding to a Scripps News inquiry. "Any illegal alien who is worried about having to wear an ankle monitor or any other GPS devices should accept the $3,000 stipend from the U.S. government and free flight home by self-deporting through the CBP Home App.”

title: Inside a Lawless ICE Raid That Tore Families Apart - NYCLU
description:
I didn’t know what to do or what to say,” Argentina Juárez-López, one of the workers seized that day and a plaintiff in our lawsuit, told the NYCLU in Spanish.
And agents arrested workers such as Argentina just for asking to speak with a lawyer.
On the first day of the new school year, agents separated over 20 workers from their children, and immediately deported some workers without due process.
“I saw many people crying for their children,” Argentina said.
“I showed them my work permit, my [social] security, and a pending asylum case I had,” M. told the NYCLU in Spanish.
text:
On September 4, 2025, as workers went about their normal morning activities, sixty armed and masked federal agents – supported by two local law enforcement agencies – stormed the Nutrition Bar Confectioners factory in Cato, New York. Officers grabbed and detained more than 100 workers. They used crowbars to open doors and even barged into a bathroom stall where one woman was using the toilet.

“Suddenly I saw military men entering with guns and balaclavas and bulletproof vests. I didn’t know what to do or what to say,” Argentina Juárez-López, one of the workers seized that day and a plaintiff in our lawsuit, told the NYCLU in Spanish. The vision of the agents descending on the factory brought her back to the memory of guerilla soldiers entering her Guatemalan village, when she and the other children would hide.

“It was the same,” she said. “They had us surrounded. They were on the roof, they were outside.”

Agents herded workers – including U.S. citizens – into a break room where they first commanded the U.S. citizens in the room to identify themselves. The U.S. citizens who identified themselves were not released; instead, they were taken to another room where workers – such as plaintiff Pedro Rojas, a U.S. citizen born in Puerto Rico – were required to show ID and give their contact information before agents would allow them to be escorted out of the factory. The workers remaining in the break room were then forcibly interrogated about their immigration status. And agents arrested workers such as Argentina just for asking to speak with a lawyer. Officers did not know her name, let alone her immigration status, when they arrested her.

While the raid took place, a body camera recorded a Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) agent’s chilling remarks comparing immigrant children to animals. Other officers listened without objection, revealing the racist underpinning of the operation.

Federal agents arrested at least 57 workers. Many were denied opportunities to talk to lawyers or their families before agents rushed them to out-of-state detention facilities as far away as Louisiana. On the first day of the new school year, agents separated over 20 workers from their children, and immediately deported some workers without due process.

“I saw many people crying for their children,” Argentina said.

Eddie, another plaintiff in the case, was deported to Guatemala after just 72 hours – despite having a work permit. He had lived in the U.S. for twenty years. Now, his wife struggles to care for their two boys alone, working overtime to try to keep the family afloat while coping with her grief over the sudden, forced separation.

“She’s got a lot of depression,” Eddie told the NYCLU.

ICE agents also forcibly separated M., who prefers to use her first initial, from her two-year-old U.S.-citizen child, sent her to a detention facility in Texas, and deported her to Guatemala even though she had a pending appeal in her asylum case.

“I showed them my work permit, my [social] security, and a pending asylum case I had,” M. told the NYCLU in Spanish. “They sent me to line up where other people were going and they took me to a van,” she continued. “After that, they took me to detention.”

The raid shattered families and communities. Officers acted lawlessly, flagrantly violating people’s constitutional right to be free from unreasonable search and seizure. And the agents did so in opposition to what they told a Magistrate Judge they were going to do that morning.

Last year, the NYCLU successfully fought to unseal the applications for the two warrants used to justify the raid, revealing that the warrants the government claimed authorized the immigration sweep did not give agents authority to seize any individual, and the government didn’t even ask the court for the authority to do so. Instead, the government only asked for authority to conduct “consensual questioning” of workers at NBC. In other words, the agents seized, separated, interrogated, and arrested workers without any justification.

That’s why, on behalf of Pedro, Argentina, Eddie, M., and their fellow workers, the NYCLU and Worker Justice Center of New York are suing a group of ICE and CBP agents, as well as the two county sheriffs that worked with them, for violating workers’ constitutional rights, including by targeting Latinx workers based on their ethnicity.

Our lawsuit argues that agents engaged in a bias-based conspiracy to seize a huge number of people even though they didn’t suspect any specific individuals of crimes. This was all in the service of meeting Trump’s goal of carrying out the largest mass deportations in U.S. history.

DHS has mounted similar dragnet operations targeted at Latinx people across the country, including in Minnesota, South Carolina, Oregon, Idaho, and more.

Our lawsuit includes some of the first civil rights claims under the New York State Bivens Act, a state law enacted this year that allows people to sue public officers, including federal officers, for violating their rights under the United States Constitution. And finally, our lawsuit seeks to allow Eddie to return to the United States so that he can be reunited with his family and continue to pursue his immigration case.

“What ICE is doing right now is an injustice against Hispanic people, all Hispanic people, to the point that it doesn’t matter if you’re Guatemalan, Salvadoran, Puerto Rican,” Pedro told the NYCLU in Spanish.

“Once they hear you speaking Spanish, they’re discriminating against you and mistreating you.”

text:
Immigrant and legal advocacy groups sued the Trump administration Thursday for violating the Fourth Amendment and other laws with the they called the government’s “arrest first, ask questions later” policy of immigrant arrests.

The 56-page lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Baltimore, accuses Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents of engaging in “warrantless arrest” that sweeps up people without cause beyond the fact that they appear to be immigrants.

It said 80% of those arrested by ICE in Maryland since 2025 had no criminal convictions and that of 1,300 arrests made in Operation Safe Community, a two-week ICE enforcement surge in Maryland and Virginia last month, less than a third had criminal convictions.

The lawsuit also said that of the more than 7,ooo street arrests in Maryland since Jan. 20, 2025, the day President Donald Trump (R) was sworn in to his second term, 93% of those arrested have been citizens of Latin American or Caribbean countries, in what one attorney called racial profiling.

“Over the past 21 months, plainclothes, masked, armed, unidentified and untrained federal agents have terrorized Maryland communities,” said Shana Kader, legal director for We Are CASA, during a news conference at the group’s multicultural center in Langley Park. “From the Eastern Shore to Park Heights to the mountains of Washington County, these agents have stalked primarily brown and Black neighborhoods, arresting those they perceive to be brown or Black immigrants without warrants and without probable cause.”

“Shame!” some people yelled after Kader spoke.

Besides We Are CASA, other groups involved in the suit are the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, the ACLU of Maryland and the National Immigration Project.

Plaintiffs include three men and one woman from Maryland, three identified only by their initials. Defendants are the Homeland Security Department and its secretary, Markwayne Mullin; ICE and its acting director, David Venturella; the Justice Department and Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Representatives from ICE and Homeland Security did not respond to requests for comment on the suit Thursday.

The lawsuit was filed on the same day We Are CASA announced Tiago Alexandre Sousa Martin was released from ICE custody and returned home after being shot by ICE agents in an Anne Arundel County neighborhood on Dec. 24.

And it comes less than a week after ICE agents who converged on a Frederick neighborhood were seen on video grabbing and pushing protestors in front of a house. At least one agent can be seen hitting a person on the ground with a baton, according to video provided by Hagerstown Rapid Response.

Austin Rose, managing attorney with the Amica Center based in Washington, D.C., said the lawsuit isn’t directly connected to the incident in Frederick.

“They [ICE agents] staked out a neighborhood for 40 hours, apparently looking for someone, and then some brave neighbors came and intervened,” said Rose, who was born and raised in Frederick. “It just shows what ICE is doing, which is they’re creating problems for themselves by just randomly showing up in neighborhoods.”

‘We are Maryland’

The named plaintiff, Samuel Guzmán, 24, is a Maryland native. He is also a member of We Are CASA and a resident of Anne Arundel County.

On June 7, Guzmán was detained by ICE agents after coming out of a 7-Eleven. Even though agents saw his identification and Guzmán pleaded that he’s a U.S. citizen, “the agents immediately handcuffed” him, put him in a truck and drove to a nearby parking lot along with other recently arrested “Latine” individuals.

“After finally reviewing Mr. Guzmán’s identity documents a second time, the agents returned him to the 7-Eleven parking lot and released him with no explanation,” the suit says. “Mr. Guzmán continues to take the same route to work on which he was arrested in June, and he faces substantial risk of re-arrest. He fears he or his Latine family members in the Annapolis area will be arrested in the future.”

A 38-year-old woman, identified in the suit as “K.M.,” was approached by ICE agents Jan. 12 while she parked her car near a friend’s house in Salisbury. Agents in six unmarked vehicles ordered her out of the car, “threatened to shoot her” and then handcuffed her. They detained K.M. for several hours at the Salisbury ICE office, interrogating her about her children and husband, who is deceased.

She was eventually released with an ankle monitor, “which causes her significant discomfort and shame at work and in public, and she must attend monthly ICE appointments.”

Similar incidents and fears were expressed by two other We Are CASA members Thursday, who went by their initials.

State Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) was on hand for Thursday’s announcement to at the multicultural center to express his support for the suit.

“As much as the Trump administration wants to terrorize us, as much as the Trump administration wants to hate us, we are Casa. We are Maryland, and we are America,” Augustine said. “We stand with We are Casa and all who are part of this suit for constitutional due process. We will fight together, and we will win because when we fight … ”

“We win,” chanted those in attendance.

title: Denver sues Trump to block ICE patrols at polling sites | Courthouse News Service
description:
WASHINGTON (CN) — The city of Denver sued the Trump administration on Thursday, asking a federal judge to issue an injunction that would bar armed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from approaching polling sites during the midterm elections.
“The specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election,” the coalition said.
The statute provides a narrow exception only if a hostile foreign power is targeting specific polling sites; it authorizes troops to defend against the attack, not engage in law enforcement activities.
“Congress banned armed federal agents at elections sites to provide and preserve free and fair elections, the rule of law, the right to vote and Americans’ confidence in the sanctity of the ballot box,” the coalition said.
Soon after, the Justice Department removed a long-standing and publicly available manual stating that federal agents are specifically barred from patrolling polling sites under the Civil War-era statute.
text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — The city of Denver sued the Trump administration on Thursday, asking a federal judge to issue an injunction that would bar armed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from approaching polling sites during the midterm elections.

The city, joined by civil rights groups Common Cause, UnidosUS and the League of United Latin American Citizens, filed the suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and argues such a move would violate a Civil War-era statute specifically criminalizing the stationing of troops at voting locations.

“The specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election,” the coalition said. “It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal immigration enforcement officers if they choose to cast a ballot.”

The coalition points to 18 U.S. Code Section 592, which Congress passed in 1865 before the end of the Civil War over concerns the president could try to influence federal elections. The statute provides a narrow exception only if a hostile foreign power is targeting specific polling sites; it authorizes troops to defend against the attack, not engage in law enforcement activities.

In 1909, Congress removed an additional exception for “keeping peace at the polls” to prevent federal authorities from using any sort of disturbance as a pretext to deploy troops.

“Congress banned armed federal agents at elections sites to provide and preserve free and fair elections, the rule of law, the right to vote and Americans’ confidence in the sanctity of the ballot box,” the coalition said. “Defendants’ disregard for that statutory framework threatens our upcoming election.”

Thursday’s lawsuit is the first of its kind and comes amid growing tensions over midterm elections, with early voting set to begin later this month.

Efforts to block the Trump administration’s proposed changes to mail-in voting have thus far failed since there is no official policy to challenge — which will likely become a point of contention in Denver’s lawsuit.

On Sept. 1, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin suggested ICE agents would be authorized to enter polling places in certain scenarios and slammed statements by Democrats that agents would be patrolling the sites as fearmongering.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place, or we’re serving a warrant,” Mullin said.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly and falsely claimed the integrity of the elections is threatened by widespread noncitizen voting. He used the claims to justify his efforts to exert unprecedented federal influence over the elections.

In April, Trump signed the executive order “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” which would create lists of U.S. citizens eligible to vote in each state and instructs the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to verified voters.

While several Democratic states sued to block the Postal Service’s ultimate policy, the Supreme Court on Aug. 24 rejected the suit, finding its claimed injury was hypothetical without an official policy. The USPS posted its final rule on Aug. 27.

According to the coalition, the Trump administration has been developing and implementing the “Polling Place Policy” since March 2026, with the first official indication of a policy coming from then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche: At the Conservative Political Action Conference, he asked why there was any objection to sending ICE officers to polls.

Soon after, the Justice Department removed a long-standing and publicly available manual stating that federal agents are specifically barred from patrolling polling sites under the Civil War-era statute.

The coalition highlighted incidents over the summer in San Antonio, Texas, Ventura County, California, and Syracuse, New York, where ICE agents entered active polling places to conduct certain law enforcement activity as clear evidence there is a policy in place.

They are specifically requesting a federal judge issue an injunction to block the “Polling Place Policy,” declare the feds have no authority to order armed officers to a polling site and enjoin federal officers from operating or carrying weapons near any ballot dropbox, curbside voting location or other voting site.

“Judicial review of the Polling Place Policy is appropriate now to declare that, except as narrowly defined by law under 18 U.S. Code Section 592, the federal government may not send armed officers to polling sites, as that would violate the prohibition on federal ‘armed men’ at election sites and interfere with the conduct of a free and fair election,” the coalition wrote. “Defendants should not be permitted to cast the pall of federal force over the ballot box as we head to the polls in the coming days.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.

In mid-August, GEO Group appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit for the third time.
It invoked a different type of immunity, qualified immunity, a judicially created doctrine that shields public employees from civil lawsuits unless they violate a person’s clearly established legal rights.
The 10th Circuit disagreed, noting a judge’s decision unrelated to qualified immunity does not authorize a defendant to immediately appeal.
Similarly, the 10th Circuit pointed out that Kane had not decided the qualified immunity issue one way or the other.
text:
The Denver-based federal appeals court dismissed an attempt by The GEO Group on Wednesday to appeal a trial judge’s non-existent decision two months before the company is scheduled to face a civil trial over alleged trafficking violations at the Aurora immigration detention facility it operates.

The class-action lawsuit, which has been pending since 2014, alleges that GEO Group violated the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act by requiring detainees to clean not just their personal space, but the common areas of the detention center under threat of solitary confinement. Those actions allegedly ran afoul of the law’s prohibition on knowingly coercing labor out of another person through serious harm or threats of serious harm.

The plaintiff detainees also alleged GEO Group unjustly enriched itself by paying them only $1 per day through a “voluntary” labor program.

In mid-August, GEO Group appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit for the third time. On previous occasions, GEO Group challenged the class-action nature of the case and the denial of its claimed immunity defense. Both the 10th Circuit and, this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the substance of the second appeal could not be addressed until after the November 2026 trial.

In April, GEO Group moved to end the case in its favor without a trial. It invoked a different type of immunity, qualified immunity, a judicially created doctrine that shields public employees from civil lawsuits unless they violate a person’s clearly established legal rights. U.S. District Court Senior Judge John L. Kane heard arguments in early June and said he would rule “in the very near future.”

Two months later, GEO Group filed its third appeal, challenging a decision that Kane had never made.

“GEO filed its motion over four months ago, and it has been over two months since this Court heard oral argument,” its lawyers wrote. “Allowing the litigation to progress any further — with trial less than three months away — would destroy the protections GEO is entitled to under qualified immunity.”

Attorneys for the plaintiffs countered that Kane never denied qualified immunity, meaning there was nothing to appeal.

One day later, Kane himself issued an order deeming the appeal “frivolous.”

“In this case, GEO has waited twelve years to assert qualified immunity. It now contends that a delay of four months in receiving a decision on the matter is a constructive denial,” he wrote.

“Moreover, GEO’s tactics serve no purpose other than to delay,” he continued. “If GEO had wanted a decision on qualified immunity before having to face the burdens of litigation, it could have raised qualified immunity sooner; it could have sought a scheduling or pretrial order that prioritized a decision on qualified immunity; it could have avoided simultaneously bombarding the Court with other substantive filings involving hefty doctrines such as government contractor protections and preemption; it could have moved for a stay specifically related to its request for qualified immunity; and it could have sought clarification on the timing of the Court’s decision.”

On Sept. 9, a three-judge 10th Circuit panel agreed to dismiss the appeal.

In an unsigned order, the panel referenced a similar scenario from January in which government defendants in a Jefferson County civil lawsuit argued a trial judge’s allowance for limited evidence was, effectively, a denial of qualified immunity. The 10th Circuit disagreed, noting a judge’s decision unrelated to qualified immunity does not authorize a defendant to immediately appeal.

Similarly, the 10th Circuit pointed out that Kane had not decided the qualified immunity issue one way or the other.

“GEO’s appeal presented this court with no order to review at all. Failure to identify an order or judgment as the subject of the appeal could be fatal to GEO’s appeal,” wrote Chief Judge Jerome A. Holmes and Judges Scott M. Matheson Jr. and Robert E. Bacharach.

The panel acknowledged the closeness of the trial date but noted that GEO Group waited 12 years after the case’s filing to request qualified immunity.

“While GEO had pursued other defenses earlier in the case, it asserted the qualified immunity defense long after discovery had closed and with trial preparation underway,” the panel wrote. “Given the procedural posture of the underlying case, we cannot say that the district court’s perceived delay in deciding GEO’s motion constitutes a refusal of GEO’s qualified immunity defense such that immediate appellate review is warranted.”

The panel dismissed the appeal.

The case is Menocal et al. v. The GEO Group, Inc.

text:
PALM BEACH COUNTY, Fla. — A new federal hotline aimed at reporting suspected commercial driver's license fraud is putting truck drivers and the companies that employ them under increased scrutiny, while raising questions from transportation safety experts about whether the effort will improve safety or encourage profiling and unreliable accusations.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recently launched the tip line, asking the public to report suspected CDL fraud by calling 866-347-2423.

WATCH BELOW: ICE CDL fraud tip line raises profiling concerns

ICE CDL fraud tip line raises profiling concerns

Federal officials say the initiative is designed to crack down on dangerous or improperly licensed commercial drivers operating on U.S. roads.

"Too many American lives have been lost or permanently changed because illegal aliens who have no business being on our roads have been granted CDLs," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement released by the Department of Homeland Security. "ICE and our federal partners, including the Department of Transportation, will be cracking down on CDL fraud so that not one more American life is lost to a reckless illegal alien behind the wheel of a semi-truck."

The hotline announcement comes as federal and state officials continue investigating cases involving allegedly fraudulent commercial licenses, including a deadly Florida crash that drew national attention.

For more than a year, WPTV has reported on concerns surrounding CDL oversight and training standards. One case involved Harjinder Singh, who is accused of making an illegal U-turn in a semi-truck on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County, causing a crash that killed three people.

Among the victims was the mother of Angeline Daudin.

"I wasn't able to see her and say, 'I love you, Mom,'" Daudin said following the crash.

Officials have alleged Singh's CDL was issued illegally in California. He remains in the St. Lucie County Jail while the criminal case proceeds.

Federal officials have pointed to cases like that as justification for increased enforcement and public reporting efforts targeting what they describe as fraudulent and illegal CDL practices.

But James Lewis, a transportation safety expert witness and former police officer, said he is skeptical the hotline will produce meaningful safety improvements.

"It seems like it's the flavor of the week," Lewis said.

Lewis argued that ordinary motorists have no reliable way to determine whether a truck driver is properly licensed or whether fraud was involved.

"There's no way that anyone who would be calling this tip line could actually know if this person has a valid license or not," he said.

He warned the hotline could instead lead to profiling of immigrant communities based on assumptions rather than evidence.

Lewis noted that some of the examples highlighted in federal messaging have involved immigrants from countries including India and Haiti, but he said fraud within the CDL system predates recent immigration concerns.

"Americans have been abusing the CDL system for years," Lewis said. "That's been going on long before Pakistanis and Indians started immigrating."

Lewis said one of the deeper issues is the persistence of "fast-track" CDL schools that promise licenses in just days despite federal training requirements established by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration in 2019.

The federal rule requires extensive behind-the-wheel and classroom training for new commercial drivers. Lewis said some programs advertising licenses within three to five days are operating in ways that undermine safety standards.

Recently, Florida officials shut down 10 CDL schools for alleged violations, while regulators nationwide have increased scrutiny of training programs that fail to meet federal standards.

Lewis said the larger concern is inexperienced drivers operating heavy commercial vehicles alongside everyday motorists.

"You have completely inexperienced, untrained people out there in a tractor-trailer loaded with stuff, driving next to your family in a minivan, and it's pretty scary," he said.

Rather than investing in a public hotline, Lewis said he believes federal and state governments should devote more resources to trained Department of Transportation officers already responsible for roadside inspections and weigh station enforcement.

"What I would really like to see is additional manpower, time, and pay for these DOT-trained state officers who already do the random inspections and the scale house inspections," he said.

WPTV asked both DHS and ICE to respond to Lewis' concerns about profiling and the reliability of public tips. The agencies referred questions back to ICE's original announcement about the hotline.

"I'm skeptical," Lewis said.

text:
By Susan Heavey

WASHINGTON, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Trump administration has proposed eliminating a 60-day ⁠grace ⁠period that allows certain immigrants, including skilled ⁠workers on H-1B visas, to stay in the United States and find a new sponsor after losing ​their job, according to a government notice posted online on Thursday.

Under the planned rule change, published in the Federal Register by the U.S. Department of ‌Homeland Security, those with H-1B and certain ‌other temporary work visas would have to leave the country as soon as their employment ends — a potential blow to top American tech ⁠companies that rely ⁠heavily on foreign workers.

It is the latest step by U.S. President Donald Trump to limit ​legal immigration since returning to office in January 2025. His administration has also introduced higher visa fees for skilled workers and recently paused immigrant visa appointments at U.S. missions globally while it implements a new training program.

Companies affected by the change could see some disruption, DHS wrote in its proposal, but it said ​the jobs could go to American workers instead. In some situations, immigrant workers who leave could potentially reapply if their employer ⁠petitions ⁠for them, it added.

"DHS presumes that ⁠they will either offer ​the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers or go through the I-129 petition process depending on their workforce requirement," the ​notice said.

The 60-day grace period, in place ⁠since 2017, allows foreign workers time to find another U.S. job or get their affairs in order — whether selling a home or pulling children out of school — before leaving the country.

"Many H-1B workers have been here for years, and they and their families have established themselves in their communities," said Gabriel Chin, a professor at the UC Davis School of Law. "I see no legitimate reason to force them to leave because they are ⁠changing jobs."

VISAS CRITICAL FOR TECH COMPANIES

H-1B visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies ⁠seeking talent from India and China, allowing them to fill roles where there is sometimes a lack of qualified U.S. workers.

Consultancy companies such as Deloitte, PwC and Ernst & Young as well as outsourcing firms such as Tata Consultancy Services , Infosys , HCL Tech and LTIMindtree are top H-1B sponsors.

Lawyers for Berardi Immigration Law, which specializes in business-related immigration issues, said the move would "sharply compress the timeline HR teams have to manage layoffs and offboarding for foreign national employees."

“It seems like every week this administration announces a new step to make life more difficult for immigrants in the U.S. and the companies and communities that rely on them," said Todd Schulte, president of FWD.us, an immigration advocacy group.

If implemented, the change would also apply to E-1 ⁠international trader visa holders; E-2 commercial vehicle operator visa holders; L-1 short-term work for executives or managers with international companies; O-1 visas for people "with an extraordinary ability" in science, sports or the arts; and TN professional workers.

It would also affect H-1B1 skilled worker visa holders from Singapore and Chile and E-3 specialty worker visa holders from Australia.

The rule is subject to a ​two-month public comment period before it can be finalized.

(Reporting by Susan Heavey; Additional reporting by Kristina Cooke ​and Anzar Mehraj; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Andrea Ricci, Rod Nickel)

text:
Timing: This Is a Proposed Rule

This is not yet a final rule. The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on September 11, 2026, which will trigger a 60-day public comment period. DHS will review public comments before determining whether to issue a final regulation.

Major Change: Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period

Currently, H-1B, L, O, and TN workers who are laid off may receive a discretionary grace period of up to 60 days (or until the end of their authorized stay, whichever is shorter) to:

Find a new employer;

File a change of status;

Apply for adjustment of status; or

Otherwise maintain lawful presence in the United States.

DHS now proposes to eliminate that provision entirely.

If finalized, foreign nationals would generally be expected to leave the United States immediately upon cessation of the employment or activity that formed the basis of their status, unless they already possess another independent lawful basis to remain in the country.

Out of Status the Next Day

DHS makes clear that, under the proposal, a worker who stops performing the employment or activity underlying their status would be considered to have failed to maintain status beginning the day after the employment ends.

The agency states that this would restore its historical policy prior to the 2017 implementation of the grace period rule.

Immigration Consequences Could Be Significant

DHS notes that once a worker fails to maintain status:

The individual may become removable (deportable) under INA §237(a)(1)(C).

DHS could issue a Notice to Appear (NTA) initiating removal proceedings.

The individual may become ineligible for certain future immigration benefits.

Depending on the circumstances, unlawful presence consequences could arise under existing immigration law.

Why DHS Is Proposing the Change

DHS argues that the current grace period:

Disconnects lawful status from the employment or activity that forms the basis for admission.

Creates administrative burdens for USCIS adjudicators.

Complicates determinations regarding maintenance of status.

Is not required by statute.

The agency states that eliminating the grace period would better align the regulations with the statutory framework governing employment-based nonimmigrant classifications.

text:
A federal judge has ordered the immediate return of the father of a U.S. Marine who was detained at the gates of Camp Pendleton last fall and deported to Mexico without a hearing.

“The Court cannot fathom more ‘extreme circumstances’ then [sic] an unlawful deportation without justification, notice, or any opportunity to be heard,” the judge wrote in the 10-page order, adding that Esteban Rios Sosa “should not have been detained at all, much less removed.”

Rios Sosa and his wife Luisa Rodriguez have lived in Oceanside for decades. Last September, they were with their son Steve Rios, who’s a Marine, trying to visit their daughter – who’s married to a Marine – at Camp Pendleton. They were stopped at the gate and Rios Sosa and Rodriguez were detained, taken to the federal building in downtown San Diego and released with ankle monitors, told to come back a few weeks later to check in with ICE.

When they returned to the federal building in early October, they were detained again. Federal agents led them away in handcuffs as Rios Sosa wore what his son said was his lucky shirt, a red T-shirt that reads “Proud Dad of a U.S. Marine.”

Rodriguez was taken to the Otay Mesa Detention Center and Rios Sosa was immediately deported to Mexico.

But his attorney says both have pending U visa applications. In a court filing, Rios Sosa’s attorney said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had notified them in 2024 that their applications were bona fide but could not be granted immediately because the agency had reached its cap on U visas for the year.

As part of that process, Rios Sosa and Rodriguez were granted what’s known as deferred action, which his attorney said serves as essentially protection from enforcement, as well as work authorization while they wait to make it through the backlog.

Local

Because of that deferred action, after about three weeks in detention, an immigration judge ordered Rodriguez released.

Then in July, Rios Sosa sued the federal government, arguing they violated his right to due process in deporting him without a chance to see an immigration judge. On Tuesday, a federal judge agreed, ordering his immediate return to the U.S.

“The government made promises to Mr. Rios Sosa to not engage in this kind of arbitrary enforcement against him,” said his attorney, Monika Langarica, the deputy legal director of the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law. “The government’s actions to renege on those promises, to break those promises, I think really resonated with a lot of people who take the government at its word and who believe the government when it says it's not going to do a certain thing.”

When asked about Rios Sosa’s case, the Department of Homeland Security has repeatedly alleged he is a violent criminal. Back in October, they said he was charged with domestic violence and aggravated assaulted with a deadly weapon. When reached for comment on the lawsuit, ICE in August called him by the incorrect name – Mauricio – and said he was “charged with inflicting corporal injury on spouse, assault with a deadly weapon, and damage of power lines.”

Rios Sosa has continually maintained those allegations are false. DHS has never provided evidence of those charges and Langarica said the government never filed anything related to those claims in court. ICE did not respond to request for comment on the judge’s order for Rios Sosa’s return.

“I think the government has had many opportunities to make this right, and unfortunately, they didn't do that,” Langarica said.

The judge also ordered the government to restore Rios Sosa’s prior immigration status “as if his October 2025 removal never occurred.”

Langarica said she’s working to get him back quickly, after being separated from his family for nearly a year and missing the birth of his grandson.

“He and the family are just overjoyed,” she said, “and really, really ready to be back together.”

DALLAS, Texas -- Republicans have gathered in Dallas for the closing day of the party’s midterm convention that aims to highlight President Donald Trump ’s influence and boost enthusiasm among GOP voters ahead of November’s midterm election. Speakers at the two-day event have derided Democratic candidates as extremists and offered defenses of Trump’s war in Iran.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance were among those to address the crowd.

Trump pledged Wednesday during the convention to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further fan inflation concerns and exacerbate the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit.

Missouri’s Republican secretary of state has ordered local election authorities to use its 2022 congressional map instead of a congressional map backed by Trump after the Supreme Court struck it down earlier today. The decision means Missouri will run the general election with a different congressional map than was used in the primary.

An appeals court on Thursday upheld a block on Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting.

Here's the latest:

The two-day Republican midterm convention in Dallas has ended.

The president stopped to pump his fist as he slowly walked off stage and balloons fell inside the arena.

Many were walking off with giant balloons and a few people tried to manage the long poles of delegate signs.

Trump concluded with a final plea: “Go out and vote.”

He turned the microphone over to opera performer Christopher Macchio, who belted out a soaring rendition of “America the Beautiful” as balloons fell.

Trump lingered and swayed to the music.

The president went on an extended riff about the size of his crowd in the American Airlines Center, the roughly 20,000-seat venue hosting the convention.

“Look at it,” Trump said. “The highest rafter, no empty seats.”

“Look at the upper ring. Look, everything is taken,” he continued. Even the “rich people boxes” were filled, he said.

However, nearly the entire upper deck was empty.

The media, he complained, will report that the room had empty seats.

Finally, after nearly three minutes of boasting, he acknowledged the elephant missing from the room.

“I gotta do a little bit better in the back,” he said.

“I’m not happy with it. That’s not good. I shouldn’t have looked up there,” he added.

Trump closed out the Republican convention by claiming the stock market had hit 80 highs, the job market is strong and he’s delivering on all of his promises to voters.

The happy talk in Dallas is a contrast to the bleak mood on Wall Street.

The S & P 500 is on a four-day losing streak, instead of setting new records. U.S. oil futures topped $100 a barrel as worries about the Iran war persist. And the inflation and high interest rates that Trump pledged to fix are causing new financial jitters.

The interest rate on 10-year U.S. Treasury notes on Thursday rose above 4.9%, meaning that the expense for mortgages, auto loans and other forms of debt has increased in ways that could slow growth.

The president said he didn’t plan to speak much Thursday at the Republican convention after his keynote address on Wednesday.

But he went on to riff anyway.

“We were a laughingstock all over the world,” Trump said, referring to his predecessor. “But we took that dark age of America and turned it into the golden age of America.”

Lee Greenwood was on stage to sing “God Bless the USA” as Vance left the stage and Trump walked out.

Vance and Trump shook hands as the vice president walked off.

The vice president said that Democrats have evolved into a group that stands against America, saying that the country should belong “to those that love it, not those that hate it.”

Vance touched a series of culturally loaded issues on race and immigration.

He took offense at the suggestion by Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, that Vance’s own grandfather would object to his marriage to a woman of Indian descent.

Vance said that Democrats now find sympathy with the terrorists responsible for the 9/11 attacks in 2001 but not people like his grandfather.

“The Democrats are the party of hatred,” Vance said. “They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it.”

Vance implored undecided voters to recognize the Trump administration’s record and not hand control of Congress to Democrats.

“Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there. Look, I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single issue. I’m not asking anybody to agree on every single policy,” Vance said at the GOP midterm convention. “What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months.”

Without explicitly mentioning the Iran war, the vice president invoked conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who “hated war,” according to Vance.

“That was his view. Now, of course, there are people who love what we’ve done and people who don’t. I’m not here to litigate the disagreements between Charlie and some of the people that he disagreed with,” he said.

Vance claimed that “we actually took on big pharma and lowered drug costs for all of our citizens.”

Federal data shows that U.S. prescription drug prices fell 0.9% in July and are down 3.1% from a year ago, the steepest year-over-year drop since 1963. The White House said these plunging prices resulted from Trump’s “most favored nation” drug deal with pharmaceutical firms and the TrumpRx website.

But drug pricing experts say the real picture is more complicated, noting that other factors, including a law from former President Joe Biden’s time in office that allowed Medicare to negotiate with pharmaceutical companies, are potentially more significant contributors to the latest consumer price index figures.

Vance took a swipe at James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate.

He praised Trump for coining a nickname: Talafreako.

For his part, Talarico and his supporters have embraced that nickname, printing it on shirts and adopting it as a badge of honor.

Like many speakers across the two-day convention, Vance pointed to comments Talarico has made about religion and transgender Americans, including saying God is nonbinary.

“I got to say, a guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Vance said.

Vance addressed speculation about his presidential ambitions.

“JD 48!” a woman yelled loudly from the stands, a reference to the next president, who will be the 48th. That prompted chants of “JD!” and “48!”

Vance responded by saying his focus for now is the midterms.

“We gotta take care of business this November and then we’ll worry about what comes next,” he said.

Vance invoked his family as he credited the president with building a bright future, while attacking the “far left” for working against their “birthright.”

Vance, the father of four including a six-week-old son, defended the nuclear family, which he said was being attacked by Democrats. He said he wants the same thing for American families as he does for his own.

“I want them to keep what they’ve earned when they work hard. And that is the birthright that I’m talking about. That is the country that Donald J. Trump is fighting every single day to defend and to build upon,” he said.

Vance opened his speech with an apparent defense of administration efforts to reduce immigration in the U.S.

Vance said voters were tired by factory closures, drug overdoses and crime and then pivoted to immigration.

“And we were tired of being called racists for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous,” Vance said.

The statement revealed the delicate politics at play on immigration. Vance falsely claimed during the 2024 election that Haitian immigrants in his home state of Ohio were abducting and eating pets, a falsehood that Trump repeated.

“History will record that your father was a great man,” Vance said.

He recalled being nervous to give his speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention less than two years after being elected to his first role in politics as an Ohio senator.

“As I addressed the country on the biggest stage of my life in the front row, right about there,” he said, pointing in front of him, “my dear friend Charlie Kirk was smiling and cheering me and reminding me that I had a good friend right here in the convention hall.”

Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, who took over as the leader of the Turning Point organization he founded, “has carried on his mission with more courage and resolve than most of us will ever be asked to show,” Vance said.

The vice president walked onto the stage after a secret riser behind the podium was revealed with a curtain raise, showing people waving American flags.

The crowd in the arena rose to their feet to welcome Vance as a hype video about him played on screens.

While Vance was met with cheers, the reception did not seem quite as loud as the welcome Kennedy and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt got as they took the stage.

The president’s son said followers of the “Make America Great Again” movement will keep Kirk’s fight for conservatism alive.

Trump Jr. said that Kirk had inspired a movement to stand up to leftists.

“We will not back down,” Trump Jr. said. “We will not fold. We will honor Charlie by carrying his torch to save this nation that we all love so dearly.”

Trump Jr. said that Democrats wanted to “shove down our throats” a “hellscape.”

As Republicans gather in Dallas, the president is also deploying his cash in key midterm races.

No Going Back PAC Inc., which a person with knowledge of the situation said is connected to Trump’s MAGA Inc., has been buying up airtime during the convention. So far it has reserved more than $68 million in advertising.

The person was not authorized to speak publicly about the funding arrangement.

— By Thomas Beaumont

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lamented what he cast as the transformation of the Democratic Party of his father and uncle at the midterm GOP convention.

The son of a former U.S. attorney general and nephew of President John F. Kennedy, the secretary said the “irony of my presence here is inescapable.”

He enumerated his view that the party had abandoned working Americans for elites and said he found a new home in the Republican Party, eliciting loud cheers and applause.

“The Democratic Party, in short, lost its way,” he said.

A video marking the Sept. 11 attacks included images from the devastation and clips of then-President George W. Bush’s visit to ground zero and triumphant first pitch in the 2001 World Series.

It also included images of then-New York real estate figure Donald Trump striding into Manhattan and talking to media about employees for his business who were working at the time of the attack.

The video later turned to images of some Democratic figures who have been critical of U.S. foreign policy and offered more callous statements of the calamity.

The segment wrapped with images of Trump as president, suggesting he had shielded the U.S. from further similar attacks, as presidents since Bush have also done.

In the end, quiet, respectful applause lightly fluttered across the arena.

Christopher Macchio’s soaring tenor spiraled through the American Airlines Center, the strains of “Ave Maria” in an almost silent convention center.

It was the most solemn and poignant moment of the convention, a tribute to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on New York, Washington, D.C., and Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

As Macchio’s voice filled the arena, the floor was darkened, though two beams of light stretched upward, reminiscent of the Twin Towers. Convention goers illuminated their mobile phone flashlights, giving the fitting illusion of candlelight.

The basketball arena’s screens fluttered with images of passenger aircraft striking the World Trade Center towers in New York, footage of frantic Manhattanites and debris-covered police, fire and rescue workers.

A narrator intoned “2,977 innocent people lost their lives,” as familiar videos transitioned to home videos of families.

“Always remember who they are,” the narrator said solemnly. “Say their names. Honor their sacrifice. Defend Freedom. Never forget September 11.”

Lawler, facing reelection in a battleground district this year, appealed to “common sense Democrats and independents” from the GOP midterm convention stage.

It was a different tone compared with the near constant attacks on Democrats.

“While I’m honored to be in this arena with so many fellow Republicans tonight, my message is really aimed at common sense Democrats and independents across the country tuning in and still undecided about their vote in November,” he said.

In an emotional presentation, Lawler appeared on stage with the family of Sheridan Gorman, who was fatally shot this year in Chicago. Officials have charged a man they say was illegally in the country with her slaying.

Ross Ulbricht, the founder of the underground website used for selling drugs, thanked Trump for pardoning him last year after being sentenced to life in prison in 2015.

“You gave me my life back, sir,” Ulbricht said while choking back tears.

Some in the crowd at the Republican midterm convention shouted that his plight was similar to that of those imprisoned for participating in the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. He said Trump was also a “target of weaponized government” after the indictments and investigations after his first term.

Ulbricht said there are hundreds of “decent Americans” who Trump freed from prison.

“I’ll be a block,” Trump said on Fox News’ “The Ingraham Angle.” “I’ll end up being a blocker.”

The president suggested he still might be able to strike deals with Congress.

He also defended his promise to give $5,000 payments to each American if Republicans preserve their congressional majorities and said he might not need congressional approval.

He also said that faster economic growth would help to pay down the $40 trillion national debt over time. Growth so far is running lower under Trump than his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden.

GOP nominee Mike Rogers said his opponent is being funded by “terrorist groups like the Muslim Brotherhood,” but offered no proof to back up his claim.

Rogers sought to portray Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee and an epidemiologist, as a terrorist sympathizer because of his relationship with the podcaster Hasan Piker, a liberal online commentator and critic of Israel.

“They treat our country like it’s the villain,” Rogers said of his opponent and Piker.

El-Sayed distanced himself from Piker last month.

The normally festive and rowdy crowd inside the American Airlines Center quickly hushed. On the screen was a face known to many of the thousands in the basketball arena, as his voice, just as familiar, came back to life for just a few minutes.

During a five-minute homage to Kirk, the conservative organizer and former President of Turning Point USA shot to death a year ago, the Republican midterm convention sat uncharacteristically quiet.

Video of Kirk speaking and working with young adults, for which he became known as a speaker on college campuses, rolled on the huge screen, while his voice echoed through the silence.

At the short program’s end, a polite round of applause rippled through the seats.

Lucas Miles, a pastor and a Turning Point vice president, kicked off a tribute to Charlie Kirk on the one year anniversary of his death.

“They could take the man,” Miles said. “They could not take the mission.”

He ticked off a list of Turning Point’s accomplishments: thousands of chapters, more than a billion social media views.

“Turning Point is not dead,” Miles said. “The organization Charlie founded is still growing.”

Mike Johnson suggested that differences with Democrats have become irreconcilable, saying “next year the communists will be in Congress.”

“It now falls to us to fight to preserve the country that we love,” Johnson said. “It’s being attacked from within.”

The Trump presidency has been defined by a broader radicalization among Republicans and Democrats alike.

Democrats portray Trump as a corrupt actor who has violated the norms and constitutional standards governing the country, whereas Johnson and others at the GOP midterm convention have said that Democrats are now beholden to political radicals that should be rejected.

The House speaker claimed he has led “the most productive Congress in 80 years.”
