One motion seeks answers on whether Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is using government contractors ThunderCat and Palantir to obtain immigrant taxpayers’ information, in violation of a February 2026 court order won by the advocates that blocked ICE from using or accessing Internal Revenue Service (IRS) data in its possession.

The second motion seeks to reveal the details of the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) transmission of hundreds of immigrants’ information to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in March of 2025. The agency has provided only a heavily redacted record of this transmission, undermining public accountability and creating concern from advocates that it may currently be violating the law.

Today’s motions were filed by Asian Law Caucus, Greater Boston Legal Services (GBLS), and Keker, Van Nest & Peters LLP in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of groups that provide taxpayer services and advocate for the rights and needs of immigrant communities: Community Economic Development Center of Southeastern Massachusetts (CEDC), National Korean American Service and Educational Consortium (NAKASEC), National Parents Union (NPU), and Undocublack Network (UBN).

IRS and SSA abuse of taxpayer data circumvents strict privacy law and exposes taxpayers and families to risk of immigration enforcement

The new filings come after DHS awarded a $10 million contract to ThunderCat Technology, LLC in June 2026 to provide “Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) data” and analytics to the Homeland Security Investigations unit of ICE. The filings also follow revelations that ICE has unlawfully shared confidential Medicaid data with Palantir through a Microsoft Teams chat, leaving that data saved in multiple cloud locations. Palantir conducts extensive work for both IRS and ICE, providing the latter an enforcement targeting tool and an opening to access multiple IRS databases. Protected taxpayer data in the hands of a third-party ICE contractor would represent an attempt to circumvent the federal court order – another example of the Trump administration ignoring the law.

“The government cannot outsource its way around the law. That’s why we are demanding answers to find out whether ICE is potentially sharing and obtaining protected taxpayer information through seven-figure contracts to tech companies, in violation of a federal court order,” said Josh Rosenthal, workers’ rights program director at Asian Law Caucus. “Putting protected taxpayer information in the hands of private tech giants puts all of our privacy, safety, and rights at risk. We will continue fighting to get answers and hold our government accountable.”

“A court order is only meaningful if the government cannot evade it through contractors or conceal whether it is complying,” said Sarah Salomon, partner at Keker, Van Nest & Peters LLP. “These motions seek straightforward answers about who received protected taxpayer and Social Security information, how that information has been used, and whether federal agencies are following the law. Immigrant families are entitled to the privacy protections Congress gave them, and we will keep pressing for transparency.”

In 2025 ICE, the IRS, and the SSA formalized agreements and began the transfer of massive data sets. Protected by strict federal privacy laws, the information held by the IRS and SSA can only be released to other parties, including other agencies, under specific and limited circumstances. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration in 2026 released a report pointing to serious concerns about the transmission and safeguarding of information with DHS. Taxpayer and immigrant advocates have raised alarm over the exposure of over one million taxpayers’ sensitive data that puts their communities at risk of potential arrest, detention, and deportation without due process.

text:
Whether Immigration and Customs Enforcement can continue construction on a controversial planned detention center outside of Gilroy could come down to one messy detail: toilets.

Santa Clara County and the state are seeking to block the facility, arguing the federal government violated state land use laws and administrative procedures when it began construction. Attorneys for Santa Clara County argue, among other things, that if the facility opens according to its current blueprints, its “ill-conveived” sewage plan poses a “risk of septic overflow.”

The county’s misgivings are straightforward: more people, more toilet trips, more strain on the existing septic tanks that were designed to serve a small agriculture company with no more than 40 employees — not its new tenant, which could have more than 100 people, including 50 employees, in and out every day.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But attorneys for the federal government argue county officials are overestimating how many people will be working and detained inside the facility — and therefore how many people might be using the toilets.

At a hearing in the case in San Jose on Tuesday, debate centered on the septic tanks, and the capacity of the site itself. Now a California judge is considering the county’s arguments that the facility could cause hazardous waste to spill into waterways because ICE and Elmwood Capital Group, the property owner, are relying on a connection to a sewage line and plumbing infrastructure that doesn’t actually exist in the rural area.

“They’re up a certain creek without a paddle,” Santa Clara County Counsel Tony Lopresti told the Chronicle.

The county’s legal team has also argued that it would be difficult — if not impossible — for Elmwood Capital to create an adequate septic system or plumbing connection to fit the needs of the ICE agents, visitors and detainees who would frequent the site.

Stacey Bosshardt, an attorney representing the site’s landlord, called the inclusion of the nonexistent plumbing line in site plans a “mistake” at Tuesday’s hearing.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

U.S. District Judge Eumi K. Lee said she expects to issue a decision by Sept. 15. On Tuesday, she extended a stay halting construction at the site at 7240 Holsclaw Rd. starting July 13. The lawsuit has garnered national interest, and is seen as a test case for how local governments could potentially fend off the construction of unwanted immigration detention centers by utilizing land use and environmental laws.

Detention center or ‘holding center’?

The dispute over how taxed the facility’s toilets would ultimately be reflects an impasse between ICE and the county over how big and how full the building would actually be.

Attorneys for the federal government argued in court that the facility itself wasn’t a “detention center” that would be holding people overnight, and therefore wouldn’t strain the sewage system as much as the county’s attorneys suggested. They called it a “holding center,” though the federal government’s own bid for a contractor said it was seeking space for a 4,000-square-foot “detention center.”

The county has consistently referenced site plans that say the facility could hold up to 150 people. Bosshardt, the property’s attorney, described those blueprints as “largely accurate” but also said they are still a “draft” plan and not final. Court filings also detail that as many as 60 members of the public could be in and out of the office within a day to meet with ICE agents for appointments. The current office in Morgan Hill where agents work doesn’t have as much space for meetings nor does it have any holding rooms or cells.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In court Tuesday, the federal attorneys said the site would hold about 10 detainees for no more than 12 hours at a time. The federal government’s own filings, however, also said the “maximum” number of people held could be higher than that. Since President Donald Trump took office, ICE has consistently kept people in cells and holding rooms designated for quick stays or processing for days overnight without beds, medical care or basic hygiene products.

County attorney Rajiv Narayan said in court he expects the Santa Clara facility would request a waiver from the federal government to hold people longer than 12 hours, which has become routine under Trump, who has sought to deport millions of immigrants from the country. When Lee questioned the defense about the building’s estimated capacity, Johann said the figures had not been completed and ICE had not “committed” to a number.

“That’s just not how the law works, thankfully,” Lopresti told the Chronicle about site planning.

The county’s attorneys wrote in court filings that the existing plumbing includes one main septic tank with a capacity of 600 gallons per day and two other systems that serve floor drains in nearby buildings. If a total 150 people were on site per day, peak waterflow would reach 15,000 gallons, the filing said.

Even if the number is lower than 150, it will still be greater than the 40 the system is currently built for, county attorneys said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Federal attorneys said the county’s estimates “lack support” and called environmental impacts “speculative.” They argued the more material impacts of the facility being blocked would be ICE not being able to perform its duties. The absence of a new office could place a “significant burden” on those who have to regularly meet with ICE, since the Gilroy facility is supposed to replace an existing location in Morgan Hill, attorneyssaid. Without a replacement, immigrants facing removal proceedings could have to travel even farther for appointments.

“The plaintiffs are offering nothing more than hypothetical future harm,” Department of Justice attorney Pamela Johann said in court.

But the site plans also include the addition of a gym, showers and food prep areas. That would mean even more wastewater, Lopresti said, with nowhere for it to go other than the tanks.

In order to meet sewer needs, the county argues the federal government and its landlord would need to design and build a sewer main connection — which would require miles of excavation work across country roads and private property — or construct a much bigger septic system with a leachfield 12 times the length of each of its existing 500-foot drain sites.

“This isn’t some sort of hypothetical NIMBY argument,” Lopresti said. “It’s a very real thing I think speaks to how absurd it was for them to try to barge through with this without taking the necessary steps.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The federal government began seeking out a new space for ICE in the broader San Jose region in 2021. But construction on the facility didn’t begin until at least this spring.

In court, the federal government argued that because the previous tenant had an office space and a lab, the “general use” would not change because it would still mostly be an office with an added holding center. If the property’s “use” doesn’t change, it wouldn’t be subject to the same level of zoning scrutiny or change-of-use requirements by law.

Lee seemed unimpressed with that argument.

title: Immigration court's unusual locations raise due process concerns - KOSU
authors: Ximena Bustillo, Steve Inskeep, www.kosu.org, steve-inskeep
description:
Why is she being sent from the Hyattsville Immigration Court to Falls Church?
INSKEEP: OK. Where are immigrants being told to go if they're not being told to go to immigration court?
But neither is a building that usually has in-person immigration court hearings.
BUSTILLO: The immigration court agency at the Justice Department declined to confirm if these were new hearing locations.
All of this, advocates say, further erodes the trust in these immigration courts that are under supervision of the president.
text:
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:

We have some news for you this morning about immigrants summoned for court hearings. They're called in for these hearings, but not at normal immigration courts. NPR's Ximena Bustillo has been covering these courts inside the Justice Department for almost two years and has some reporting on where the immigrants are being sent. Ximena, hi.

XIMENA BUSTILLO, BYLINE: Hi.

INSKEEP: So what'd you find out?

BUSTILLO: Well, I heard a weird rumor from some of my sources. A few immigration attorneys in the Greater Washington, D.C., area - that's Maryland and Virginia - told me that they had clients or people hoping to retain them who came to them with notices to appear at immigration court.

Now, these notices themselves are normal. If someone is here without legal status, they may get one in the mail, and that starts their removal proceedings. This is also the process where immigrants get to argue why they should not be deported. But immigrants who had previously been scheduled at Maryland or Virginia courts were instead told to go somewhere else, a place their attorneys had never before seen scheduled for an in-person hearing. Here's two attorneys, Lucelia Justiniano and James Reyes.

LUCELIA JUSTINIANO: This has to be a mistake. Why is she being sent from the Hyattsville Immigration Court to Falls Church? That makes no sense.

JAMES REYES: I honestly thought it was a glitch. I was like, 15 years - there's no way. This is just a glitch in the system.

BUSTILLO: And both attorneys have been practicing in the area for over 10 years.

INSKEEP: OK. Where are immigrants being told to go if they're not being told to go to immigration court?

BUSTILLO: So one was actually the offices for the Federal Emergency Management Agency in Washington, D.C. And the second is the headquarters for the agency that runs immigration courts in Falls Church, Virginia. But neither is a building that usually has in-person immigration court hearings.

INSKEEP: And how does the administration explain this?

BUSTILLO: The immigration court agency at the Justice Department declined to confirm if these were new hearing locations. But they did say that they will continue to make scheduling adjustments, including opening new hearing locations as needed to, quote, "ensure all cases are handled in a timely and lawful manner." NPR has since learned that FEMA employees on Friday were notified that their headquarters conference rooms would be used by the DOJ and the Homeland Security Department.

INSKEEP: OK. So random conference rooms are becoming courtrooms. But are the immigrants still seeing a judge when they get there?

BUSTILLO: Yes. So I was told - and I asked many people coming out of these buildings. And they did confirm they did see an immigration judge - though that judge happened to be appearing remotely on a TV screen, often in the original court, like Baltimore, Hyattsville, where they were supposed to appear. And now remember, these are administrative judges. So they're also a lot more like other federal employees under direction of the president.

INSKEEP: Right. They're not part of the judicial branch, but the executive. What are the concerns about having an unannounced location for your court hearing?

BUSTILLO: Well, it adds to the confusion. And the risk is that if immigrants miss their hearings, that gives the immigration judge ability to issue an automatic final order for their deportation. And groups tracking these orders say they've really increased in the last few months. And NPR identified two cases where immigrants did not receive a notice in the mail about the change of venue. And in one instance, the immigrant only knew because they used an application called MigraConnect, which sent them a notification about the new time and place.

INSKEEP: How do the added locations fit into the immigration strategy of the administration?

BUSTILLO: The administration is trying to both reduce the court backlog and increase the number of people that it can deport. And that strategy does appear to be working. The number of cases pending is falling for the first time in about a decade, according to government data. And in order to reach that goal, immigration judges are scheduled to hear hundreds of cases in a day. And they're being trained to deny immigrants' requests for more time. All of this, advocates say, further erodes the trust in these immigration courts that are under supervision of the president.

INSKEEP: NPR's Ximena Bustillo, thanks so much.

BUSTILLO: Thank you.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
The Trump administration is proposing to eliminate a rule that gives many H-1B visa holders up to 60 days to remain in the United States after losing their jobs, potentially forcing thousands of foreign workers and their families to make immigration decisions almost immediately after employment ends.

The Department of Homeland Security unveiled the proposed regulation Thursday. It would remove the 60-day grace period available to workers in several employment-based nonimmigrant classifications, including H-1B visas widely used by technology companies and other employers seeking highly skilled workers.

The proposal is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on September 11 and will then enter a 60-day public comment period. The current grace period remains in effect while the rulemaking process continues.

If the regulation is finalized as proposed, covered workers would generally begin failing to maintain their immigration status the day after their qualifying employment ends unless they have another legal basis to remain in the United States.

The Current Rule Gives Workers Time After a Job Loss

Since 2017, federal regulations have allowed certain employment-based visa holders whose jobs end before their authorized stay expires to remain in the country for up to 60 consecutive days, or until their existing authorized period ends, whichever comes first.

The rule covers H-1B workers along with people holding E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, and TN status. Their dependent family members can also benefit from the grace period.

The protection is discretionary, not guaranteed. USCIS can shorten or eliminate the period based on circumstances including immigration-status violations, unauthorized employment, fraud, national-security concerns, or criminal convictions.

For workers who receive the full period, the time can be critical. A person who loses a job can use the window to pursue employment with another qualifying employer, apply to change immigration status, seek adjustment to permanent residence when eligible, or make arrangements to leave the country.

H-1B workers also have a special portability provision that lets eligible workers begin employment with a new employer once a qualifying H-1B petition has been filed, rather than waiting for USCIS to approve it.

Removing the grace period would sharply narrow the time available to reach that point.

DHS Wants Immigration Status Tied More Closely to Employment

DHS argues that the 60-day period separates a worker's legal status from the employment that originally justified admission to the United States.

Under the administration's reasoning, employment-based nonimmigrant classifications exist because the individual is performing the job or activity underlying the visa. When that employment ends, DHS says authorization to remain under that status should end unless another lawful basis for remaining in the country already exists.

The agency also points to the administrative work involved in applying the current rule.

USCIS says that from fiscal year 2018 through May 20, 2026, more than 1.9 million petitions and applications potentially required officers to determine if the grace period applied. Officers may have to establish exactly when employment ended and decide if circumstances support granting, shortening, or eliminating the discretionary period.

DHS now says those individualized determinations consume resources for a benefit that Congress did not expressly require.

The Proposal Would Reach Beyond H-1B Workers

Much of the attention surrounding the proposal will likely focus on H-1B visas because of their importance to the technology sector, but the regulatory change is substantially broader.

Workers covered by the proposal include treaty traders and investors, specialty occupation workers from Australia, Chile, and Singapore, intracompany transferees, individuals with extraordinary ability or achievement, and certain Canadian and Mexican professionals working in the United States under the TN classification.

Family members whose immigration status depends on the principal worker could also be affected.

DHS estimates that an average of about 65,752 covered workers per year experienced an employment cessation or employer change from fiscal years 2021 through 2025 based on the agency's proxy data. About 99 percent of that population held H-1B status.

The agency cautions that its records do not show precisely how many people actually relied upon the grace period.

Its data show that an average of 3,795 covered workers per year had a new employer submit a Form I-129 petition within the possible 60-day window. Others pursued adjustment of status, a change or extension of status, or certain employment authorization.

DHS Acknowledges Workers and Employers Have Relied on the Rule

One of the more significant portions of the proposal addresses what happens when a federal agency reverses a policy that people and businesses have organized their affairs around.

DHS acknowledges that foreign workers, employers, and family members may have made decisions based on the expectation that workers would have some time to respond after employment ends.

Employers may have recruited people who recently lost another job on the assumption that the worker could remain in the United States while a new petition was prepared. Workers may have bought homes, established families, enrolled children in schools or made career decisions knowing that losing a job would not ordinarily require an immediate departure.

DHS says it considered those reliance interests and concluded that the government's interests in changing the rule outweigh them.

That discussion could become important if a final regulation is challenged in federal court.

Supreme Court administrative-law precedent permits federal agencies to change policies, but an agency generally must acknowledge the change, provide a reasoned explanation, and account for serious reliance interests created by the earlier policy.

DHS cites that precedent directly in the proposed regulation, including FCC v. Fox Television Stations and Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm.

The unusually detailed reliance discussion appears designed in part to establish the administrative record supporting the policy reversal before a final rule is issued.

Losing a Job Could Trigger Much Faster Immigration Consequences

Under the proposal, a covered worker whose qualifying employment ends would generally need to leave the United States immediately unless another legal basis permits the person to remain.

DHS states that the worker and dependent family members would be considered to be failing to maintain their nonimmigrant status beginning the day after the principal worker's employment or qualifying activity ends.

That would transform the immigration consequences of an ordinary layoff.

Under the existing system, an H-1B employee who suddenly loses a job has a limited period to search for another employer willing to file a petition. The proposed system could require the worker to pursue a new employment arrangement from outside the United States if another lawful status has not already been secured.

DHS acknowledges that the change could lead to more departures following job losses. The agency also recognizes that employers seeking to hire recently terminated foreign workers could experience delays or temporary productivity losses if those workers have to leave the country before returning through a new approved petition.

The proposal could have an especially visible effect during large corporate layoffs, where dozens or hundreds of visa-dependent employees may lose their jobs on the same day.

A Final Rule Could Face an Administrative Law Challenge

Publication of the proposal does not change the current immigration rules.

Interested parties will have 60 days after publication in the Federal Register to submit comments, including evidence concerning economic effects, employer reliance, family disruption, and other consequences of eliminating the grace period.

DHS will then have to consider significant comments before issuing any final regulation.

A legal challenge could follow if the administration adopts the rule. Opponents could seek review under the Administrative Procedure Act and argue that DHS failed to adequately justify its departure from the policy adopted in 2016 and implemented in 2017, particularly if the final administrative record does not sufficiently address reliance interests or the consequences identified during public comment.

DHS has already begun building its response to such arguments.

The proposed rule repeatedly emphasizes the Secretary of Homeland Security's statutory authority over the time and conditions of admission for nonimmigrants. It also expressly acknowledges the government's change in position and explains why DHS now believes the grace period conflicts with the structure of employment-based nonimmigrant status.

For now, H-1B workers who lose their jobs still have access to the existing discretionary grace period.

title: Class-action lawsuit filed in Md. over DHS 'arrest first, ask questions later policy' - WTOP
description:
“He was kidnapped by ICE agents outside a 7-Eleven in June, despite his protests repeatedly that he was born in this country,” said Austin Rose, managing attorney for the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.
“Guzman vs. DHS challenges this racist, unlawful policy and practice of arrest first, ask questions later,” said Shana Khader, legal director of We Are CASA.
“Federal law is clear: immigration agents need a warrant to make an arrest,” said Sonia Kumar with the ACLU of Maryland.
“What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.
“ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” the statement from the spokesperson said.
text:
A group of Maryland residents from throughout the state, by way of the immigrant rights group CASA, have filed a class-action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security over sweeping immigration-related arrests that have been carried out in recent months.

According to the complaint, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is adhering to “a consistent policy: aggressively stop people who they perceive to be Brown or Black immigrants and immediately arrest them without a warrant and without making the individual assessments required for such warrantless arrests.”

It accuses ICE of violently crashing into and detaining people without warrants or even investigations — something described as “arrest first, ask questions later” in violation of three other court rulings since President Donald Trump took office in 2025.

One plaintiff in the case is identified as Samuel Guzman of Anne Arundel County, a U.S. citizen who was born in Maryland. In the complaint, it said he was detained in a 7-Eleven parking lot in Annapolis, put in restraints and taken to another parking lot where he was held with other Latino individuals.

“He was kidnapped by ICE agents outside a 7-Eleven in June, despite his protests repeatedly that he was born in this country,” said Austin Rose, managing attorney for the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. “The ICE officer said to him, ‘If you are an American citizen, why don’t you speak better English?’”

The three others are listed only by their initials and have been in the United States for at least one, sometimes two decades. They hail from Prince George’s, Montgomery and Wicomico counties. The complaint says all four have been illegally arrested by ICE and believe they’re at substantial risk of being arrested again.

“Guzman vs. DHS challenges this racist, unlawful policy and practice of arrest first, ask questions later,” said Shana Khader, legal director of We Are CASA.

The complaint asks a federal judge to certify anyone as class representatives in the case “who, since January 20, 2025, have been or will be arrested in this District for alleged immigration violations without a warrant and without a pre-arrest, individualized assessment of probable cause that the person is in the United States unlawfully,” as well as “anyone who, since January 20, 2025, have been or will be arrested in this District for alleged immigration violations without a warrant and without a pre-arrest, individualized assessment of probable cause that the person poses an escape risk.”

The lawsuit also asks a judge to declare the current policies in violation of the Fourth Amendment and to force the government to stop making warrantless immigration arrests without probable cause of an immigration violation.

“Federal law is clear: immigration agents need a warrant to make an arrest,” said Sonia Kumar with the ACLU of Maryland. “That’s the rule. That’s the rules they’re supposed to follow. There’s one exception: a narrow, specific, deliberately limited exception created by Congress for when agents have probable cause that someone’s here unlawfully and that they are an escape risk. It is an exception. It is not and was never meant to be a blank check for hunting people down while they’re trying to get to work or take their kids to school or just go about their daily lives.”

DHS provided a statement to WTOP attributed to a spokesperson that denied the allegations they engaged in illegal practices, and pushed back on suggestions ICE agents are targeting the Hispanic population.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” the statement said. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. — NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity. ICE has authority for lawful arrests under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices.”

The agency also highlighted several arrests made throughout Maryland that it announced in 2025 and early 2026 that it dubbed “the worst of the worst” — immigrants who came to the country illegally and were convicted of murder, sexual abuse and other felonies.

“ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” the statement from the spokesperson said.

Similar cases filed in D.C. and other states have been upheld against the government.

“We hope that we can achieve the same result that we did in D.C., which was a significant curtailing of the amount of warrantless arrest there,” Rose said. “It doesn’t solve the problem entirely, and it still takes more and more work. And in the D.C. case, they violated the injunction, we had to go back again and get it enforced.”

Immigration judges work for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review and are part of the executive branch, not the federal judiciary.
The Trump administration has fired more than 100 immigration judges since January 2025, according to Bloomberg Law.

text:
A former San Francisco immigration judge is suing the Trump administration, alleging she was fired just days after raising alarms about what she described as unlawful and unconstitutional treatment of a detained child.

Chloe Dillon, who served as an immigration judge in San Francisco, filed suit Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The complaint alleges she was terminated in August 2025 in retaliation for whistleblowing, about 48 hours after she emailed a supervisor about what she described as potential statutory-law and due-process violations involving ICE’s detention of an unaccompanied minor after a court hearing.

According to the complaint, Dillon said the detained minor could not be placed in expedited removal proceedings and had the right to have his already-filed asylum application considered first.

The lawsuit alleges violations of the Whistleblower Protection Act, the First and Fifth Amendments, the Appointments Clause and Article II.

Dillon also alleges she had previously objected to a 2025 directive requiring immigration judges to grant all ICE motions to move cases to different court venues. Her supervisor allegedly told her that “the White House” was watching the issue and warned her against resisting the directive.

The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges work for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review and are part of the executive branch, not the federal judiciary.

The lawsuit comes amid a wave of firings. The Trump administration has fired more than 100 immigration judges since January 2025, according to Bloomberg Law. MS NOW reported at least 135 had been fired since Trump returned to office. Other fired immigration judges have separately sued, alleging discrimination based on gender, age, ethnicity or prior advocacy for immigrants.

In a separate case, a Merit Systems Protection Board decision found the attorney general may remove immigration judges at will, though that decision is under appeal.

San Francisco’s immigration court, where Dillon worked, permanently closed Sept. 4.

The Texas Republican-led legislature’s 2025 effort to flip Democratic House seats through gerrymandering triggered a wave of redistricting bills across the country in Republican and Democratic states.

However, the Texas GOP might have inadvertently made it harder for Republican nominee Tano Tijerina to unseat Cuellar. Tijerina was elected as a judge in Webb County as a Democrat before switching parties in 2024.

Trump was the first Republican presidential candidate in a century to win several counties throughout the district, including Cuellar’s home of Webb County. However, Cuellar won reelection in 2024 and is fighting for his 12th term. Many Trump supporters, particularly among Texas’ Latino population, no longer support him. 1 in 5 Texas Latinos now regret voting for him, according to a recent UnidosUS poll.

“A lot of these voters, they may have liked Trump in 2024, but they're not consistent Republican voters,” said Erin Covey, Cook Political Report analyst. “It's better to think of them as more independent voters who are open to being persuaded.”

In a sit-down interview with Medill News Service, Cuellar said that the Texas GOP looked at the wrong data when it redrew the map, by voting along party lines to pass a rare mid-decade redistricting bill known as HB 4 in August 2025. After months of lawsuits over alleged racial gerrymandering behind the bill, the lawsuit challenging HB 4 was stayed by the Supreme Court in December. The stay allows the map to take effect for at least the 2026 midterm election.

Texas draws new electoral maps every 10 years based on the Democratic Performance Index, or “DPI,” data. DPI is a specialized political map that measures the partisanship of voting areas based on local-level voting history and weighted election averages.

Rep. Todd Hunter (R-TX), admitted the maps were redrawn to favor the districts that swung in favor of Trump in 2024 according to the select redistricting committee report Hunter authored.

“[HB 4] seeks to revise the composition of the districts for the election of members of the U.S. House of Representatives from Texas by replacing the 2021 map with a new map to reflect the increased statewide vote for the Republican presidential nominee,” he wrote.

Several polls suggested that the Texas GOP’s reliance on Trump voters, without accounting for other features of the Texas voting bloc, made it unlikely the party would pick up five seats in the House of Representatives in November. But experts believe they will still gain some.

“I think there's a much better chance that they end up flipping maybe three seats as a result of the new map,” said Covey.

The Texas Partisan Index is a voting analysis tool published every two years after each statewide election by a local news organization called The Texan. The index looks at the Republican-to-Democratic partisan leanings of each legislative district and county in Texas, based on data obtained from the Texas Legislative Council and the Secretary of State.

The TPI initially found that following the 2024 election, Texas’ 28th Congressional District leaned 51% Democratic. The latest TPI, updated after the redistricting bill was passed, shows that the district is now 53% Democratic.

Bill King, a senior fellow at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, said Republicans are “much more unlikely” to win seats in the three redrawn South Texas districts, including the 28th Congressional District.

“In fact, they cut the margin so thin down there, and they relied on what we think are some false premises,” King said.

Cuellar elaborated on those false premises King alluded to. Cuellar said the Republican Party misunderstood South Texas’ voting history and the influences on Latino Trump supporters in 2024 would vote for other Republicans down-ballot.

“What they did is they looked at South Texas or the narrative by the Republicans that Hispanics voted for Trump and voted for Republicans,” Cuellar said. “But if you look at those numbers . . . here in Webb County, we had some Republicans running. The Democrats won. So it didn't happen in 2024. Trump won, but the people said, ‘I'm voting for this local Democrat.’”

Gov. Greg Abbott denied the redistricting was racially discriminatory but said in a Fox News interview, “Four of the five districts we’re drawing are going to be Hispanic districts; they happen to be Hispanic Republican districts.”

In Texas, 55% of Latinos voted for Trump. In the 28th District, Trump won Webb County, which is 90.6% Latino, and Zapata County, which is 93.6% Latino. An overwhelming majority of those Latinos are Mexican-American.

Cheyenne Rodriguez, a Zapata County resident who identifies as Hispanic and voted for Trump, told Medill News Service that border security was a key issue for her decision to vote for Trump. She feels that support for Trump in her area is strong but quiet.

“There's a lot of people who are hardcore-not Trump- and then they ended up voting Trump; you see it a lot,” she said. “I mean, I don't really see a whole bunch of Trump flags or people celebrating stuff like that. But it's just the general vibe, you know, like, you can relate on the subject. Ain't nobody gonna be voting for Biden. I'm sorry, but no.”

Despite Trump’s historic Latino support, King said polling since redistricting shows that many Latinos are shifting against Trump.

“The polling seems to show that they're having some real buyer's remorse on Trump and the Republicans, and it's likely to flip back this time to more traditional results that we've seen,” he said. “If that's the case, they probably don't pick up any of those seats in the [Rio Grande Valley], and might even lose another one that's vulnerable.”

According to a 2025 UnidoUS poll, 66% of Texas Latino voters now disapprove of Trump.

“The drivers of that erosion are telling: the cost of living and inflation (44%), immigration enforcement in American cities (33%), job and wage stagnation (26%), and the war in Iran (25%) top the list. Latino voters are not just disappointed; they are making the connection between this administration’s policies and the economic pain they feel every single day,” UnidosUS wrote in its analysis.

While Latino voting blocs in other states have found issues with Trump’s immigration policy for moral reasons, Bill King explained that Latinos in Texas are “complicated” and have found Trump’s immigration policies hurt their wallet.

“If you go online, you'll see a lot of business people down along the [South Texas] valley talking about the difficulty in finding workers,” he said. “The fact that, like I mean, every time somebody gets deported or self-deports or doesn't come here, that's one less customer for a restaurant. It's one less tenant for an apartment owner. It's having the economic effect down the valley that they're not happy about. Latinos in Texas are very much economic voters.”

The majority-Latino Maverick County used to fall squarely within the 28th District, but redistricting has split it up.

Luis Ruiz, former chairman of the Democratic Party in Maverick County, said most Latinos in Texas, “especially Tejano Latinos,” don’t support Trump’s immigration policies.

“Why? Because most of us see it not as a personal issue. But rather as a financial issue. If it hurts our pockets, we don’t like it. That is going to cause a big problem in 2026 and 2028,” he said.

text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. (CN) — A federal judge on Thursday questioned the federal government’s delay in restarting diversity visa application processing, after a court order blocked three policies that paused applications.

On Aug. 28, Senior U.S. District Judge Edward Davila granted in part a preliminary injunction to temporarily reopen the processing of visa applications. He also granted in part class certification of subclasses for those whose diversity visas, either under an Immigration Services or the Department of State policy, were on indefinite hold.

At Thursday’s hearing on an emergency motion to enforce Davila’s order, attorney Curtis Morrison, representing dozens of applicants, said the U.S. State Department sent cables to consular offices on “how to deflect and turn away plaintiffs and class members,” and said he heard from his clients that they were turned away from interviews in Paris and Kigali, Rwanda, on Thursday morning.

“It is plaintiffs’ position that there have not been good faith efforts,” Morrison told the court, saying the department “made things worse” and cancelled all interviews for applicants in September. Morrison said it was concerning, because the fiscal year for processing applications ends at the end of September.

Nag Young Chu, with the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said the cancellation of interviews had to do with a training initiative to provide for “adequate training” and was not directly related to Davila’s order.

Chu explained a department cable was sent out Thursday morning to consuls with guidance on prioritizing the recently cancelled interviewees and that the policies blocking application processing are no longer in effect.

Davila, a Barack Obama appointee, questioned why it took almost two weeks after the court order for the government to send a cable and restart interviews.

“That seems like a binary to me, a switch up and down,” he said. “I don’t understand the disconnect from engaging again.”

Chu said restarting the application processing was not binary and many internal discussions on how to adjudicate the pending applications need to take place. Additionally, he said, reconsideration by consular officials of applications that were denied solely due to department policies would require a manual search.

Under the diversity immigrant visa program, the Department of State holds a lottery in which it randomly selects noncitizens from countries with historically low rates of U.S. immigration for the opportunity to apply for a green card. If an applicant is in the U.S. under a different visa at the time of selection, they must a submit form with Immigration Services to adjust their status to permanent resident.

Selection to the program does not guarantee a visa, just the ability to apply for one. Generally, the Department of State selects up to 55,000 immigrants to start the application process for each fiscal year.

In December 2025, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department issued two policies that place indefinite holds on green card applications and adjustment of diversity visa status.

And in February, the State Department issued a notice pausing visa approval from 75 countries, requiring consular officers to refuse all immigrant visa applicants until the agency develops new guidance for consular officers to assess if an applicant might become dependent on public assistance once in the U.S. The notice was issued with no date on lifting the pause.

A class action was filed in June in Northern California federal court and names President Donald Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Director Joesph Edlow, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as defendants.

Because of the possibility that the government will be unable to process thousands of applications by the end of the fiscal year, Davila asked for a briefing from both parties about what a remedy could be if the government fails to follow the court’s order in a timely manner.

He said the recommendation to restart interviews in three to seven days may be a “herculean feat” but should be attempted. He asked both parties to attend status hearings three days a week until the end of September to keep the court informed on the government’s progress.

text:
TOPEKA — A U.S. District Court judge issued an order forbidding enforcement of a bipartisan Kansas law adopted in 2004 that allowed certain immigrant students at public colleges and universities to pay in-state tuition rates rather than higher out-of-state rates.

Beneficiaries of the controversial state statute have been community college or university students who were brought to the United States as children, completed a high school education in Kansas and agreed to seek citizenship while pursing a degree in higher education.

The judge’s injunction takes effect immediately, but it was unclear how it would be implemented on individual campuses across Kansas.

The state law was challenged by the U.S. Department of Justice based on a premise the program violated federal immigration law, incentivized illegal immigration and unconstitutionally discriminated against U.S. citizens.

U.S. District Judge Holly Teeter, a nominee of President Donald Trump, issued a permanent injunction Wednesday night that relied on the Justice Department’s arguments to justify invalidation of the Kansas tuition program.

“The central problem here is that there are United States citizens and nationals who pay full nonresident tuition when an unlawfully present alien is eligible to pay a lower rate on the basis of residence,” the judge said in the decision.

Teeter said state statute was preempted by federal law “because it confers a postsecondary education benefit on an unlawfully present alien based on a state-defined residency conclusion without making that same benefit generally available to United States citizens and nationals regardless of their residence.”

Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach, a longstanding opponent of the tuition statute, collaborated with the DOJ on the legal challenge and jointly proposed a consent judgment blocking the law.

In defense of the state’s tuition statute, Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly sought to intervene and seek dismissal of the lawsuit.

Ryan Kriegshauser, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Kansas, said during a news conference Thursday that the court ruling meant Kansas couldn’t extend in-state tuition benefits to immigrant students without providing the same benefit to U.S. citizens.

“No longer will illegal aliens enjoy the benefit of lower in-state tuition in Kansas,” Kriegshauser said. “This decision has been a long time coming. In fact, I looked at this statute 20 years ago as a law student and a law clerk. It violated the supremacy clause then as it does now.”

Jessica Swonger, staff attorney with the ACLU of Kansas, said the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund and the ACLU of Kansas filed a motion in July to intervene on behalf of students impacted by U.S. v. Kansas.

“This is a disappointing denial of the rights of those most impacted by the current administration’s cruel crusade against students in Kansas to participate in a lawsuit that will directly impact their future,” Swonger said. “The court has allowed the Department of Justice, in collusion with Attorney General Kobach, to slam the door on hardworking Kansas students, even though Kansans have long supported providing all children in our state the opportunity to learn.”

In June, the DOJ filed its complaint against Kansas and endorsed a proposed consent decree to permanently forbid future use of the tuition law.

“Kansas’ unconstitutional and un-American laws should never have been passed in the first place and are prohibited by federal law,” said Brett Shumate, an assistant attorney general in the DOJ’s civil rights division. “The Department of Justice has won on this exact issue in Texas, Oklahoma, Kentucky and Nebraska, and we will take this fight to any states that fail to put American citizens first.”

During the 2026 session of the Kansas Legislature, the House and Senate passed Senate Bill 254 to prohibit people without authorization to be in the United States from receiving state and local public benefits, including in-state tuition at public colleges and universities.

Kelly vetoed the measure and denounced the bill as damaging to the state’s economy and to workforce development. The Republican-controlled Legislature failed to produce two-thirds majorities necessary to override the governor.

“There are many ways that we could, and should, work together to fix this country’s broken immigration system,” Kelly said when she filed the motion to intervene in the lawsuit. “In pursuing higher education, these young Kansans are a net-benefit to our entire state, gaining the education and training needed to be valuable members of our workforce and contribute to our economy.”

In February, Kobach issued a nonbinding legal opinion that concluded the tuition law known as KSA 76-731a conflicted with federal law.

“For years, Kansas universities have been violating federal law by giving in-state tuition rates to illegal aliens, while nonresident U.S. citizens have to pay much more in tuition,” Kobach said. “The governor tried to intervene in this case, because she wanted to continue giving in-state tuition benefits to illegal aliens. With this decision, the court rejected her illogical arguments, and once again, U.S. citizens will be treated better than illegal aliens by Kansas universities.”

text:
proposed rulemaking titled “Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period.” The proposal, signed by Secretary Markwayne Mullin and carrying DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 (RIN 1615-AD22), would strike 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) from the regulations. That single paragraph is what currently allows a nonimmigrant worker whose employment ends mid-petition to remain in the United States for up to 60 days without being treated as out of status. The proposed regulation can be found here: https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-18631.pdf

If finalized as written, the rule would mean that an H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, or TN worker, along with that worker’s spouse and children, would be considered to have failed to maintain status the day after employment ends, and would be expected to depart the United States immediately unless separately authorized to remain.

The grace period is still in effect today. Nothing changes unless and until DHS issues a final rule. But the comment window is open now, and DHS has specifically asked the public to weigh in on reliance interests. That request deserves close attention, and I will come back to it below.

What the current rule does, and where it came from

DHS created the up to 60-day grace period in the 2016 AC21 final rule, Retention of EB-1, EB-2, EB-3 Immigrant Workers and Program Improvements Affecting High-Skilled Nonimmigrant Workers, 81 FR 82398 (Nov. 18, 2016), effective January 17, 2017. The stated purpose was to enhance job portability, stability, and flexibility for high-skilled workers, and to make it easier for U.S. employers to hire and transition nonimmigrant talent.

Under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2), a covered worker gets up to 60 days, or until the end of the authorized validity period, whichever is shorter. The worker is not authorized to work during that window, but is not treated as having not been out of status either. That breathing room is what makes it practically possible to be the beneficiary of a new I-129 change of employer petition, file an I-539 change of status, file an I-485 where eligible, apply for a compelling circumstances EAD, or even wrap up their affairs and depart the country.

Two features of the existing rule matter for the current debate. First, the grace period has always been discretionary, and USCIS can shorten or eliminate it when adjudicating a later benefit request. Second, DHS never built a mechanism to track its use, which is why the agency now has to rely on proxy data.

What the proposed rule would do

The regulatory text is short. DHS would remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), redesignate current paragraph (l)(3) as the new (l)(2), and revise 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) to delete the cross reference to the 60-day grace period. The practical consequences are considerably larger than the text suggests.

Status would end the day after employment ceases. DHS states plainly that under the proposal workers and their dependents “would be considered to be immediately failing to maintain their nonimmigrant status the day after the principal alien’s employment or activity ceases.” The preamble repeatedly frames the expectation as immediate departure.

Dependents fall with the principal. Because derivative status is tied to the principal’s status, spouses and children would lose status at the same moment. DHS’s own figures put the dependent population at roughly 208,187 per year on a five-year average, and 1,040,935 for FY 2021 through FY 2025 combined.

The 10-day grace period would not fill the gap. DHS notes in a footnote that the 10-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(1) applies only “after the validity period ends,” so by its terms it does not reach a worker terminated during an approved validity period. The company that lays off an H-1B employee two years into a three-year approval leaves that employee with no cushion at all.

The compelling circumstances EAD would be harder to reach. DHS proposes to rewrite 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) so that it references only the periods authorized by 214.1(l)(1) plus other periods of admission before a validity period begins or after it expires. Because an initial compelling circumstances EAD requires the applicant to be in a qualifying status on the filing date, removing the 60-day bridge substantially narrows the window in exactly the involuntary job loss scenario the CCEAD was designed to address. DHS’s own data shows only 49 CCEAD filings in the relevant population across five fiscal years, so this is a small program, but it is one of the few safety valves that exists.

The downstream consequences are not small. Failure to maintain status carries deportability exposure under INA 237(a)(1)(C)(i), potential accrual of unlawful presence and the resulting three and ten year bars under INA 212(a)(9)(B), adjustment bars under INA 245(c)(2), and a negative factor in future discretionary adjudications. The agency also acknowledges that H-1B petitioners would remain liable for the reasonable cost of return transportation abroad for a beneficiary dismissed before the end of the authorized admission period.

The rule does not resolve how portability interacts with the change. H-1B portability under INA 214(n) is statutory and is not amended here. Neither is the preamble clear about how a terminated worker who is no longer “maintaining status,” but whose I-94 has not expired, is supposed to be treated for portability, extension of stay, or change of status purposes. That ambiguity is one of the more consequential gaps in the proposal.

DHS’s stated justifications

The agency offers two. The first is statutory alignment: each covered classification is defined by reference to specific employment or activity, so DHS now believes lawful status should end when that employment ends. Though, the regulation seems to align with the goals of AC21. The second is administrative burden. DHS counted over 1.9 million petitions and applications from FY 2018 through May 20, 2026 on which adjudicators potentially had to assess whether the grace period applied, and concludes it should not spend limited resources on a discretionary benefit Congress did not require.

DHS also candidly acknowledges that it is reversing its own 2016 position, and cites Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm and FCC v. Fox Television Stations for the proposition that an agency may change course if it explains itself. However, this is something that requires a lot of heavy lifting.

On the population affected, DHS estimates that an annual average of 65,752 primary beneficiaries experienced cessation of employment or changed employers, with 328,758 over the five-year period, and that 99 percent of that group was in H-1B status. Of that five-year total, 5.77 percent had a new I-129 filed within 60 days, 1.70 percent filed an I-539, 0.59 percent filed an I-485, and under 0.1 percent filed a CCEAD. DHS uses I-129 withdrawal data as a proxy and admits it undercounts, since several classifications have no withdrawal notification requirement at all. The quality of that proxy is itself a fair subject for comment. Frankly, the data seems off based on what has seemingly been the case.

DHS considered and rejected three alternatives: eliminating the grace period for only some classifications, shortening rather than eliminating it, and keeping it but imposing stricter evidentiary requirements. Anyone who would prefer one of those alternatives should say so on the record, with support.

The comment period, and why the reliance interests request matters

Comments are due 60 days after publication. Based on the September 11, 2026 publication date, that puts the deadline at November 10, 2026, with the electronic docket accepting submissions until midnight Eastern at the end of that day.

Comments must be filed through the Federal eRulemaking Portal at regulations.gov under DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364. USCIS is not accepting comments by mail, email, hand delivery, courier, or on digital media. Every submission is posted publicly without change, including any personal information it contains, so think carefully about what identifying details you include. DHS notes that the most useful comments cite a specific portion of the rule, explain the reason for the recommended change, and include data, information, or authority supporting it.

Now the part I would flag above everything else. In Section IV.D, DHS acknowledges the reliance interests at stake, and it does so in some detail. The preamble recognizes that employers made business arrangements assuming terminated workers could start new employment without departing, that workers and their families made career and personal plans, and that affected families bought houses, paid taxes, and invested in their communities. DHS then concludes that any such reliance “would be misplaced” because the grace period was always discretionary, citing the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Wages and White Lion Investments for the idea that a belief about how an agency will exercise its discretion is not a serious reliance interest.

And then DHS says this: it “invites comments on any potential impact of this rulemaking, including comments on any potential reliance interests that are implicated by the provisions of this NPRM.”

That invitation is the single most important sentence in the document for employers and workers. An agency reversing a longstanding policy must consider serious reliance interests, and a failure to do so is a classic basis for holding a rule arbitrary and capricious. But courts review the administrative record, and the administrative record is built during the comment period. If the only characterization of reliance in the record is DHS’s own assertion that reliance here is “misplaced,” that assertion is much harder to challenge later. Concrete, documented, first-person accounts of reliance are what turn a conclusory dismissal into a genuine record problem.

Call to action

File a comment before November 10, 2026. Generic opposition helps very little. Specificity helps a great deal.

If you are an employer, describe what you actually do today. How many mid-validity terminations and rehires do you handle in a year? What does it cost you when a hire has to consular process from abroad instead of transitioning in the United States? How long do visa appointments take at the posts your workforce uses? What happens to project timelines, client commitments, and staffing when a candidate disappears for weeks or months? If you have restructured, acquired, or downsized in reliance on the ability to redeploy workers, say so. Attach numbers.

If you are a worker or family member, describe the plans you built around the current rule. A mortgage, a lease, a school year, a spouse’s employment, a pending green card case, a child approaching 21. DHS said reliance here is misplaced. The record should reflect whether that is true in the lives of the roughly 65,000 workers and 208,000 dependents the agency itself identified each year.

If you would accept a narrower rule, say which alternative and why. DHS rejected partial elimination, a shortened grace period, and an evidentiary-requirements approach. Comments supporting one of those preserve the argument.

Address the gaps. The interaction with H-1B portability. The collapse of the compelling circumstances EAD filing window. The absence of any transition or grandfathering provision for workers already in the United States. The reliability of I-129 withdrawal data as a proxy for grace period usage.

Reddy Neumann Brown PC is preparing comments on this proposal and is available to help employers develop and submit their own. If you would like to discuss how the rule would affect your workforce, or if you have questions about your status following a termination under the rules as they exist today, please contact our office.

Reddy Neumann Brown PC located in Houston, Texas, has been serving the business immigration community for over 25 years and is Houston’s largest immigration law firm focused solely on U.S. employment-based and investor-based immigration. We work with employers, employees and investors helping them navigate the immigration process quickly and cost-effectively.

By: Steven Brown

Steven A. Brown is a Partner at Reddy Neumann Brown PC, where he leads the firm’s Litigation Team, addressing delays and denials of immigration benefits, FOIA requests, and policy and regulatory challenges. Steven is dedicated to delivering practical and effective solutions for clients facing unreasonably delayed or unlawfully withheld immigration benefits, including Employment Authorization Documents (EADs), advance parole, green cards, 221(g) decisions, EB-5 delays, and other immigration-related matters. His litigation efforts were instrumental in Shergill, et al. v. Mayorkas, a landmark case that led to the U.S. government recognizing that under the INA, L-2 and E visa spouses are authorized to work incident to their status, eliminating the need for separate EAD applications. This case has transformed work authorization for thousands of families across the United States.

title: Inside the 'Shadow Surge' Driving ICE Arrests to New Heights - The Marshall Project
authors: Geoff Hing, Doug Livingston, Lauren Villagran
description:
Trump’s new pick to run the department, Markwayne Mullin, promised to pursue the president’s goals with more cooperation from local law enforcement and less public backlash.
In Florida, ICE logged more than 7,000 immigration arrests, more than triple the number in that month the year before.
So far in 2026, ICE recorded more immigration arrests in Hamilton — a city of fewer than 65,000 residents — than anywhere else in Ohio.
Immigrant advocates in Chicago and St. Louis say calls to hotlines for legal services and to report ICE arrests increased dramatically in July.
Data collected during those calls shows more than half of immigration arrests in St. Louis and eastern Missouri were made by police during a traffic stop.
text:
After federal immigration agents ended their aggressive enforcement blitzes in the streets of Minneapolis and Chicago, President Donald Trump promised mass deportations with “a little bit of a softer touch.”

Less focused on targeted cities, this quieter approach has led to a surge in immigration arrests across the country.

Arrests began climbing gradually in March and by July had risen sharply. In nearly every state, arrests exceeded the number from the same period the year before. A Marshall Project analysis of Immigration and Customs Enforcement data published by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA found that in many places the surge in enforcement has been dramatic. Even without a focus on high-profile operations, immigration arrests more than doubled in 15 states and Washington, D.C.

Republican-led states and communities across the country offered up their own law enforcement agencies to help, from the Texas and Florida highway patrols to sheriffs departments in Ohio and local police in Missouri.

A Department of Homeland Security press release reported ICE made nearly 51,000 arrests in August, higher than any month on record.

“We call it the ‘shadow surge,’” said Jill Garvey, director of States at the Core, a nonprofit that supports grassroots organizations confronting authoritarian threats. “It’s this much quieter, but no less violent or deadly, enforcement.”

Public outrage exploded in January when federal agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an enforcement mission called Operation Metro Surge. Their deaths marked a turning point in the Trump administration’s campaign to round up and deport immigrants without authorization to be in the United States.

After months of flashy, made-for-media enforcement — agents piling out of a rented Penske truck at a Los Angeles Home Depot, rounding up hundreds of Korean autoworkers at a plant in Georgia, arresting a 5-year-old boy in a bunny hat in Minneapolis — Trump fired Border Patrol commander-at-large Greg Bovino and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Trump’s new pick to run the department, Markwayne Mullin, promised to pursue the president’s goals with more cooperation from local law enforcement and less public backlash. Congress had already approved tens of billions of dollars to fund that mission.

The enforcement that has followed has been widespread, diffuse and harder for the national media to track. It’s also been measurably more effective.

ICE’s stepped-up enforcement looks different across the country. Federal authorities have cracked down on commercial truck drivers and arrested people at airports who had overstayed their visas. ICE has continued arrests of immigrants in neighborhoods and public places like hardware store parking lots. These operations can still be chaotic, like a raid of a Memphis bar that began as a state investigation into gambling and drugs and ended with immigration arrests, or immigration agents striking protestors with batons and dragging them from the porch of a home in Frederick, Maryland. In some states, immigrants are still most frequently brought into ICE custody through a transfer from a prison or jail, but increases in other kinds of arrests have led to a summer surge.

Roughly 2,000 state and local law enforcement agencies have signed agreements with the federal government to conduct immigration stops or hand over immigrants who are in local jails. Since ICE reset its tactics, arrests from these programs have grown considerably.

Texas and Florida, each led by Republican governors with possible national aspirations, have emerged as Trump’s top enforcers.

Texas accounted for a quarter of all immigration arrests in July. In Florida, ICE logged more than 7,000 immigration arrests, more than triple the number in that month the year before. Both states have directed their state troopers to conduct immigration stops. In Florida, the arrests often begin when people are stopped for traffic violations or driving without a license, said Palm Beach immigration attorney Jackie Delgado.

“They are not being taken to a jail and being booked in and seeing a judge,” she said. “They’re skirting the justice system and heading directly to ICE.”

Other states, including Missouri and Ohio, are blips on the nationwide scale of immigration enforcement. But each has seen arrests climb as local police lean into the cooperation agreements with ICE.

In 2024, neither state had a single local police agency enforcing immigration laws for ICE through what are colloquially called 287(g) agreements — a reference to the federal regulation that created the program. Today, 130 law enforcement agencies in Missouri and 20 in Ohio have signed up.

“The signing of these 287(g) agreements has really turned all of our local law enforcement into these ‘show me your papers’ forces,” said Gabby Eissner, advocacy strategist at the St. Louis-based MICA Project, which provides low-cost and pro bono legal services to immigrants. “People are getting picked up at traffic stops, and those traffic stops are happening because of the color of their skin.”

Since June, ICE has set new monthly records for signing up local law enforcement partners, according to a Marshall Project analysis of agreements listed on the agency’s website. With greater swaths of the country patrolled by ICE’s local partners, advocates say it’s getting harder to distinguish routine traffic stops from targeted immigration arrests.

“The 287(g) agreements and the cooperation with local law enforcement are making it challenging for people to document what’s happening in their communities,” said Garvey, who leads the authoritarian watchdog organization.

In Southwest Ohio, the quietly expanding immigration machinery is on full display in Hamilton, the seat of conservative Butler County. There, Sheriff Richard Jones has had an “Illegal Aliens Here” sign outside the jail for two decades. He quickly inked 287(g) agreements after Trump returned to office last year.

Jones told The Marshall Project that 44 of his deputies, or about a quarter of his law enforcement personnel, are ICE-trained to identify undocumented immigrants. They initiate most of the hundreds of stops that have led to ICE arrests in the county, but police officers working for other local departments also call his deputies, widening the net.

So far in 2026, ICE recorded more immigration arrests in Hamilton — a city of fewer than 65,000 residents — than anywhere else in Ohio. Arrests there more than quadrupled this year compared to the same time period last year, and nearly all of those arrests are tied to 287(g) agreements.

Jones said he expects to bring in $20 million in revenue this year from the agreement with the federal government. That money outweighs the daily protests outside the county jail. He estimates that 4,700 immigrant detainees have come through the jail in the past 18 months.

“A few of them get released from here and don’t get deported,” he said. “But it’s not many.”

Even with broader collaboration between federal immigration agencies and state and local law enforcement, ICE’s data shows that in July, half of arrests were of people with no prior contact with the criminal justice system. This percentage has grown along with the increase in arrests.

ICE and Customs and Border Protection have more funding than ever to conduct immigration enforcement, with more than $200 billion allocated since Trump took office last year. Congress approved about $70 billion of that funding in June. That cash infusion is greater than the fiscal 2026 budgets for the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration and U.S. Marshals Service combined, according to the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law.

ICE has so far used the money, which can be spent through fiscal 2029, to more than double its personnel, hire more charter flights for faster deportations and expand its technology to include “shock gloves” and robot dogs.

Cities are still targets for immigration enforcement, with less fanfare. Immigrant advocates in Chicago and St. Louis say calls to hotlines for legal services and to report ICE arrests increased dramatically in July.

The St. Louis Rapid Response Hotline has fielded nearly 9,000 calls for help dealing with immigration arrests over the past year, according to the Ashrei Foundation, which runs the hotline. Data collected during those calls shows more than half of immigration arrests in St. Louis and eastern Missouri were made by police during a traffic stop. The same pattern is evident in Chicago.

“They are quieter arrests,” said Alycia Jameson, a Chicago-based immigration attorney. “It’s a lot of suburbs. It’s a lot of traffic stops. It’s not the Midway Blitz Operations [in Chicago] — it’s not that. But the numbers are really up.”

text:
Armed federal agents are planning to patrol voting locations during elections and the courts need to act now to stop it from happening, alleges a lawsuit filed by a group of civil rights organizations and the city of Denver.

The effort is intended to get out ahead of any attempt by the Trump administration to use law enforcement to hinder voting. And it aims to counter what one group calls “an intentional climate of fear and intimidation,” that threatens to chill participation among minority communities.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday, asks a federal district court in Washington, D.C. to declare such activities unlawful and block the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from carrying them out.

“The specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election,” the lawsuit reads. “It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal immigration enforcement officers if they choose to cast a ballot.”

DHS Chief Markwayne Mullin said recently that he would only dispatch ICE to polling areas “to conduct civil immigration and customs enforcement operations.” But that still runs afoul of federal election laws, according to the lawsuit.

Specifically, ICE’s plans violate a U.S. Code section from the Civil War era that prohibits military and federal officers from ordering armed agents to “any place where a general or special election is held,” under penalty of fines, imprisonment and disqualification from holding office.

The code only makes one exception: “to repel the armed enemies of the U.S.”

The pro-democracy organization Common Cause said it helped file the lawsuit, in part, to stop rumors about armed federal agent deployment that have been circulating among the communities it works in.

“Every week is a new headline and scare for naturalized citizens and communities of color, about ICE or other law enforcement at the polling places,” the group says on its website. “This intentional climate of fear and intimidation stops now.”

Two other organizations on the lawsuit, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) and UnidosUS, represent a huge contingent of Latino citizens who’ve expressed fear that armed and-or plainclothed federal officers could approach and possibly arrest them as they try to vote or work at polling locations.

Their complaint compiles a long list of statements made by Trump administration officials and actions taken by ICE agents that explain why Latino voters harbor these concerns.

In February, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said she couldn’t “guarantee that an ICE agent won’t be around a polling location in November” during a press conference. A month later, Justice Department official Todd Blanche, now the attorney general, asked at a conference, “Why is there objection to sending ICE officers to polling places?”

Blanche and Mullin have also said in congressional hearings and to the press that they would deploy armed agents to polling areas to serve warrants and conduct other law enforcement operations where they suspect threats.

The lawsuit also points to actual instances of ICE agents making arrests and approaching suspects at polls during elections this year. Earlier this year, in San Antonio and in Ventura County, California, groups of agents descended upon voters during elections.

Also in June, two agents confronted a poll worker in Syracuse to probe her about online comments she made about ICE.

“The result is that as citizens go to the polls this fall, they are confronted by the possibility of armed force—agents carrying guns who may stop them based on how they look and what language they speak, detain them forcefully, interrogate them, and prevent them from seeking help,” the lawsuit reads. “Even citizens who are not specifically confronted by ICE agents may be intimidated from voting by the presence of ICE agents at or near voting sites.”

The city and county of Denver is involved with the lawsuit because a large portion of its population are Mexican, Vietnamese and Ethiopian immigrants – “making it a likely target for ICE activity during the midterm election,” the lawsuit reads.

According to the complaint, the county clerk has already begun trainings for its elections staff on how to de-escalate interactions with federal agents and how to identify agents when they’re not in uniform. It also describes how rumors of armed agents showing up at polls have made the difficult job of recruiting poll workers even tougher.

“The possibility of confronting armed federal agents in the course of these duties is expected to cause concern and anxiety for election judges attempting to complete their duties, and individuals may no longer be willing to perform this work,” the complaint reads. “Losing large numbers of election judges during the election cycle would impair the Clerk’s ability to administer the election, impose significant costs to train replacement judges for that election, and hinder the ability to timely tabulate and report results.”
