title: Tracking the numbers behind Trump's immigration offensive - CNN
authors: Catherine E. Shoichet, Alex  Leeds Matthews, Annette Choi, Kate Carroll
description:
The latest data on immigration enforcement paints a revealing picture of the Trump administration’s crackdown.
Since President Donald Trump’s promise to lead the largest deportation operation in US history, CNN has been tracking key numbers.
At least 20 people have been shot by on-duty ICE and CBP agents during the second Trump administration.
At least 57 people have died in ICE custody since the start of the second Trump administration, according to ICE statistics.
But a CNN analysis found that the death rate has spiked on a monthly and annual basis under the second Trump administration.
text:
The latest data on immigration enforcement paints a revealing picture of the Trump administration’s crackdown.

Arrests are soaring, immigrant detention has skyrocketed nearly 70% since early 2025, the pace of deportations is intensifying and the death rate in detention reached its highest point since the pandemic.

Since President Donald Trump’s promise to lead the largest deportation operation in US history, CNN has been tracking key numbers. The charts below show what’s happening beyond the headlines, and how the immigration offensive has ebbed, flowed and often intensified on multiple fronts.

The data on this page will be updated as new information is released, so check back for changes.

Immigration arrests are changing

The Trump administration claims immigration authorities’ arrests are focusing on major criminals it calls “the worst of the worst.” But the data reveals that most of those arrested don’t have criminal convictions on their records, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University (TRAC).

The Department of Homeland Security takes a different view on the numbers. The agency says nearly 70% of people arrested by ICE have been convicted or charged with a crime in the United States — including the pending charges in that calculation. And White House border czar Tom Homan has stressed that prioritizing national security threats doesn’t mean others are exempt.

“If you’re in the country illegally,” he says, “you’re never off the table.”

But critics of the administration’s approach argue that officials are misleading the public about their priorities.

“DHS inflates the number of ‘criminal’ arrests by including people with pending criminal charges, because many criminal charges do not end in convictions, and an ICE arrest denies them due process and their day in court,” says David Bier of the libertarian Cato Institute.

As the number of immigrant arrests soars, there’s another shift: US Customs and Border Protection officers are handling far fewer arrests than they once did.

As restrictions at the US-Mexico border have increased and enforcement efforts have increasingly focused on the interior of the country, ICE is now largely tasked with making those arrests. Though we’ve also seen CBP officers playing a more visible role in some immigration operations inside the US.

Shootings by federal agents are drawing scrutiny

Aggressive tactics playing out in public have become a frequent sight in the Trump administration’s immigration offensive, with some federal authorities shattering car windows and tackling their targets during arrests or other operations. And as enforcement continues, the use of deadly force during operations has drawn increasing scrutiny.

At least 20 people have been shot by on-duty ICE and CBP agents during the second Trump administration.

DHS officials have repeatedly argued that ICE officers are facing a significant increase in assaults against them.

“ICE and CBP are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and themselves,” a DHS spokesperson told CNN last year. “Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.”

Immigrant rights advocates and some local leaders have accused DHS of endangering American communities by using aggressive tactics.

Two shooting deaths during ICE operations drew national attention this summer as arrests ramped up in July. DHS has said it’s investigating those controversial shootings, and others that occurred earlier this year. State and local authorities are also investigating some of the shootings. Federal officials’ initial responses have described the uses of force as justified, even as the shootings have sparked protests from critics who argue agents are abusing their power and who question the thoroughness and approach of federal authorities’ investigations.

The pace of deportations is increasing

DHS says the Trump administration has deported 985,000 people, but hasn’t provided a detailed breakdown of that number by federal agency. In addition to ICE removals, which are tallied in regular data releases by the government, US Customs and Border Protection also removes individuals apprehended at the US-Mexico border, and the Coast Guard conducts repatriations.

ICE’s recently released preliminary data for the current fiscal year, which ends September 30, shows removals at their highest levels in recent years.

Both those pushing for more deportations and immigrant advocates who oppose the crackdown argue that officials should release more data about deportations so the public can better track what’s going on.

ICE is detaining more people

By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70% from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

And officials say they’re hoping to grow ICE’s detention capacity even more.

Detention deaths are on the rise

As the number of people detained has grown, more people are also dying in ICE custody.

At least 57 people have died in ICE custody since the start of the second Trump administration, according to ICE statistics. That tally doesn’t include deaths of those recently released from ICE custody. In June the agency announced it was ending its policy of reporting those deaths to the public.

The trend has sparked concern from those who track these numbers and see them as a troubling indicator of widespread problems in the detention system that they argue have intensified with policy changes made by this administration.

At least 10 of the deaths were presumed suicides, and some of the individuals who died had pre-existing medical conditions. A CNN investigation found deadly outcomes in more than a dozen cases could be linked, in part, to substandard treatment by at-times understaffed medical teams dealing with escalating detainee populations, according to a review of autopsy reports, court records and interviews with detainees and experts.

DHS disputes allegations of medical neglect and poor conditions that advocates link to the growing death toll. “Being in detention is a choice,” the agency argues, stating that undocumented immigrants can opt to self-deport using the US program that offers a $2,600 stipend to those who choose to leave.

“As bed space has rapidly expanded, we have maintained (a) higher standard of care than most prisons that hold U.S. citizens — including providing access to proper medical care. For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives,” a DHS spokesperson said, adding that detainees also receive food, water, bedding, clean clothing and dietician-certified meals.

DHS also argues the rate of deaths in ICE custody has remained consistent. “There has been NO spike in deaths,” the spokesperson said. But a CNN analysis found that the death rate has spiked on a monthly and annual basis under the second Trump administration.

In a June analysis, Physicians for Human Rights and Human Rights First argued the death rate has more than doubled since Trump’s second term began.

“Urgent action is needed to address this crisis and prevent further deaths,” the organizations said.

description:
Debt bondage happens when overseas recruiters charge workers high fees to access jobs in Canada.
From agriculture and food processing to tourism, construction and domestic work, debt bondage is a growing concern in Canada, fueled by international poverty and unscrupulous agents.
The Temporary Foreign Worker Program The TFWP gives Canadian employers access to international workers to manage severe work shortages.
The International Labour Organization and other groups say 50 million people around the world live in modern slavery, more than half of them in debt bondage.
“They could continue with a complaint but often feel very unmotivated, so we’ll have to abandon their claim.” Million-dollar question How to rid the world of debt bondage?
text:
Debt bondage happens when overseas recruiters charge workers high fees to access jobs in Canada. Advocates say major changes to law and policy are needed to prevent it.

Southeast Asian and eastern European women, hired as domestics but forced into jobs as sex workers. Jamaican, Guatemalan and Mexican workers toiling in agriculture. Vietnamese women working in the nail-care industry. Filipino men framing houses in the construction industry.

Many of them may be workers charged outrageous fees for the promise of well-paying jobs. They may take out extremely high loans to get here and face exorbitant fees for housing, food, travel and passports, essentially getting trapped in a hard-to-escape cycle of work and debt.

From agriculture and food processing to tourism, construction and domestic work, debt bondage is a growing concern in Canada, fueled by international poverty and unscrupulous agents. Government programs like the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) can be both a blessing and a curse.

The Temporary Foreign Worker Program

The TFWP gives Canadian employers access to international workers to manage severe work shortages. On one hand, the TFWP supports cornerstones of the Canadian economy and offers jobs in industries like construction and agriculture. But it can create conditions of servitude, since international workers may have to pay “agents” in their home countries to access jobs. This is a form of debt bondage, defined by Calgary-based Action Coalition on Human Trafficking (ACT) as a situation “when someone is forced to pay off a loan by working for little or no payment. Debt bondage is one of the most common methods of exploiting victims of human trafficking.”

The TFWP requires an employer to get a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) before hiring temporary foreign workers. The LMIA must show that employees will have a positive or neutral effect on the economy and that the employer has attempted to fill positions with Canadian workers. Workers receive a non-negotiable, employer-specific work permit, which ties them to a job at a particular location.

The challenges? International workers may pay brokers illegal recruitment fees (often by borrowing money) to access these jobs, sometimes in the tens of thousands of dollars. According to an article in The Conversation, workers “come from more than 80 different source countries. Of that number, 110,000 are low wage,” in jobs often marked by “unpaid wages, limited access to timely health care, unsafe working conditions, overcrowded accommodations, abusive working conditions, questionable payroll deductions and non-payment of accrued overtime.” According to the federal government, in 2025, the TFWP issued more than 162,000 permits, with almost half of those involving jobs in agriculture and farming. Psychological and physical abuse and long work hours are additional hazards, according to ACT.

Contemporary slavery?

According to a 2024 CBC story, a report by Tomoya Obokata, the United Nations’ special rapporteur on contemporary forms of slavery, called Canada’s TFWP “a breeding ground for contemporary forms of slavery” with “workers being underpaid and going without protective equipment… employers confiscating documents, arbitrarily cutting working hours and preventing workers from seeking health care,” as well as creating conditions for sexual harassment and abuse. However, then-Immigration Minister Marc Miller “objected to the use of the phrase ‘contemporary slavery’ in reference to the temporary foreign worker program.”

Amanda Aziz is a staff lawyer at BC-based Migrant Workers Centre, a non-profit created to “promote and advance access to justice for migrant workers by providing legal support, system navigation, advocacy, research, public education and engaging in law and policy reform initiatives.” In a telephone interview, Aziz says Obokata’s statement was “very welcomed by my organization and many others working with migrant workers. It is very accurate, and unfortunately nothing really has improved since that report” came out. The International Labour Organization and other groups say 50 million people around the world live in modern slavery, more than half of them in debt bondage. Aziz says it is reasonable to estimate the number of workers caught in debt bondage in Canada in the “tens of thousands.”

Canadian laws targeting debt bondage include section 279 of the Criminal Code (Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labour) and Bill S-211 (Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act). Bill C-16, the Protecting Victims Act, received Royal Assent in June 2026 and aims to update and “strengthen protections for victims of exploitation, gender-based violence and coercion.” Ontario created Bill 41 (the Protection from Coerced Debts Incurred in Relation to Human Trafficking Act) to prevent credit reporting agencies from including coerced debts in consumer reports and ban the collection of debts forced upon human trafficking survivors. Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta all have Trafficking Acts providing legal remedies and civil protection for trafficking survivors. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario all forbid the charging of fees to secure jobs.

“The problem is, the federal government… seems to be in denial with respect to some of the core causes of a lot of the abuse and exploitation in these temporary programs,” says Aziz. Limiting workers to one employer and a non-negotiable work permit with no flexibility creates “an incredible power imbalance more so than with Canadians or permanent resident workers. The fact that it’s temporary and totally reliant on [an] employer … you are going to see a very awful system, situations of abuse and exploitation, just by virtue of the way we’ve set up this system.”

Huge debts and reduced opportunities

A federal government study found that being “far from home, without their familiar social system and their potential social supports, was seen as an important factor in individuals’ vulnerability to coercion and exploitation… Economically, traffickers often saddle their victims with huge debts leading to dire consequences in cases of non-payment and/or make promises of future prosperity. For international victims, threats of being exposed to immigration authorities are another form of control.”

Aziz says that while the federal government is attempting to improve the situation, it is also making “a mad rush to reduce the number of temporary residents,” wrongly blaming them for negatively impacting housing and social services. This shifts the focus away from positive measures like “proactive [workplace] inspections and enforcement.” According to Aziz, trying to reduce the number of temporary residents has just made the situation worse. For those who are legitimately working in Canada and trying to find a path to permanent residence, “we’ve pulled the rug out from under so many of these workers.”

The struggle for steady work has created a predatory industry full of “unscrupulous representatives and agents who are getting rich off fraudulently promising workers that they can help them get a new job if they just pay [and telling workers] they’ve got ‘connections’ with employers. It has created this situation of desperation [with] workers now having a much harder time renewing their temporary residency and then turning to these really awful agents and representatives who are taking advantage of the situation,” says Aziz. Promises of jobs – both real and fake – drive workers to pay up to $70,000 for a chance to work in Canada.

Aura Freedom International is “a grassroots organization working in Canada and internationally to end violence against women and human trafficking through advocacy and education.” In a phone interview, founder and CEO Marissa Kokkoros calls debt bondage a form of coercion, “because the trafficker will say, ‘you owe me 10 grand for your travel, your housing, your recruitment fees, your food,’ and that could be for labour trafficking or sex trafficking. And they say, ‘you must work until your debt’s paid off,’ and then they’re going to add excessive, ridiculous fees on top of it.”

According to ACT, “traffickers may tell victims that they have incurred debt due to expenses associated with transportation, housing, food, and documents such as work permits and visas. Often, traffickers will pile more on top of the initial debt, citing costs such as interest on the initial debt, ongoing costs of food and housing, and additional necessities like medication.” This can include coercive debt like lines of credit, personal loans, and credit cards.

Complaints stuck in red tape

For international workers, getting out of debt bondage involves:

Ensuring their own physical safety;

Using specialized helplines to contact organizations that assist with shelter and emergency help;

Keeping notes and records of names of exploiters, living/working conditions, and coercive financial obligations; and

Reporting the crime and using the available resources to nullify coerced debts.

If mistreated workers want to file a complaint, those grievances are often stuck in a complicated system of overburdened investigators and overbooked tribunals. In general, there is a six-month limitation period to make a complaint, with up to two years for temporary farm workers.

In BC, human rights complaints are taking longer to get to a tribunal, there are often language barriers, and “by the time you get an investigator [to look into the complaint], the worker may already be back in their country,” says Aziz. “They could continue with a complaint but often feel very unmotivated, so we’ll have to abandon their claim.”

Million-dollar question

How to rid the world of debt bondage?

“That is the million-dollar question,” says Aziz. “In our office we often see these schemes getting more sophisticated and difficult. Players in a worker’s own country start the recruitment scheme and collect tens of thousands of dollars, and then they have a representative in Canada who does the immigration work.” How do authorities enforce the rules, and get to those overseas recruiters who receive the money? “Recruitment fees are illegal across the country. No one is permitted to charge a worker a fee to get placed in a job [but] it can take years to identify recruiters, and longer for that person to finally be arrested or investigated.”

A better future includes more effective enforcement. “If we get rid of the structures that create incentives to sell jobs to workers by not having our system focused on employer-specific work, I think that could go a long way,” says Aziz.

Prevention involves “empowering and building up our communities to resist and to not have any need for some trafficker who’s going to promise [workers] everything they’ve ever wanted,” adds Kokkoros. Aura Freedom has provided submissions to government studies and “brought survivors to the table,” but they note that the issue “is so much deeper, and we really have to go upstream because legislative efforts are just band-aids that happen after the exploitation” has already happened. The real focus must be education, advocacy, and prevention, says Kokkoros.

Long-term, access to justice demands faster investigations and a commitment by all – from employers and law enforcement to the tribunal system and politicians – to make the system more transparent, rigorous, and fairer to workers.

text:
Folks,

Greetings from the Burgh, where Payday is wrapping up a ton of projects here before our multimedia editor Amos Wolf goes on parental leave.

65% Towards Parental Leave Goal

Good news, folks, we are now 65% of the way towards our parental leave goal. Amos is getting ready to take off on Friday for the birth of his first child and it would soothe everyone’s anxiety if we could hit this goal today.

ICE Arrested 50 Immigrant Workers in PA Hospital Raid

Last week, ICE raided a construction site at the new Geisenger hospital facility in the central Pennsylvania community of Danville. Now, it’s been announced that at least 50 immigrants were detained in the raid, making it the largest workplace ICE raid in Pennsylvania this year.

Immigrants’ rights advocates were horrified. Activists say that Danville local police assisted ICE in the raid.

“ICE monitored us with drones, watched our vehicles, and intercepted us on the roads. Alongside local police, they waited for us. With the support of local police, they used their power to intimidate us, to let us know we have no rights and that they will take anyone away they encounter,” one eyewitness told the Patriot-News. “Since then, my fellow co-workers are terrified, and no one wants to work. I am afraid and filled with uncertainty.”

For more, check out the Patriot-News.

ICE Raids Pittsburgh’s Latino Beechview Neighborhood

Beechview is the largest Latino neighborhood in Pittsburgh and for the past two days, reports indicate that ICE has been on a rampage throughout the neighborhood. ICE targeted the popular Mexican grocery store Las Palmas.

Now, neighborhood businesses are saying that business is down as immigrants fear shopping there. Our partners at Frontline Dignity are calling people to show up and shop in the district.

“When fear makes people afraid to leave their homes, our neighborhood businesses feel that impact too,” said Jaime Martinez, the founder of Frontline Dignity. “We can respond by making sure our immigrant neighbors and the businesses that serve this community know they are not standing alone.”

For more on how to respond, check out friends at Frontline Dignity.

Report: Immigrant Workplace Threats Double Under Trump in California.

A new report from the California Labor Commissioner’s Office shows that workplace threats against immigrants have more than doubled under Trump. From KQED:

Supervisors threatening to call ICE? That’s nothing new. But with federal agents dramatically detaining so many people under the Trump Administration, workers are taking the threat seriously. And many decide it’s not worth the risk to complain about wage-theft, harassment or other workplace issues.

“But it doesn’t have to be real, it can just be said and the people are fearful,” said Jaime Arteaga with the North Coast States Carpenters’ Union. “It can be a rumor. Somebody might say we might get deported and that shuts everything down. The workers are not going to come forward.”

State figures show complaints of retaliation involving immigration threats have spiked under the first and current Trump administration. Relatively few workers will go to the authorities, but the California Labor Commissioner’s Office reports about 200 complaints involving immigration threats since 2025. That’s nearly as many as during the entire four years of President Joe Biden’s administration.

For more, check out KQED.

Labor Lab Launches New Union Busting Cost Calculator

The anti-union busting website Labor Lab has launched a new calculator that allows workers to find in-depth profiles of the anti-union lawyers working against them and how much they are being paid.

Drawing on filings from the National Labor Relations Board and Department of Labor, the tool has data and background on more than 800 consultants, 8,000 law firms and 21,000 attorneys working in union busting.

“These tools advance LaborLab’s vision of providing resources that can help directly empower workers to organize their workplaces,” said Bob Funk, executive director of LaborLab. "We envision worker-organizers, union staffers and labor attorneys using the search tool to identify unions that have previously dealt with a particular anti-union attorney or consultant, learn from their experience and share that information with other workers.”

For more, check out the new tool at Labor Lab.

Eiffel Tower Workers Strike Over Visit That Excluded Female Staff

Finally, workers at the Eiffel Tower went on strike today after female workers were forced to leave the tower so that a right-wing sect of Hindus associated with Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) could visit.

"Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation," the staff union said in a statement. “Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present."

For more, check out Euronews.

title: 'The White House was watching': Fired immigration judge alleges retaliation by DOJ
authors: Zack Stanton, Laura Barrón-López, Fallon Gallagher, Julianne McShane, The Associated Press
description:
The White House is watching this.” “Prior to the Trump administration, I can’t imagine hearing something like ‘the White House is watching you’ from my ACIJ,” Dillon told MS NOW, referring to her supervising assistant chief immigration judge.
Dillon was never told who at the White House was tracking immigration judges’ decisions.
Unlike federal judges, immigration judges sit within the executive branch, working for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review.
In a similar case involving other fired immigration judges, the Merit Systems Protection Board ruled that the attorney general may remove immigration judges at will because they are “inferior officers” and that the constitutional removal power overrides statutory job protections.
Critics — including fired immigration judges, immigration lawyers and Democratic lawmakers — have argued that this structure threatens judicial independence, making these judges susceptible to political pressure.
text:
A former immigration judge filed a first-of-its-kind whistleblower complaint against the Justice Department on Thursday, alleging that she was fired two days after she reported that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents “had unlawfully detained an unaccompanied minor who had just been in her courtroom,” according to a complaint filed in federal court Thursday.

Chloe Dillon, an immigration judge in San Francisco until her dismissal last spring, also alleges that she had been warned months earlier that the White House was tracking her rulings on a new Trump administration policy that she had found unlawful.

“I really felt that it was my duty, knowing that this was happening, to say I can’t be part of what I feel like is an illegal action,” Dillon told MS NOW. The timing of her firing, she said, seemed “too coincidental”: No other judges in San Francisco were fired that day, nor was her termination part of a mass dismissal.

The policy at issue had come down last April, when San Francisco immigration judges were told that any and all requests by ICE to move a case to a different court venue should be granted. Dillon pushed back, arguing that the directive was contrary to the law and could hurt a noncitizen’s right to counsel.

Dillon’s supervising assistant chief immigration judge then “informed her that ‘the White House’ was watching the issue and cautioned her against resisting the directive,” states the complaint, filed in federal court in the Northern District of California.

Recalling the conversation, Dillon said she told her superior that she believed “this policy violates the law.” Her supervisor, as she summarized it, told her to be careful: “The White House is watching this issue. Like, do you really want to push this? The White House is watching this.”

“Prior to the Trump administration, I can’t imagine hearing something like ‘the White House is watching you’ from my ACIJ,” Dillon told MS NOW, referring to her supervising assistant chief immigration judge.

Dillon was never told who at the White House was tracking immigration judges’ decisions.

“You don’t make decisions based on what the president or what someone else wants you to decide,” Dillon said, describing the code of conduct immigration judges have long followed. “You make the decision based on what the law is, what the evidence is in front of you, and the application of those facts and that evidence to the law.”

The White House and DOJ did not respond to requests for comment.

Unlike federal judges, immigration judges sit within the executive branch, working for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review. The administration has reportedly fired at least 135 of them since Donald Trump returned to the White House, and has maintained that the president and attorney general have the full constitutional authority to remove them.

More articles

The argument has so far held up. In a similar case involving other fired immigration judges, the Merit Systems Protection Board ruled that the attorney general may remove immigration judges at will because they are “inferior officers” and that the constitutional removal power overrides statutory job protections. That decision is being appealed.

Critics — including fired immigration judges, immigration lawyers and Democratic lawmakers — have argued that this structure threatens judicial independence, making these judges susceptible to political pressure. Since the start of Trump’s second term, the administration has fired judges and weakened and narrowed due-process protections for people facing deportation. It also has repeatedly pressured judges to rule in its favor. It now refers to them as “deportation judges” and has issued recruitment materials invoking Judge Dredd, the authoritarian comic-book lawman who serves as judge, jury and executioner.

Even as it fired judges, the department recently swore in its largest-ever class of new ones. Then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said at the time that the administration “is committed to re-establishing an immigration judge corps that is dedicated to restoring the rule of law in our nation’s immigration system.”

Dillion is unconvinced that is what is happening.

“I think there’s undue pressure from the top on how to rule,” she said. “And I believe that there are also directives that make it difficult for them to preside over cases fairly and impartially.”

She is one of several fired immigration judges to challenge their terminations during the Trump administration. Others have filed lawsuits against the Justice Department, alleging that they were fired because of their gender, age or ethnicity.

“This is a slippery slope. Where does it end?” Dillon said. “The point of the immigration court is to offer people a fair proceeding. The point is to do justice. The point is to allow people to present their case and have their case decided on the facts and the law, and not have it be a predetermined outcome. It’s just about affording fairness, which is what people think America stands for.”

text:
Update: This story was updated with a response from DHS on Thursday, Sept. 10 at 10:30 a.m.

Wisconsin U.S. Rep. Gwen Moore (D-Milwaukee) traveled to Leavenworth, Kansas, on Wednesday to visit an immigration detention facility where two Milwaukee women are being held, interview them and check on their welfare. Reyna Elizabeth Garcia and Estenderly Marte Polanco were both arrested during a surge of arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in early July.

Their arrests were described as excessive and violent by advocates from Voces de la Frontera, who monitored the surge and who joined Moore on the Kansas visit. Moore said that the Leavenworth ICE facility currently holds 450 people but is designed to hold more than 1,000. She said she saw signs of rapid expansion. Moore fears that the facility will quickly fill up with more people. “They are building so they can fill this thing up with twice as many detainees,” she said.

Garcia and Polanco told Moore that they are being treated as human beings, Moore said. Detainees are allowed to leave their cells and be in a common area during the day, and the facility has plans for an area where detainees will be able to exercise and get access to sunlight. Moore observed various meals being prepared including kosher and vegetarian options, indicating that the facility is making an attempt to meet dietary needs, although the food appeared to be of low quality.

Most of the people held at Leavenworth are not criminals, Moore said. Still, she said, “it is a very depressive setting, it is definitely a prison, and they are aggressively building.”

Officials at the facility denied any medical neglect, Moore said, and the detention center has doctors on call, but no full-time medical staff within the facility itself.

“We had some hard questions for the ICE officials,” Moore said. “We were very curious to see where the murders and rapists were, and they were unable to show us that.”

Garcia was arrested in late May along with her brother and fiance after ICE agents in unmarked vehicles followed them as they were leaving a local grocery store in Milwaukee. Her fiance, Galo Suárez, was later released and told by ICE agents to walk away and to not look back or else he’d face consequences, he said during a Voces press conference after the arrest. Polanco was arrested the same weekend while driving with her 11-year-old son, who was in the back seat when ICE agents pulled her out of her car. During the arrest, agents split Polanco’s lip, threw her to the ground, and at one point placed her in a position where she couldn’t breathe, she said. In both arrests, agents were described by witnesses as mocking and insulting the people they were arresting.

After her visit, Moore described Garcia as extremely depressed. Polanco checks on her, Moore said, adding that Polanco has a strong faith in the power of prayer and uses this to help lift Garcia’s spirits.

While Garcia’s fiance was released the same day he was arrested, Moore said that the family later learned that her brother had been deported. Polanco said that she told the agents that she was scared about what would happen to her child, who was born prematurely. He remains traumatized after witnessing her arrest, Moore said, and blames himself for his mother’s detention.

Garcia told Moore that she left Nicaragua because “the politics put me in danger,” only to find herself in a similar situation in the U.S.

Moore criticized the historic level of funding for ICE in recent budgets — more than $120 billion — and said her Democratic colleagues worked together to stop further allocations in the most recent budget reconciliation bill. At Leavenworth, she said, she wondered where all the money was going. “I was looking for the sauna,” she joked. The privately run facility is operated by CoreCivic, which sold the facility to the federal government for $238.4 million — about $300,000 per bed. Moore said it is comparable to other prisons that don’t bring in nearly as much money.

In response to questions from the Examiner about Moore’s visit, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security called Moore’s criticisms of the facility “baseless and false.”

“If she doesn’t like our country’s immigration laws, she should focus on changing them–not political theater,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

“Individuals in ICE detention continue to have access to on-site medical care, community emergency transport services, emergency room care, hospital admissions, and off-site specialty care,” the spokesperson added.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” the spokesperson wrote. “They are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers. Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.”

title: 'They're terrorizing the whole neighborhood': Beechview residents describe heightened ICE activity
description:
Beechview — the hilly epicenter of Pittsburgh’s Latino community — has been a hot spot of ICE activity for months.
But the full scope of immigration operations in the neighborhood remains hazy as ICE stays mum about its activity.
“They’re terrorizing the whole neighborhood right now,” said Shelbin Santos, owner of Peruvian restaurant Chicken Latino.
Several Frontline responders — who document scenes of supposed ICE activity — were present throughout Beechview on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Though Martinez said the activity is nothing new in the region, he said the recent jump in Beechview activity appears to be more aggressive.
text:
Latino business owners in Pittsburgh’s Beechview neighborhood say they’re terrified by what they describe as a recent increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity involving several tense confrontations with masked agents and people being detained.

Beechview — the hilly epicenter of Pittsburgh’s Latino community — has been a hot spot of ICE activity for months. But the past two weeks have been especially intense, according to Monica Ruiz, executive director of Beechview-based immigrant advocacy nonprofit Casa San Jose.

It’s culminated in at least two detentions and two tense confrontations at Las Palmas, a popular Latino grocery store, witnesses told TribLive. But the full scope of immigration operations in the neighborhood remains hazy as ICE stays mum about its activity.

“They’re terrorizing the whole neighborhood right now,” said Shelbin Santos, owner of Peruvian restaurant Chicken Latino.

Last Wednesday, agents detained a man outside of Mexican Sazón Lichita, a restaurant a few doors down on Broadway Avenue from Chicken Latino, she said.

Kaylyn Torijano, daughter of Mexican Sazón Lichita owner Liz Torijano, said the customer had just left the shop with a carry-out order when agents detained him.

A video she captured of the incident shows at least four agents, most masked, in tactical gear — including one with a vest reading “Fugitive Operations” — seeming to detain a man outside a truck with another man inside, though the truck’s tailgate blocks part of the camera’s view.

Fugitive Operations teams are a subgroup of ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division.

Agents have also appeared Tuesday and Wednesday at Las Palmas grocery store, also on Broadway Avenue.

On Tuesday, agents in two black SUVs surrounded a white work van outside the store and detained at least one man, according to Ruiz.

The agents also tried to enter the store, but Joey Berumen, a part of the family that owns Las Palmas, told them to leave the property.

“Immediately, all my employees got scared, and so I locked the whole building down,” Berumen said.

The interaction between Berumen and the agents, captured without audio by security cameras at an auto body shop across the street, was hostile and expletive-laden, Berumen said.

After about two minutes, the agents left.

They returned Wednesday morning, however, and yelled at Berumen by name before doing a sharp U-turn on Broadway and departing again, according to Ruiz, who said she witnessed the encounter.

“They’re targeting them, and they’re doing it on purpose,” Ruiz said.

ICE did not answer TribLive questions about agent behavior or whether it had recently stepped up operations in Beechview, though spokesman Jason Koontz did confirm the agency is active in the neighborhood.

“Citizens and legal residents should find reassurance in the presence of trained law enforcement officers removing criminals and illegal aliens from their streets,” Koontz said in a statement.

Losing business

Regardless of immigration status, Beechview residents are fearful, Berumen said — including the roughly 15 employees at the grocery store — who he said were “scared and frustrated.”

He said he remained resolute in keeping the agents away from the store.

“My whole family has been here for 30 years, and I’m not going nowhere,” Berumen said. “You don’t scare me at all.”

Speaking to TribLive in Spanish as her daughter translated on Wednesday morning, Liz Torijano said she would usually be sold out of empanadas by 9:30 a.m., but her typical Latino customer base has not been coming into the shop because of the recent incidents.

That’s left her with a warmer full of food.

Kaylyn Torijano said she hands out cards informing immigrants of their rights and others with contact information for Casa San Jose.

She said she also monitors a WhatsApp group of local neighbors who send heads-up messages when they spot agents.

At Chicken Latino, Santos said, foot traffic had also practically ground to a halt, forcing her to limit hours for her employees.

“We’re losing so much business, it’s crazy,” Santos said. “Even the ones who have papers are scared to come out. You’re just scared to come out because of the way you look.”

Beechview’s immigrants both supplement Allegheny County’s declining population and contribute to its economy by working and opening businesses, Ruiz said.

But she said the recent activity has had a chilling effect on the economic buzz.

“It’s empty,” Ruiz said. “These businesses help our economy.”

For its part, local rapid response and immigrant rights group Frontline Dignity will be increasing patrols in Beechview and coordinating with community groups, according to its executive director Jaime Martinez.

Several Frontline responders — who document scenes of supposed ICE activity — were present throughout Beechview on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Mateo Mattos, director of Radio Las Palmas — a Spanish-language FM station inside the store — also said hosts will air information about ICE sightings.

text:
Photo: Demonstrators gather outside the dormant Hudson Correctional Facility on September 13, 2025, protesting reported plans by the Trump administration to turn it into Colorado’s newest immigrant detention facility. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)

This story by Chase Woodruff appeared on Colorado Newsline on September 9, 2026.

The town of Hudson has refused for months to take any steps to review and enforce its zoning code as it applies to a planned immigration detention center there, say the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to block the facility — and three Hudson residents are now joining them.

Wendy Homstad, Caden Grosshans and Emily Shanks, all residents of Hudson, were added as plaintiffs alongside Weld County resident Janet Carlson and the nonprofit Together Colorado, in an amended complaint filed Tuesday in state court, the group said. Carlson is a neighbor of the dormant prison known as the Big Horn Correctional Facility, which operated as a private prison for the Alaska Department of Corrections from 2009 until 2013, but her property is not within town limits.

The GEO Group, a private prison company, has announced a five-year contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen the facility as a 1,200-bed immigration detention center. But the lawsuit, filed in July against the town of Hudson, its town council, its planning commission and Planning Director Jennifer Woods, alleges that a conditional use permit for the site, approved by voters in 2008, is now void after more than 12 years of vacancy.

“I’ve gone to meeting after meeting, and I’ve watched my neighbors do the same, and every time the answer is the same: it’s not our problem,” Shanks said in a statement Wednesday. “I’m not asking Hudson to take a side in a national debate. I’m asking Hudson to follow its own rules, the same rules it would make anybody else follow.”

Hudson officials have maintained that the town “does not have authority to approve or deny federal use of this private facility.”

Attorneys for the town filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit last month, arguing the plaintiffs lack standing to bring the case. Together Colorado “lacks any connection to the Town,” they argued, while Carlson “lacks a direct connection to the Town,” and the injuries both plaintiffs claimed in the initial complaint were “presently speculative and cannot be determined until a remote time in the future.”

The amended complaint, however, points to Hudson’s own estimates, in its Water Supply Master Plan, that the reopened facility’s water consumption could reach 230 acre-feet annually, nearly doubling the town’s average water use over the last 20 years.

“The reopening of the [Big Horn Correctional Facility] will reintroduce demands that the Town has not anticipated for some time,” the plan says.

“Once the (facility) reopens, Hudson no longer can use the [Colorado-Big Thompson Project water] dedicated for the prison to meet other water demands within Town,” it continues. “This drives the need for Hudson to immediately shift its approach to use other water resources to meet its water demands.”

Other concerns cited by town residents in the new complaint relate to a projected increase in 911 calls, a trend observed in other rural ICE detention centers run by GEO, and the risk of public health emergencies like the tuberculosis case state officials have been barred from investigating at GEO’s facility in Aurora.

“After hearing about deaths and disease outbreaks in other detention centers, including a tuberculosis outbreak at the GEO-operated facility in Aurora, Plaintiffs Homstad and Grosshans have also grown concerned about the public health risks posed by the Facility, which could spread to the community through Facility staff and visitors, and the strain on the Town’s limited emergency services infrastructure,” the complaint reads.

Despite months of residents raising concerns about the facility through public comment periods and other official channels, town officials have declined to formally explain their position, review the alleged violation, “adopt an official code revision, or issue a conditional use permit” for the facility, the suit alleges.

“Hudson has had every opportunity to sit down, answer questions, and follow the process laid out in its own code,” said David Seligman, executive director of Towards Justice, the progressive legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs. “Instead it has chosen silence, and now litigation.”

Immigration advocates and Colorado Democrats have been staunchly opposed to the Hudson facility’s potential use as an ICE detention center since last year. The Aurora facility, which has long been the target of criticism from activists over allegations of inhumane conditions and dehumanizing treatment, is Colorado’s only currently operational ICE detention center.

GEO seeks to intervene

In his second term, President Donald Trump has pledged to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” aiming to remove all of the estimated 12 million immigrants in the country without permanent legal status, regardless of how long they have been in the country, the legal status of their family members or whether they have criminal records.

Together with CoreCivic, another large private-prison company, The GEO Group is expected to be the prime beneficiary of a multibillion-dollar windfall for expanded immigration detention services authorized by Republicans’ 2025 spending and tax cut law. Last year, GEO chairman George Zoley spoke during an earnings call about the “attractive opportunity for investors” presented by “the unprecedented growth opportunities we anticipate will materialize over the balance of this year and next year.”

Attorneys for GEO moved to intervene in the case last month so that the company “can seek dismissal of this lawsuit and, if necessary, defend its substantial interest in performing its contracts with the property owner and ICE.”

The plaintiffs say their case only concerns the town of Hudson’s application of its zoning laws. They’re seeking a court order requiring town officials to comply with the “relevant procedures for amending the Land Development Code and/or granting or amending a conditional use permit.”

“This case concerns only the Town’s own authority and duties under the LDC — not the validity, meaning, or performance of any contract to which GEO is a party,” the plaintiffs in an August 31 filing said. “GEO’s efforts to intervene in this matter will do nothing other than needlessly complicate this litigation.”

text:
A coalition of advocacy groups and a Democratic-led city on Thursday filed a preemptive lawsuit seeking to block the Trump administration from deploying armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling sites ahead of November's midterm elections.

The lawsuit asks the federal district court in Washington, D.C., to declare unlawful any plans to have armed agents at polling places and to prohibit federal officers from carrying weapons near voting locations or other sites where votes are collected.

"The specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election," the lawsuit read. "It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal law enforcement if they choose to cast a ballot."

The lawsuit specifically named the Department of Homeland Security and ICE as defendants, as well as their respective leaders, Markwayne Mullin and David Venturella. It was filed by the liberal-leaning legal group Democracy Forward, on behalf of the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause, UnidosUS and the city of Denver.

The suit cited a provision of federal law that makes it a crime for officials to oversee or order the deployment of "any troops or armed men" to "any place where a general or special election is held," unless such a deployment is needed to repel "armed enemies of the United States."

Although some MAGA personalities, like Steve Bannon, have called on ICE to "surround the polls," Trump administration officials have denied concrete plans for such deployments, while at the same time not categorically ruling out the presence of agents at polling sites under some circumstances.

During a news conference in New York City earlier this month, DHS Secretary Mullin said that "ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places."

But Mullin said ICE could be at polling places if there's "a threat" to such sites or if agents are serving a warrant for someone they've "been actively tracking down."

"If we're serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be," Mullin said when pressed again on the issue.

ICE's deportation branch is mainly in charge of locating, arresting, detaining and deporting people who entered the U.S. illegally or otherwise violated federal immigration law. Its Homeland Security Investigations branch has historically focused on dismantling criminal activity with an international nexus, but has increasingly been assigned to help with immigration enforcement and investigations into alleged voter fraud.

“We will continue to fight to make sure that there are basic standards of human dignity met in anywhere that our taxpayer dollars are funding,” she said.

text:
Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador were in limbo Wednesday as a deadline neared for the Trump administration to decide if they should end, as they have for hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries.

The Temporary Protected Status designation expired Wednesday but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens. If the Department of Homeland Security takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days.

READ MORE: We may finally know what makes a country 'unsafe' for TPS deportations: a bromance with Trump

DHS said in a statement Wednesday that it will announce a decision on El Salvador "at the appropriate time" and that protections would remain in place until then.

About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of homeland security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits.

In Florida, an estimated 45,000 Salvadorans are at risk of losing the legal protections and work authorization they have relied on for years, Florida Immigrant Coalition Executive Director Tessa Petit said in a statement.

"These are Florida workers, parents, homeowners, business owners, students, neighbors, and community members who have spent decades putting down roots in the only country many of them have known as home," she said. "The Trump administration must immediately extend TPS for El Salvador and stop treating longtime members of our communities as disposable."

Petit also wants Congress to approve legislation that would create a permanent pathway to legal status for all TPS holders and others who have spent decades living, working, and contributing to the U.S.

“We have seen what happens when this administration strips communities of their protections: families are thrown into uncertainty, workers lose their livelihoods, and people who have spent decades building lives in America suddenly find themselves targeted for deportation," she said. "Salvadorans deserve permanent stability, dignity, and a pathway to citizenship.”

Trump administration has ended protections for more than a dozen countries

During President Donald Trump's second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. In addition to El Salvador, only people from three other countries remain protected with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon.

The Trump administration obtained a major victory in June when the Supreme Court ruled that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS.

Tom Homan, Trump's "border czar" who has advocated for ending TPS, said Tuesday that the decision rests with the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"If it expires, it's up to the secretary," Homan said when asked about TPS. "Temporary protected status means temporary. Let's face it, El Salvador is a much safer country than it's ever been now with a new president up there."

Congress created temporary protections in 1990

TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026.

El Salvador has been a Trump ally

Once one of the most violent places in the world, El Salvador has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador's travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders.

Bukele has been an ally of Trump's policy of mass deportations and El Salvador was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison also known as CECOT.

Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture, and disappearances in the Central American nation's prison system.

Trump received Bukele at the White House in April 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. In July 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington, the Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits.

Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of the country's gross domestic product, according to El Salvador's central bank.

This story has been corrected to show that TPS has ended for people from 13 countries during Trump's second term, not 14.

text:
The number of federal immigration detainees in Kentucky jails is growing dramatically, but the public knows less and less about them, including whether or not they have criminal records, according to new reports on federal efforts to deport more people.

Some information on U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainees in Kentucky jails is hard to find, a new report from the League of Women Voters of Kentucky says.

The League’s analysis found a few online rosters at Kentucky jails that house federal immigration detainees are unclear on the local crimes charged or status of the detainee. Three do not list people who are in ICE custody.

“Kentucky jails belong to us, the people of Kentucky, so we should know how immigrants are being treated,” wrote League President Jennifer Jackson in a letter about the report. “The people held there are human beings, so Kentuckians should insist on their human rights.”

The League, a group that has been tracking ICE data statewide for a few months, also said in the latest analysis a dozen jails across Kentucky are being paid to house ICE detainees and most do not have a criminal conviction; more than 60 jails in the state have voluntarily placed ICE holds on people arrested locally; most jails that provide ICE custody are overcrowded because of federal roles; and two jails and more than 50 law enforcement agencies have partnerships with ICE.

In November, about 12 local police agencies and three jails in Kentucky had partnerships with ICE under 287(g) agreements. Two bills were filed in the 2026 legislative session to direct Kentucky State Police or local law enforcement agencies to enter such ICE agreements, but they did not get floor votes.

According to data from Relevant Research, Kentucky jails are housing about 1,200 people for ICE as of July.

Last week, progressive think tank Kentucky Center for Economic Policy said in an analysis that arrests through the 287(g) agreements have grown in recent months. In November 2025, there was one arrest in Kentucky through the agreement program. In July 2026, there were 70.

After its report, the League of Women Voters sent letters to leaders in counties with the greatest participation in ICE detention: Boone, Bourbon, Campbell, Christian, Daviess, Fayette, Grayson, Hopkins, Jefferson, Kenton, Laurel, Oldham and Woodford. Among the group’s requests were providing more fully transparent inmate lists and evidence about the treatment of detainees.

The full analysis said jails in Bourbon, Boone, Grayson, Hopkins, Laurel and Oldham counties include ICE detainees in their roster listings. Those people can be identified by an immigration charge listed or that the arresting officer or agency is listed as ICE, Immigration or the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The League said Campbell, Christian and Kenton counties do not list people there in ICE custody. Daviess County “appears to include people in ICE custody in its public roster, but not in a way that makes that status clear, as it may include people arrested by other federal agents, like U.S. Marshals. Fayette and Woodford counties’ “approaches are unclear to the League.”

Matt Mudd, a spokesperson for Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg, said Louisville Metro Department of Corrections “does not house individuals who are in ICE custody,” but it does honor detainer requests from ICE to hold people 48 hours beyond their scheduled release for local offenses. The American Civil Liberties Union of Kentucky criticized the practice in August, saying it reviewed data that showed a nearly 300% increase in the average number of monthly detainer requests since the city’s policy change last year. Mudd said the cost for the holds “is negligible, and LMDC has not increased its budget to accommodate these holds.”

“To protect individual information, names of those subject to an ICE detainer are not released. Furthermore, information related to immigration detainers is subject to confidentiality requirements of federal law. The individual’s attorney may request additional information in person with proper identification while in person at LMDC,” Mudd added. “However, all local charges for individuals in custody at LMDC are available on a searchable public website that shows all allowable information.”

Mudd also referred to the state law governing conditions for jails, such as the requirement to provide inmates three nutritious meals a day to inmates and health and mental health evaluations and treatment.

ICE detention in Kentucky has made headlines in recent months. U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, a Democrat who represents Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, joined two of his House colleagues to visit the Campbell County jail in July to review conditions for ICE detainees there.

“Trump and Republicans in Congress gave ICE billions in taxpayer money to target and terrorize immigrants in our communities,” McGarvey said in a Wednesday statement to the Kentucky Lantern. “At a bare minimum, we as taxpayers deserve transparency about where our neighbors are being taken and how they’re being treated.”

McGarvey joined family members of a Louisville woman, Sarafinah Bukirwa, who was detained by ICE in calling for better medical care for her while she was in the Grayson County Detention Center in July. Bukirwa, who has sickle cell anemia, was not getting all of her medications, her brother said, but the jailer denied the claim. Bukirwa was later released in August by a federal judge and after her family paid her bond.

text:
Washington, D.C. — The largest and oldest Latino civil rights membership organization in the United States, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), joined by Common Cause, a voting rights organization with nearly one million members, UnidosUS, the nation’s largest Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization with more than 300 affiliates nationwide, and the city and county of Denver, Colorado, filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s policy of authorizing armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to enter polling places to conduct immigration enforcement operations during the 2026 midterm elections.

The lawsuit challenges a policy confirmed and clarified by U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin on September 1, when he said that ICE officers could enter polling places to serve warrants or conduct other immigration and customs enforcement activity. The suit explains that the policy violates, among other laws, a federal law that has prohibited anyone from sending armed federal personnel to polling places for more than 150 years, and that the presence of armed officers is intimidating and threatening.

The lawsuit comes as early voting is set to begin in several states later this month and just weeks before Americans across the country cast their ballots in the November 3 midterm elections.

Congress first enacted the prohibition against armed federal personnel at polling places in the final months of the Civil War to protect free and fair elections from federal interference. Under federal law, armed federal personnel may not be ordered, brought, kept, or maintained at a place where an election is being held except when necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.

The complaint alleges that the administration’s new policy directly defies that prohibition by authorizing armed ICE officers to enter polling locations for ordinary immigration enforcement, including serving warrants and detaining people suspected of being unlawfully present in the United States. It also explains that the new policy violates the federal prohibition on arbitrary and capricious government action.

“The right to vote is foundational to our democracy and yet this administration continues in its endless attempts to weaken the very institutions it is entrusted to protect,” said Juan Proaño, CEO of LULAC. “The outcomes of elections define the future for all of us, and in America, voters should be able to cast their ballots without fear of intimidation by armed ICE officers at polling places. We are proud to join this litigation and fight to protect fundamental American freedom.”

“Putting armed officers in polling places is a tactic used by dictators, but we won’t be scared out of exercising our rights,” said Common Cause President & CEO Virginia Kase Solomón. “No American should ever have to walk past armed federal law enforcement just to cast a ballot, yet this administration has adopted a policy that allows exactly that. Everyday Americans refuse to be silenced by the administration’s continuous efforts to meddle with our elections. From taking legal action to stop this policy to leading the nation’s largest nonpartisan Election Protection program, Common Cause is fighting alongside voters to keep our elections free, fair, and accessible.”

“Sending armed ICE officers to polling places is not immigration enforcement — it is voter suppression, plain and simple,” said UnidosUS President & CEO Janet Murguía. “All Americans — including Latino voters — have a constitutional right to cast their ballot without fear of interrogation, detention, or family separation. This case is about protecting voters, preserving confidence in our elections, and ensuring that every eligible voter can participate free from intimidation.”

“The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American,” said Denver Mayor Mike Johnston. “Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

text:
BURLINGTON — U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Congresswoman Lori Trahan conducted an unannounced visit to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Burlington Tuesday, their first surprise visit since ICE was compelled in court to allow such visits earlier this year.

In a joint statement released Wednesday, Trahan and Warren said they exercised their “constitutional responsibilities to conduct oversight” when they made the visit.

“Immigration attorneys and community advocates have shared deeply worrisome testimonies with our offices of individuals being detained by ICE for multiple days without access to adequate food, medical care, or sleeping conditions,” said the two members of Congress. “During the hour-long inspection of the Burlington facility, we walked through every part of the area in which people are detained. We witnessed over two dozen individuals held for processing, questioned ICE regarding our constituents’ concerns, and pressed for more humane treatment of those in custody.”

They said they would “continue showing up and fighting for transparency, decency, and accountability.”

The two join the ranks of other members of the Massachusetts congressional delegation to conduct a surprise visit to the facility since a court ruled earlier this year that ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, cannot prevent lawmakers from inspecting their facilities even without the visit being prearranged.

U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton made a similar visit last month, though he claimed to have been prevented from going beyond the facility’s lobby for about 30 minutes while his staff observed multiple vans leaving the property. Moulton had conducted an unannounced visit last year as well, before DHS began barring lawmakers from making surprise inspections. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey and U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern have made similar visits to the building this year.

The string of inspections and prearranged tours by lawmakers at the Burlington ICE building stems from reports of poor conditions for immigrant detainees inside the building, which has been a home to ICE operations since 2007. After President Donald Trump returned to office last year, the building became a focal point in the discourse over his immigration crackdown due to it being where most detained immigrants are brought first when they are arrested by ICE in Massachusetts.

It has also turned into the focus of local protests against ICE, with multiple groups holding weekly demonstrations going back to spring 2025 when the initial reports about the conditions inside began to emerge.

Those groups include Bearing Witness, which began protesting every Wednesday at the facility that April, and Justice 4 All Thursdays at ICE, which began its weekly demonstrations last September.

Both groups gathered at their usual spot on a grassy area across from the building’s entrance Wednesday for what they called “Hold ICE in Contempt Day,” which organizers said was aimed at urging judges in Massachusetts to “to hold ICE accountable for violations of court orders.”

Jared Berezin, one of the organizers of the Bearing Witness protests, and Todd Palmer, who started Justice 4 All Thursdays, stood together at the demonstration Wednesday and listed a number of incidents in American history where court orders were used against activists.

“When a judge orders ICE officials not to transfer an individual out of Massachusetts, but ICE defies that order and flies them out of [Hanscom Air Force Base] no one is held in contempt,” said Berezin. “When a judge orders ICE to produce a detainee’s arrest warrant and ICE refuses, no one is held in contempt. When a judge orders ICE to release someone but ICE officials keep them locked up anyway, no one is held in contempt. If any of us were to defy an order from a judge we would be fined and jailed, yet judges in Massachusetts and across the country treat ICE officials as if they are exempt from judicial authority.”

Palmer said he and Berezin are “calling for accountability in the courts.”

“We need our federal judges in Massachusetts and across this country to use their powers of contempt. We are not calling for judicial activism, we are calling for judicial action,” said Palmer.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed to no longer count immigrants without green cards in the 2030 census or ask about race and ethnicity, part of an overhaul that would redefine who counts as a U.S. resident in the eyes of the federal government.

The sweeping measures would upend a process that helps determine the allotment of congressional seats, billions of dollars in federal funding and policies to address systemic disparities.

The proposed regulation, published online on Wednesday, would not count noncitizens without green cards in the 2030 census, a significant departure from the process stipulated by the Constitution to occur every 10 years. Historically, the census has asked Americans about their race and ethnicity and counted all U.S. residents regardless of their immigration status.

The overhaul also would bar the U.S. census from asking Americans about their sexual orientation.

While the proposal is likely to face legal challenges, the changes would not only remove immigrants who lack legal status from the official population count used to determine congressional seats, but also immigrants who are in the United States legally and have yet to secure green cards or citizenship. As a result, areas with more immigrants, which tend to vote Democratic, could lose representation and federal funding.

The proposed overhaul, as well as removing questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation from the census, could have major implications for collecting the federal data used to inform antidiscrimination policies and civil rights protections.

“If we don’t have the data in order to see that there’s problems, then we’re sticking our heads in the sand,” said Kimball W. Brace, the president of Election Data Services, an organization working with Democratic and Republican local governments on census and election issues. “We won’t see it. We won’t get a feel for what’s happened.”

An overhaul of the census count would face significant hurdles. The 14th Amendment calls for “counting the whole number of persons in each state,” rather than just citizens. And the rule would take effect only after the 2028 presidential election, meaning a new administration could come in and reverse the changes. Under the U.S. Constitution, Congress is tasked with carrying out the census; however, it has delegated decisions on the census to the Commerce Department.

But some researchers said Trump’s decision to try to resurrect his first-term effort to reshape the census could create a chilling effect and reduce participation.

As part of the proposal released Wednesday, the administration said it was considering including a question in the census about the immigration status of participants, something civil rights groups have warned would deter immigrants with and without legal status from filling out the form out of fear of government retaliation.

“The Trump administration is trying to omit pieces of the population that they don’t feel are real Americans,” said William H. Frey, a demographer at the Brookings Institution. “And in many ways, pulling back some of the trends and important policies that came into effect since the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s.”
