text:
U.S. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Phoenix, conducted a surprise oversight visit of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Phoenix on Wednesday after reporting last week by the Arizona Mirror showed that detainees are staying longer and in larger numbers than in previous years.

Ansari cited the Mirror’s reporting for prompting her to conduct the visit, the 13th time she has visited ICE detention and temporary hold facilities to provide congressional oversight.

The ICE facility Ansari visited Wednesday is in a midtown Phoenix office building that is home to the Arizona headquarters for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE. It sits next door to the Arizona Attorney General’s Office and has been the subject of weekly protests that began last summer, some of which led to clashes between protesters and ICE officers.

The Phoenix ICE District Office, while being the primary base of operations for ICE in the Grand Canyon State, also houses a temporary hold facility. It features 10 holding cells that can hold upwards of 150 people. The facility has no beds, no on-site medical services, limited access to food and no shower that is accessible to detainees. According to ICE, it is meant to house people for no more than 12 hours.

But as ICE has implemented President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda and immigration agents have sought to meet high quotas for arresting immigrants, detention sites have become more crowded and short-term facilities are being used for longer than intended.

As reporters waited outside for Ansari to brief them on what she saw inside, multiple people could be seen going in and out of the building for immigration appointments with ICE. Workers were also replacing windows that had been shot at in July.

“I am very concerned about medical access, given what severe medical neglect we have seen at the detention centers, as well as the holding facility in Mesa,” Ansari said in an interview with the Mirror prior to the visit.

Records obtained by the Mirror found that the Phoenix Fire Department responded to the facility 11 times between December 2025 and March 2026. Almost all of those calls resulted in a detainee being sent to a local hospital on a “Code 3” response, meaning emergency services drove with their lights and sirens on to the hospital.

“I’m really alarmed that we know people have been held here for longer than they should have and over capacity, it is completely unacceptable,” Ansari told the Mirror in an exclusive interview, referencing the Mirror’s reporting which found the average length of time detainees have been staying at the facility has gone from between eight and 10 hours to 20 hours.

When Ansari visited the facility Wednesday, it housed 29 detainees, she said.

Ansari said ICE officials had told her that a waiver issued by ICE last year removing the 12-hour holding cell limit was “lifted” in July. That waiver was vacated in federal court in June as “arbitrary and capricious” because it conflicted with ICE’s own detention standards.

She told reporters that an ICE official told her that the agency is “trying to be more responsive” to inquiries from members of Congress on conditions and are committed to not holding detainees longer than 12 hours.

ICE itself called the Mirror’s reporting on its own publicly released data “FALSE,” adding that the facility does not hold people for longer than 12 hours, despite the data showing otherwise.

Ansari was unable to speak to detainees at the facility due to a new ICE policy that bars them from doing so without prior approval from the agency.

“Every time we do an oversight visit, we are informed of a new rule,” she said.

Ansari added that oversight visits like this will continue to be important, even if the agency puts a best foot forward to members of Congress.

“I think that constant oversight is needed,” she told reporters.

When speaking with the Mirror, Ansari said she hopes her Republican colleagues also perform their oversight duties, and she warned about the possible sanitized tours that the agency provides to members of Congress. ICE previously moved detainees prior to visits.

“I absolutely urge my Republican colleagues to conduct an oversight visit,” Ansari said. “I think it is really important but what I think is more important than going is getting an authentic sense of what is going on and not accepting a standard tour by the staff members of these facilities but actually talking with detainees.”

title: Womble v. Patel | Constitutional Accountability Center
description:
A North Carolina prison denied Edward Womble, a prisoner with a hearing disability, a hearing-aid battery (and thus a functional hearing aid) for nine months.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that Title II’s nondiscrimination mandate applies to all public entities, including state prisons.
First, there is no textual carveout that excludes prison medical care from Title II’s broad prohibition on disability discrimination.
Finally, the district court erred in invoking a line of cases stemming from a 1996 Seventh Circuit decision, Bryant v. Madigan, which first posited an atextual, “judge-made” carveout for prison medical care.
That carveout is plainly at odds with Title II’s broad statutory ban on discrimination in any public “service, program, or activity.”
text:
A North Carolina prison denied Edward Womble, a prisoner with a hearing disability, a hearing-aid battery (and thus a functional hearing aid) for nine months. During that time, he was excluded from receiving aural overhead announcements, including calls for meals and religious and medical events, because of his disability.

Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) bars discrimination by public entities, providing that “no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded from participation in or be denied the benefits of the services, programs, or activities of a public entity, or be subjected to discrimination by any such entity.” That bar creates an affirmative obligation on public entities to provide accommodations that allow people with disabilities to meaningfully access public services, programs, and activities. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that Title II’s nondiscrimination mandate applies to all public entities, including state prisons. And the statutory text is clear: medical care is a service under Tite II.

Nonetheless, the district court below dismissed Womble’s failure-to-accommodate ADA claim because, it said, that claim was actually challenging inadequate medical treatment. Womble appealed, and in September 2026, CAC filed an amicus brief in the Fourth Circuit supporting his claim. Our brief makes three principal points.

First, there is no textual carveout that excludes prison medical care from Title II’s broad prohibition on disability discrimination. Second, even if there were such a carveout, Womble’s request for a hearing-aid battery was an intervention to accommodate his hearing disability under Title II (and thus restore his access to overhead announcements), not medical treatment at all. Finally, the district court erred in invoking a line of cases stemming from a 1996 Seventh Circuit decision, Bryant v. Madigan, which first posited an atextual, “judge-made” carveout for prison medical care. That carveout is plainly at odds with Title II’s broad statutory ban on discrimination in any public “service, program, or activity.”

text:
Popular Roadless Rule conservation measure protects 44 million acres of U.S. Forest Service lands from destructive and expensive roadbuilding and logging and supports outdoor recreation

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) joined a bipartisan coalition of 164 Members of Congress led by Representative Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.-06) and Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) in urging the Trump Administration to abandon its proposal to rescind the Roadless Rule, a guardrail protecting 44 million acres of National Forest System lands.

In a letter to the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Forest Service, the lawmakers criticized the lack of meaningful public engagement, calling for the Department to extend the comment period, hold in-person public meetings, and conduct full Tribal consultation. The lawmakers also demanded the Trump Administration halt its rescission effort and instead focus on successful implementation of this bedrock policy.

“Since its adoption in 2001, the Roadless Rule has served as a cornerstone of public lands conservation, now protecting approximately 44 million acres of National Forest System lands across 37 states,” wrote the lawmakers. “These areas provide clean drinking water, critical wildlife habitat, carbon storage, and world-class recreation opportunities. Iconic landscapes such as the Tongass National Forest in Alaska, the Gila National Forest in New Mexico, and the George Washington National Forest in Virginia exemplify the ecological, cultural, and economic importance of these lands.”

“By avoiding the construction and maintenance of new roads, the rule saves taxpayers billions of dollars,” they continued. “The Forest Service already faces a road maintenance backlog of nearly $6 billion across its existing system. Expanding road networks into remote and often economically unviable areas would only increase these costs.”

“After 25 years of successful implementation, the conclusion is clear: the Roadless Rule is effective, widely supported, and essential to responsible forest management. Rescinding it would undermine decades of progress and impose unnecessary environmental and fiscal costs,” they concluded.

The full text of the letter can be found here.

Senator Cortez Masto has consistently fought to protect Nevada’s treasured outdoor spaces. She successfully defeated a proposed mass public lands sell off in the One Big Beautiful Bill and opposed Steve Pearce for Director of the Bureau of Land Management because of his decades-long record opposing public lands. The Senator is a champion of conservation efforts in the Lake Tahoe Basin. She has introduced legislation to permanently codify fee-free days of public service of federal lands.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration wants to overhaul the U.S. census to exclude noncitizens who don’t have a green card from the country’s next population count in 2030, according to a Wednesday notice in the Federal Register.

The document, which will officially be published Thursday, could mean major changes for how millions in federal funding is allocated to states, as well as affect the population numbers for determining the number of U.S. House members in each state. The House is made up of 435 lawmakers apportioned among congressional districts in the 50 states.

The move is likely to face legal challenges, as the changes run counter to the U.S. Constitution’s 14th Amendment that directs representatives in Congress to be appointed based on the “whole number of persons in each State,” excluding Native Americans “not taxed.”

The amendment language does not specify immigration status. The states handled immigration enforcement until the federal government took over in 1882 with the passage of the Chinese Exclusion Act.

The proposed changes would exclude any noncitizens who do not have lawful permanent residence, or a green card, which could result in millions being excluded from the population count. That would include immigrants in the country without legal authorization, those with some form of temporary legal status, refugees and asylum seekers.

The unauthorized immigrant population — that includes noncitizens who have some form of limited legal status — has grown to more than 15.8 million since mid-2024.

The Trump administration argues that noncitizens who are not green card holders should be kept out of the census count because “they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States,” according to the document.

The proposal also calls for removing several questions pertaining to sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, and suggests adding a question relating to citizenship, which President Donald Trump has pushed to include since his first term. But the Supreme Court in 2019 kept the question off the 2020 census.

The Trump administration wants those demographic questions removed from the census because the survey “should be colorblind and should not be distorted in any way by questions about immaterial personal characteristics, such as race,” the proposal says.

The census has collected information about race and ethnicity since 1790, the first survey count in the U.S.

text:
A massive immigration operation is happening in Memphis. It’s been underway for just under a year now—hundreds of arrests, streets filled with officers. But most people I talk with have never heard of it. Why?

As I previously documented for this magazine, the occupation of one of America’s largest majority-Black cities began last September: ICE arrived in Memphis along with more than a dozen local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. Today, more than 1,200 officers are still stationed there as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, according to a spokesperson from the US Marshals Service.

You might not have heard about this just because there’s a lot going on (gestures everywhere). Also, Tennessee’s Republican governor supports the task force, and the Trump administration has framed it as a crime-fighting operation rather than an immigration operation, so it’s gotten less coverage than, say, ICE’s actions in Minneapolis. But there’s another reason why this surge hasn’t gotten much attention: It’s harder to record ICE in Tennessee than it is in many states.

Just ask Hunter Demster, who runs a soup kitchen and has spent the last year driving around Memphis with his phone, trying to document immigration arrests so he can post the videos online. With help from the ACLU, he and other activists sued the task force in May for allegedly violating their First Amendment rights to record by, among other measures, invoking Tennessee’s Halo Law.

Passed last year, the Halo Law makes it a crime for someone to come within 25 feet of an officer after they’ve been warned to step away. Demster’s lawsuit accuses agents of using the statute inappropriately. Now he’s sharing evidence to show what he means.

In a video published this week, you can watch as Demster records a group of federal officers standing on the side of the road. He’s there for 20 minutes before they pull a man out of a ditch to make an arrest. Demster tries to capture the moment, taking care to remain 25 feet away, according to his court declaration.

But the officers aren’t satisfied—they want him back even farther. “I am filming, I am not impeding, I am not doing anything!” Demster yells as an officer continues walking toward him and away from the scene, forcing him so far back that he can no longer see or hear what’s happening. Eventually, Demster, who curses in frustration, refuses to retreat any more and finds himself tackled and handcuffed.

This second video, shot from across the street, shows another view of the encounter.

Since the task force began last year, officers have invoked the Halo Law against Demster dozens of times, according to the lawsuit. Other community members have similar stories. “This lawsuit is laying out partially why you aren’t hearing as much from Memphis,” Demster told me a few months ago. “There’s an intention to operate in the shadows.”

text:
The nation's election system is in a messy legal limbo, with fights over mail-in voting, electoral maps and voter records still locked in court.

Why it matters: Americans are in the eye of the storm, with over half saying they don't think the 2026 midterms will be conducted fairly or are unsure, according to a new poll.

President Trump insists his push to reform America's elections will protect the sanctity of votes. But the administration's overhaul has left voters and states in a complicated web of litigation — with the first midterm ballots already sent out.

"Any confusion was caused by radical Democrats' litigation to stop these commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the SAVE America Act."

Driving the news: Just 45% think the midterms will be conducted fairly, a sentiment shared by 37% of independents and 48% of both Democrats and Republicans, according to a YouGov survey conducted Sept. 4-8.

It comes as Trump has spent years spreading unproven claims of widespread voter fraud, fueling a government crackdown that critics say oversteps his power.

That's left the president's election agenda in the hands of the federal judiciary.

Case in point: The administration asked the Supreme Court Tuesday to clear its modified SAVE system (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements), an online tool it integrated with Social Security data and expanded to conduct bulk searches to verify voters' immigration status.

Voting rights groups sued over what they described as an overhaul of the system, which was previously used to check eligibility for benefits, to "create comprehensive databases of American citizens."

District Court Judge Sparkle Sooknanan blocked the plan, saying government agencies had "haphazardly" pulled together "unreliable" data that states were using to "actively" remove citizens from voter rolls.

"SAVE, if it is allowed to be utilized for the purposes the administration is trying to utilize it for, will inevitably falsely flag voters as being ineligible," says Jared Davidson, counsel at Protect Democracy.

But Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices Tuesday to toss the "indefensible order" that he said threatens election integrity.

Zoom out: That was the second time in just three days that the Trump administration turned to the Supreme Court on its election-related agenda.

On Sunday, the administration made yet another appeal to the justices to allow its mail-in voting policy changes to go into effect, adding to a complicated series of injunctions and appeals over the plan.

States sued over the rule, saying it would force them to "immediately redesign" ballot envelopes and "develop new systems at breakneck speed."

"If you look at what they're trying to do in terms of restrictions on mailing outbound absentee or mail-in ballots; those are already out the door, and others are heading out the door every day," says Dan Lenz, senior legal counsel for strategic litigation at the Campaign Legal Center.

Plus, the redistricting war over the country's congressional maps flared up again in Missouri this week.

The state's election chief faces contempt proceedings for telling officials to use a redrawn map—one that the state supreme court blocked, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in, and then revived by another federal judge.

What they're saying: "The chaos is the point," Davidson says.

He tells Axios, "implementation isn't even necessarily the end game for the Trump administration here."

Lenz echoes him, arguing that muddying the waters "allows you to then contest election outcomes you don't like after the fact."

text:
The ACLU of Connecticut filed a lawsuit Wednesday challenging Hartford Immigration Court's policy of withholding records related to individual cases from the public.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for Connecticut, argues that records like case numbers, case names and in absentia removal orders - which the immigration court issues when a person fails to appear for their hearing date - should be open to the public under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which the lawsuit says has traditionally granted access to judicial records.

"The First Amendment guarantees that we the people have access to documents used to adjudicate cases like these," Dan Barrett, the ACLU of Connecticut's legal director, said in a statement. "The Immigration Court's judgments and dockets are no more secret than those of the Connecticut Superior Court two blocks across town."

A spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review said the office and the Department of Justice "declines to comment on litigation-related matters."

Unlike federal district and circuit courts and the U.S. Supreme Court, immigration courts are part of the U.S. Department of Justice. That means they fall under the Executive Branch, not the independent judiciary. In immigration court, unlike in most state and federal courts, case records are not accessible to the public. Some hearings are open, but some of the most consequential happen behind closed doors. And while the court itself records every hearing, even recordings of public hearings are considered confidential.

Last year, CT Insider filed a request under the federal Freedom of Information Act for recordings of Hartford immigration judges speaking during public hearings a reporter had attended in person. Those recordings did not identify individual defendants or include any details of individual cases. EOIR denied that request, citing an exemption to the public records law for records that "constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of the personal privacy of third parties."

EOIR also declined to tell CT Insider last year what immigration judges were hearing cases in Hartford. And while Hartford Immigration Court posts a daily list of people who have cases before in its lobby, EOIR has refused to provide information to CT Insider about upcoming hearings upon request.

"EOIR does not provide copies of immigration court records, including the posted daily docket," spokesperson Kathryn Mattingly said in a statement last October. "Immigration courts are created by statute and regulation and are not Constitutional courts of public record."

The new lawsuit comes after the ACLU of Connecticut sent a letter in July to Assistant Chief Immigration Judge Angela Munson, who oversees the Hartford Immigration Court, requesting docket numbers, case captions, the names of defendants and in absentia removal orders for May, June and July 2026, according to the complaint filed in federal court Wednesday. The ACLU made that request under the First Amendment, not under FOIA, it said. The ACLU followed up on that request via email in August, according to the complaint, which says Munson ignored those requests.

The suit names Munson and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as defendants. It asks the federal district court to order Hartford Immigration Court to produce the records and enjoin it from denying future requests.

The ACLU of Connecticut is being represented in the case by Alexa Talin Millinger of Hinckley Allen Snyder LLP, court records show. The case had not yet been assigned to a judge as of press time, nor have the defendants responded or have any hearing dates been set.

Wednesday's lawsuit marks the second time Hartford Immigration Court has come in for criticism this week. U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal sat in on about an hour of hearings in court Thursday, after which he held a press conference during which he accused the court of "intentional injustice."

More than 250 people were scheduled for hearings before one of three judges in the court on Tuesday, according to a list posted in its lobby. The sheer volume is a dramatic change from this time last year, when CT Insider observed between 20 and 40 cases at such a hearing. These new "mega master hearings," as they're called, along with staff turnover and the termination or retirement of judges, have dramatically remade the court since CT Insider spent a week there last year documenting its operations.

Blumenthal vowed Tuesday to return to the immigration court as part of what he called an "investigation" into its operations.

"I'm going to continue this investigation more aggressively and completely, because the warning signs of injustice are unmistakable," the Democratic senator said.

text:
Author: Meesha Falik

September 09, 2026

Anti-immigrant activity reached record highs at the beginning of 2025 in the United States, with a 75% increase in the number of people held in ICE detention, including a 2450% increase in the detention of people with no criminal records by early 2026. . The UK also recorded 251 anti-immigrant related events in 2025 alone. “March for Australia” recorded a wave of anti-immigrant protests across the country in late 2025 and early 2026. Slogans expressed discontent among protestors regarding a national identity they believed to be under threat from “anti-Australian” actors. Most recently, anti-immigration protests swept through Belfast following a knife attack, resulting in an assault on immigrant communities, including within religious spaces. In the previous year, England experienced a wave of anti-immigration protests similar to Australia, the United States, and other Western countries that have historically served as primary migrant destinations.

Underlying all of these movements is a collective fear that national values are being eroded by migrant populations diversity, and the belief that immigrants are taking away not only jobs and social resources, but the very facet of national identity. It is, therefore, important to hold these claims and fears to account, to understand what role migrants really play in host countries.

Migration: Fact-Checked

By the end of 2024, 3.7% of the world’s population resided in countries different from their country of origin. The percentage of global international migrants has not increased significantly since 2020, and the share of female migrants also remains relatively stable at 48% up to 2024. Up to 41.6 million individuals were reported as refugees by the end of 2025, the large majority originating from 6 war-affected countries.

Europe and North America continue to host nearly 51% of the world’s immigrant population, being desirable destinations due to the high quality of life and better infrastructure. The United States, in particular, bears nearly 17.2% of the global migrant population. First-generation migrants account for a significantly lower percentage, followed by Germany, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, and France. Interestingly, the largest share of global international migrants also comes from Europe and North America. They account for 21.6% of the global migrant population, followed by Central and Southern Asia (17.7%), and Latin America and the Caribbean (15.9%).

Migrant workers account for 4.7% of the total global population, with about 168 million migrant workers worldwide.. Remittances, money sent back to relatives in countries of origin by migrant workers, amounted to 905 billion USD in 2024, a substantial increase of 4.5% since 2023. The United Nations estimates that remittances influence the lives of one in seven people globally. This promotes sustainable development, and may, in certain cases, supplement or entirely replace foreign aid, by alleviating poverty through improved per capita income, improving the standard of living, and contributing to growth and debt stability in the receiving country, as well as fostering greater investment in the education and health sectors. While remittances alone cannot promote sustainable development in the long-run as they are meant for private consumption rather than structural investment, and carry limited positive effect without supporting economic policies, their contributing power cannot be ignored. Even then, concern among host countries highlights fears of bearing migrant costs, while their earnings are “drained out” of the country. Experts, however, suggest that only 15% of a migrant’s income leaves the host country as remittance. The remaining is reinvested into the host economy, and can help countries achieve up to 7 of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which aim to attain positive health, education and equality outcomes globally, including reduced poverty and hunger, improved well-being, sanitation, education, and economic growth, and reduced inequalities. Migrants make significant economic contributions to this end, for example, in the form of nearly $100 billion in tax revenue generated from undocumented migrants alone in 2022 in the United States.

A Two-Way Street

Research indicates that immigrant inflow may lead to positive labour market outcomes, including an increase in employment and reduced long-term unemployment. Most significantly, migration has been shown to lead to increases in per capita GDP in the long run. Given the often higher immigration education requirements regarding degrees obtained and experiences, host countries often enjoy an improved educational background of their labour force when migrant backgrounds are included. Since 2017, the education profile of migrants, both foreign born and EU-born, has increased steadily, with university graduates accounting for 32.1% and 35.2% of migrants respectively in 2025, closing the gap between 36.8% of native-born EU graduates in 2025. Similarly, in a 2022 survey, 35% of immigrant adults held college degrees, on par with 36% of US-born adults.

These statistics are relevant across contexts. European labour markets face significant challenges in the coming years due to an ageing population, with a consistent increase in median age across the continent since 2015. In the United States, the net labour force growth has been almost entirely driven by immigrant inflows and foreign-born workers since 2008, with no distinction between skill levels or legal status. For lower skilled and undocumented immigrants, their major economic contribution is still significant and comes in the form of taxes , which then supports critical social services for all American citizens, including social security and Medicaid. ageing populations through social security benefits, with migrants in some cases costing less than native-borns, and making net positive contributions to social security (paying more in taxes than they receive in benefits).

Assimilation: Systems and Theories

Sociological research has long attempted to establish the theoretical basis for the process of and perceived need for assimilation among migrant communities in host countries. These range from highlighting the necessity and benefits of integration for migrant success in host communities, to understanding how migrant diversity, including identities and culture, may be lost in the process, and what that may mean for host cultures.

Classic Assimilation Theory

In the 1920s, the Chicago School of Sociology popularized what is also known as the straight-line assimilation theory. It categorized the assimilation process as a unidirectional adoption of host culture, a process considered necessary to maintain social cohesion and allow for the upward mobility of migrant communities. The theory, originally built on the American model of integration by European settlers, sees immigrants adopting the local culture over time, suggesting the longer an immigrant has been part of the culture, the more similar to their host country’s culture they will become.

Racial Ethnic Disadvantage Model

The model highlights what may be considered a significant limitation of classical assimilation. This theory posits that even with language acquisition and cultural knowledge, assimilation may not occur. Institutional barriers in accessing work or educational opportunities may prevent or significantly prolong this process, especially as these social barriers, combined with prevalent social stigmas become more obvious to the second or third migrant generations. First-generation migrants often fail to perceive these obstacles, as they often face far more difficulty in accessing resources in their home countries. The resulting sociocultural consequences of this exclusion may lead to racial/ethnic (re)emergence, preventing assimilation from occurring.

Segmented Assimilation

Noting assimilation processes that prolong into several migrant generations, theorists concluded that the integration process may not always be as straightforward as the classical theory suggests. Instead, structural barriers, such as poor educational opportunities and lack of access to employment and other social resources, may stagnate the assimilation process or may even reverse the process. Segmented assimilation may occur when some members of disadvantaged groups outright reject assimilation, opting rather for oppositional membership and engaging in behaviors incompatible with the host culture. Others may choose a path of selective assimilation, imbibing many elements of the host culture, while retaining traditional values.

Measuring Assimilation

Immigration and assimilation are both complex topics, and cannot necessarily be boxed by simple economic or social indicators. However, they do paint an indicative picture of the role migrants play in host societies.

Economic assimilation

Measured in terms of earnings and earnings gap reduction between migrants and native-born citizens, economic assimilation attempts to map migrant income as an indicator of successful integration. Measured in the context of the number of years since migration, accelerated assimilation is observed in migrants with higher levels of education, with improving earning trajectories over 10 and 20-year periods. Earning differences are lowest when compared between migrant and native groups of the same ethnoracial identity. Some research suggests that permanent migrants (compared to migrants who leave host countries within 10 years) may reach the same earning potential as those who are native-born within 10 years of migration.

Sociocultural assimilation

Social migrant assimilation is defined by migrant participation in society, measured through socialisation, civic participation, and sense of belonging. Analysis across various regional contexts shows that long-term migrants integrate better into host society, converging with local standards, compared to shorter-term migrants who tend to socialize less. Additionally, educational background tends to predict a greater sense of belonging with the broader community rather than close social circles. When measured in terms of satisfaction, language proficiency, and ethnic enclave, sociocultural assimilation is associated with higher employment and wage rates for migrants, as well as job satisfaction and security. Social assimilation, therefore, may predict economic success for migrants, particularly during periods of economic growth.

Identity assimilation

In a similar vein, identifying with the host country and culture is often regarded as one of the strongest predictors of assimilation. Following the classical assimilation theory, researchers find that identification with the host country only increases with subsequent generations, and is strongly measured as early as the second generation. Concurrent with identity, immigrants’ civic participation is also strongly influenced by the host culture, and most migrants tend to respond positively to integration efforts in host cultures.

It is important to note that some of the most significant barriers to integration and assimilation come from ethnic and racial differences between migrant and host communities, as discrimination from native citizens’ is highlighted as the single greatest barrier faced by migrants, as well as their disadvantaged backgrounds, resulting in fewer educational or employment opportunities. However, when given the same resources and opportunities, migrants offer significant support to their host communities in various contexts.

Migrant Contributions

With assimilation, migrants make increasing contributions to their host society. High-income countries in particular reap higher rewards from inward migration.

Sociocultural Contributions

Diversity of language, cuisine, art, and sports is often considered a transcendence of ethnic and racial differences that may otherwise divide local and migrant populations.

Civic contributions

Depending on the political framework of host countries, migrants may actively participate in host societies through community, state, or federal political participation and volunteer work. 16% of the American members of Congress are first- or second-generation migrants. Most significantly, where cohesive migrant integration policies exist, improved tolerance, lower xenophobia, and greater pro-democratic governance are reinforced.

Economic contributions

Migrants tend to belong to more innovative and entrepreneurial sectors, with higher contributions to start-ups and investment in host countries, as well as taxes. A 1% increase in migrant inflow is estimated to increase native employment by 0.2%. In the United States alone, over the last 30 years, immigrants have produced roughly $100,000 more in taxes per capita than the average native citizen. Further research suggests that migrant inflows boost aggregate income over the long-run, with increasing employment ratios, labour productivity, and capital accumulation.

The Verdict

The surge in anti-immigrant sentiment across Western nations in recent years highlights a critical disconnect between political narrative and empirical reality. A deeper analysis of the impact migrants have on their host communities reveals a more nuanced picture than often believed.

Far from being a one-sided burden, migration functions as a "two-way street" that yields significant economic and social benefits to receiving and sending countries, communities, and the migrants themselves. However, to effectively address the anxieties underlying current anti-immigrant movements, public discourse must address migration as a complex but largely beneficial exchange. This will help reconcile the tension between preserving national identity and embracing the realities of a globalized world. Ultimately, understanding the true role of migrants is essential for crafting inclusive policies that balance social cohesion with economic sustainability.

Glossary

Aggregate Income: The total income earned by all individuals or households within a specific economy over a period of time

Assimilation: The process of becoming part of a larger group or culture by adopting its customs and values.

Behavioral Integration: The extent to which an individual adopts the habits, routines, and social behaviors typical of the host society.

Capital Accumulation: The increase in the stock of physical or financial assets available for production within an economy.

Civic Participation: The involvement of individuals in community life and political processes, such as voting or volunteering.

Debt Stability: The condition where a debtor’s ability to meet financial obligations remains secure and manageable over time.

Economic Sustainability:The ability of an economic system to maintain performance and resource availability for future generations.

Foreign Aid: Financial or material assistance provided by one country or organization to another

Host Country: The nation that receives immigrants or international visitors from other countries

Immigrant (Migrant): A person who moves to a foreign country to settle permanently or temporarily

Institutional Barriers: Formal rules, laws, or organizational structures that restrict opportunities for certain groups

Integration: The process of individuals or groups blending into a larger society or system

National Identity: The sense of belonging to a state or nation, characterized by shared culture, history, and values

Per capita income: The average income generated per person in a given area in a specified year

Psychological Well-being: A state of mental health characterized by positive emotions and life satisfaction

Refugee: A person who has been forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution, or natural disaster

Remittances: Money sent by a worker to a family member in their home country

Social Mobility: The movement of individuals or groups between different social or economic positions

Social Resources:The assets, networks, and institutions available within a society to support individual or collective well-being

Standard of Living: The level of wealth, comfort, material goods, and necessities available to a person or community

Structural Barriers: Systemic features of social or economic systems that limit progress for certain groups

Sustainable Development: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs

Unidirectional: Moving in one direction

Governments in the United States and Europe have recently sought new ways to deter, deflect, and deport migrants, and to redefine their rights under human rights law and refugee law for that purpose. The panelists will discuss and compare some of the efforts of the UK and US governments in that direction, including pushbacks and removals to unrelated third countries and the differing responses of the UK Supreme Court and the US Supreme Court. Speakers

Kirsty Hughes is an Associate Professor in Law at the University of Cambridge and Director of its Centre for Public Law. text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Chicago-area operation cost local businesses more than $1.2 billion last year, according to a new study.

The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago’s Great Cities Institute, found that residents of Cook County’s Latino-heavy neighborhoods made “substantially fewer” visits to restaurants and retail businesses in neighborhoods without a high concentration of Latin America-born individuals.

The decline in those “cross-community” trips corresponded with roughly $1.26 billion in “foregone commercial activity” for restaurants and retail businesses in Cook County, where Chicago is located.

Additionally, local governments in Cook County received approximately $107 million less in sales-tax revenue than they otherwise would have due to the estimated decline in commercial activity, the study noted.

“Visits to businesses in high Latin America-born neighborhoods did not increase enough to offset the decline in cross-community trips, and visits to destinations outside Cook County did not increase,” the study noted. “Within the commercial activity visible in our data, the decline therefore appears to represent foregone rather than relocated activity.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended the operation, telling The Hill that removing “criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers.”

“Let’s be clear, if there was any correlation between rampant illegal immigration and a good economy, [former President] Biden would have had a booming economy,” added the DHS spokesperson, who also highlighted multiple people with crime records that federal officers arrested during the operation.

The surge of ICE officers to the Chicago area, which the agency dubbed “Operation Midway Blitz,” began a year ago Tuesday and lasted through mid-November 2025.

During the roughly two-month operation, federal officers detained 3,841 people, 15 percent of which had a prior criminal conviction, according to a report from the Chicago Sun-Times.

Of the detainees, 2,732 have either been deported or left the country voluntarily, the Sun-Times noted.

The Trump administration launched the crackdown over the objections of Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D).

Citing the study on the economic costs of the operation, Pritzker said it caused “real damage” to businesses in the state. The governor also touted the work of the Little Village Chamber of Commerce in helping businesses rebuild.

text:
Federal immigration authorities have sent a resident of St. Paul, Minnesota, to Guantánamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba, despite the man having no criminal record and being a legal resident of the U.S.

Adam Abdullah, 31, is an auto mechanic who was born in Somalia and came to the U.S. seeking asylum in 2023. He has regularly checked in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) since he began living in Minnesota, and has no criminal history.

ICE officials stopped Abdullah’s vehicle on December 12, 2025, as part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Metro Surge.” In a brief interview with Minnesota Public Radio this week, Abdullah said that the agents were not forthcoming about why he was being pulled over, and seemed uninterested in respecting his rights.

“When they come to me, and I ask them why you pulled me over, they say, ‘We are immigration, so give me your work permit,'” Abdullah recounted. “And I asked them, ‘Do you have a warrant, and what’s the reason to pull me over?’ And they say, ‘We don’t need a warrant; we are immigration, and we know you are Adam Abdullah.'”

Abdullah indicated that he still hasn’t been given an explanation for why he was targeted. After being detained, he spent the next nine months moving between immigrant jails across the country — first in Albert Lea, Minnesota, then in Covington, Kentucky, and finally in Louisiana.

At that point, he was told that he was going to be deported to Somalia. But that plan was apparently changed, and he was instead sent to Guantánamo, the U.S. naval base notorious for guards torturing imprisoned people, particularly during the so-called “war on terror.”

During his interview, which lasted only 10 minutes due to restrictions at Guantánamo, Abdullah indicated to MPR that he is one of eight Somali migrants imprisoned at the naval base, some of whom, like himself, were abducted by immigration agents in the Twin Cities.

It appears that Abdullah’s civil rights are being violated, as he doesn’t have regular access to counsel, and is limited to 10-minute phone conversations when he is allowed to speak to his lawyer.

“Calls are limited to five to 10 minutes, and we don’t even know if they’re confidential,” said Marc Prokosch, Abdullah’s attorney. “And that’s the only way that we can communicate with our clients is through these phone calls that may or may not be under attorney-client confidentiality.”

The choice to send migrants to Guantánamo, as part of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, appears to be aimed at further criminalizing immigration, Yumna Rizvi with the Center for Victims of Torture explained.

“This administration wants to conflate this threat of immigration with terrorism,” Rizvi said.

Conditions at Guantánamo Bay are horrendous, reports have indicated. In August 2025, Human Rights Watch interviewed 20 Venezuelan migrants who were sent there. Those individuals described unsanitary conditions, being denied access to information about their futures and their legal cases, and isolated confinement for up to 23 hours each day. Even for the one hour a day that they were released, they were forbidden from talking to each other.

“The US government has taken immigrants to Guantánamo and subjected them to incommunicado detention in appalling conditions,” Juanita Goebertus, director of the Americas Division of Human Rights Watch, said last year. “No immigrant or asylum seeker who leaves their country in search of protection should be taken to a place like this.”

text:
By Julia Harte

Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Trump administration proposed on Wednesday ⁠changing ⁠the national census to include only ⁠U.S. citizens and permanent residents, a move that could significantly change how much ​political representation and federal funding each state receives.

The U.S. Census Bureau submitted the proposal just over a year after President ‌Donald Trump ordered its parent agency to ‌craft a new census that would block immigrants in the U.S. illegally from being counted. The bureau will ⁠conduct the next ⁠full census in 2030.

The proposed rule changes would exclude even more immigrants from ​the census, such as those in the U.S. on a temporary lawful basis. The proposed changes would also eliminate parts of the questionnaire that seek information on race or ethnicity, which have been included since the first census in 1790.

The proposal ​is open to public comment for 30 days.

Demography experts and civil rights advocates warn that both changes ⁠could warp ⁠the data used for drawing ⁠congressional and state ​legislative districts, enforcing anti-discrimination law and allocating federal funds for public services.

FEDERAL AID, POLITICAL REPRESENTATION AT STAKE

The ​effort could have "earth-shattering" effects, leaving cities ⁠and states that have relatively high immigrant populations with insufficient federal aid and political representation, said Meeta Anand, senior director of the census and data equity program at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights.

Census data "undergirds so much of our democracy and our society," Anand said. "So you'll start seeing a very inaccurate picture of our country, ⁠and then we're making political decisions, business decisions, investment decisions based on data that are flawed."

The ⁠White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump has long decried the fact that immigrants living in the U.S. illegally are included in the census, which is used to determine how many seats each state gets in the U.S. House of Representatives and state legislative districts.

In his first term, Trump tried to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census but was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled that the federal government had given a "contrived" rationale.

The U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment calls for political representatives to be apportioned based on "the whole number of persons in each ⁠State."

The administration's effort to omit immigrants in the U.S. illegally and temporary immigrants from the U.S. census comes amid its wider crackdown on both legal and illegal immigration across the country.

The Justice Department warned on September 2 that states could lose billions of dollars in welfare funding if they do not ​report all immigrants whom state agencies know to be in the country illegally.

(Reporting by ​Julia Harte; editing by Paul Thomasch and Rod Nickel)

FREDERICK, Md. (WBAL) — A protest in a Frederick neighborhood turned violent Friday night as Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers clashed with demonstrators, leaving some injured and prompting calls for an investigation.

Protesters gathered near Stoneybrook Court after ICE vehicles were spotted in the area on Thursday. By Friday, more than 100 community members had joined the demonstration, chanting and linking arms in opposition to the federal immigration enforcement activity.

“We were attacked. Our community was physically attacked by federal law enforcement officers,” Frederick City Council President Cesar Diaz said. “In the past, we’ve seen them come in, they do something, they kidnap someone and then they leave. This time, they stuck around.”

Witnesses said ICE officers appeared to be targeting a specific house and began driving SUVs onto sidewalks, ordering protesters to move.

“He started to really come at me and so I moved off. There was another woman there with me, and then, there was another protester sort of in front, like caddy-corner to me. He actually plowed into that person and started pushing them with his car,” said Soolah Kemp, a protester.

Kemp also described how a group of protesters later linked arms in front of the home.

“They were just standing there. It wasn’t like they were fighting. They weren’t. They just linked arms,” Kemp said.

Video from the scene captured the moment officers physically engaged with protesters.

“(They were) beating people with batons, kicking them, punching them, throwing people on the ground, just to attempt to get into the front door of this home,” said Tatiana Santos, who is with Indivisible Frederick Forward.

Protesters suffered cuts and bruises, with some requiring hospitalization. Frederick police eventually arrived to deescalate the situation. Witnesses said ICE officers broke into the home and later spoke with the family inside.

“We were asked to be quiet so that they could have a conversation with ICE and then ICE left,” Santos said.

Witnesses said it did not appear that ICE made any arrests during the incident.

Diaz expressed concern about the implications of the encounter.

“This is the first time that’s happened in Frederick. I think that level of action is the first time that’s happened anywhere in Maryland, and now, people are concerned. Is this the new normal? Is this an escalation?” Diaz said.

Diaz also noted that he had not seen a warrant for ICE’s activity. Community members are now calling on the Maryland attorney general to investigate the incident.

Baltimore City Councilwoman Odette Ramos, D-District 14, said some of the protesters came from Baltimore. She criticized the officers’ actions, writing: “Shame on ICE for their violent, unconstitutional behavior.”

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (CN) — Months after thousands of federal agents wrapped up a controversial winter of immigration enforcement in the Twin Cities, Minnesota and the Trump administration returned to court Wednesday to debate whether the state’s lawsuit over the surge should be thrown out.

Seeking a dismissal, the federal government told U.S. District Judge Katherine Menendez Minnesota lacks legal standing now that Operation Metro Surge has drawn down.

The state argued nothing is stopping the government from returning to Minnesota and engaging in the same “unlawful actions” that plagued its citizens earlier this year.

“If they start up these policies again, we know what’s going to happen because they’ve done it before, and there’s a very small list of cities that they are intending to target,” Minneapolis Assistant City Attorney Heather Robertson said. “It is not purely speculative to say they will come here again.”

Menendez seemed at least inclined to agree, noting the Justice Department’s unwillingness to bring a mootness argument stating the surge will not return.

“There is no suggestion that your clients have stopped any of this or that they pledge not to resume it,” the Joe Biden appointee said to the DOJ attorneys. “The challenge that you have is you’re trying to use standing to accomplish what you’re not willing to put on the table to satisfy mootness.”

Still, Menendez voiced skepticism over whether Minnesota could prove ongoing and imminent harm long after the main deployment ended.

“This interpretation of declaratory judgment claims completely swallows the imminence and immediacy of the risk of future harm,” she said. “It feels like this would allow cases to go forward no matter how long after something is over.”

Minnesota brought its initial suit in January — just days after the federal officer-involved killing of Renee Nicole Good — seeking an immediate halt of Operation Metro Surge and a declaration that the government’s actions were unlawful.

The surge saw thousands of masked federal agents descend on the Twin Cities beginning in December 2025 in what Homeland Security called the largest immigration enforcement action in U.S. history.

While the federal government claimed the operation targeted noncitizens with criminal records, local leaders and civil rights groups argued the true intent was political retaliation against “sanctuary” jurisdictions not adhering to President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda.

“They are asking you to ignore all of the allegations that [Operation Metro Surge] was a vehicle to coerce and commandeer, and are asking this court to find as a matter of factual dispute that everything about [Operation Metro Surge] was a lawful immigration enforcement operation,” Minnesota Assistant Attorney General Lindsey Middlecamp said Wednesday.

Menendez repeatedly pressed Justice Department attorneys on that point, questioning why claims of coercion shouldn’t survive a motion to dismiss.

“There could be extreme ultra vires conduct from the government,” Menendez said. “I’m supposed to accept their allegations as true, and they allege a multi-front effort by the administration to try and enforce compliance from the state and local municipalities to the executive’s stance on immigration enforcement.”

The Trump administration countered that Minnesota’s 10th Amendment, equal sovereignty and First Amendment claims fail on their merits, arguing immigration enforcement does not infringe upon state police powers and the state provides little direct evidence of political retaliation.

To support its claims of coercion and economic fallout, Minnesota shifted its legal strategy this spring. After failing to secure an initial preliminary injunction, the state filed an amended complaint in April that moved from predicting harms to detailing realized damage.

Minnesota claims the state lost over $600 million in business revenue and $240 million in wages throughout the surge across the Twin Cities and expanded its factual record to include a string of subsequent violent events after the initial lawsuit was filed, including the shootings of Alex Pretti and Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

The government argues downstream, indirect financial costs and generalized public fear are legally insufficient to confer standing, insisting states cannot sue the federal government on behalf of their citizens.

Given the operation in Minnesota has long since ended, the state now seeks a permanent judgment ruling the baseline policy underlying the surge was unconstitutional — one that would permanently bar future masked agent policies, racial profiling and roving patrols in the area.

“This is not a country where the government gets to go up to random people and say ‘show me your papers,’” Minnesota Assistant Attorney General Brian Carter said.

A key friction point remains the revocation of Homeland Security’s internal “sensitive locations” guidance, which previously restricted most enforcement near schools, places of worship and courthouses — all areas that saw increased enforcement in Minnesota.

Justice Department attorney Brantley Mayers asserted blocking or vacating the 2025 sensitive locations guidance would not stop federal agents from arresting people at those locations, as an independent statutory basis remains.

“Officers still retain statutory discretion, and we think the same is true for the sensitive locations policy,” Mayers said. “There is no legal constraint on the use of legal discretion at sensitive locations.”

While the number of federal agents in Minnesota has dropped significantly throughout the year, the state still claims the threat of enforcement remains, and the remaining agents are likely adhering to unlawful policies.

“The threat is ongoing,” Robertson said. “They are trying to coerce us to adopt their immigration policies, and they are trying to punish us for adopting policies that disagree.”

authors: Anthony L. Fisher, David J. Bier, Sydney Carruth, Laura Barrón-López
description:
In December 2025, Cruz showed up at the immigration benefits office for an interview for the petition, hoping to advance in the legal immigration process.
USCIS has increasingly collaborated with ICE since last year, reporting applicants who have records of past immigration infractions, even in cases when they might be eligible for legal status.
After almost two weeks of detention, ICE relented and gave him a bond hearing.

text:
This article is part of “In broad daylight,” an MS NOW series exploring the stories of people whose lives have been endangered, upended or cut short by Trump’s brutal immigration agenda.

Douglas Sura Cruz came from El Salvador to Illinois more than 11 years ago. He fell in love with an American, they got married, and together they have two young children who are also U.S. citizens. His wife petitioned U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for Cruz to receive lawful permanent residence.

In December 2025, Cruz showed up at the immigration benefits office for an interview for the petition, hoping to advance in the legal immigration process. Everything seemed in order. But after his interview, USCIS didn’t adjudicate his petition. Instead, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents approached him and arrested him.

Douglas has no criminal record. Still, ICE detained him.

Cruz is the victim of a new and terrifyingly common Trump administration practice of arresting the spouses, parents and other family members of U.S. citizens as they go through the standard green card process. USCIS has increasingly collaborated with ICE since last year, reporting applicants who have records of past immigration infractions, even in cases when they might be eligible for legal status.

Cruz was taken to the notorious Broadview ICE facility, which had been sued months prior to his arrival there by the American Civil Liberties Union for “overcrowding, unhygienic conditions, lack of medical care, and deprivation of adequate food.” The lawsuit details that a single bathroom is shared among detainees in the overcrowded cells with “poor sanitation, clogged toilets, and blood, human fluids, and insects in the sinks and the floor.” Although the district court eventually ordered some conditions to be improved, the ACLU accused the government of withholding evidence showing whether it had complied with the order.

Outside the detention center walls, Cruz’s wife and children stared down financial destitution, deprived of their primary financial support. Normally, under any other administration, including the first Trump administration, ICE and Border Patrol detainees can seek bond if they aren’t dangerous and they have sufficient ties to the community and are not deemed a flight risk. But Cruz had run into a second devastating and unprecedented policy shift from last year: the administration’s refusal to grant bond hearings to people who entered without inspection.

Even serious criminal suspects get a bond hearing before trial. This policy meant that Cruz could face months behind bars before the outcome of his case. He filed a habeas corpus petition with a district court to force the administration to give him a bond hearing. His attorney wrote that his detention imposes a “substantial deprivation and burden that puts [him] and his family at risk without his support.”

More articles

Thanks to this anti-bond policy, almost 10,000 people each month are filing habeas petitions just like Douglas Cruz in attempts to free themselves from deplorable conditions in ICE custody. ∂

Fortunately, Cruz’s counsel was able to convince the judge that the no-bond policy was illegal and unconstitutional, and the judge ordered ICE to grant him a bond hearing. After almost two weeks of detention, ICE relented and gave him a bond hearing. Based on typical spending per detainee, his stay in detention likely cost the government more than $2,500, for less than two weeks.

Cruz was fortunate to receive some form of legal justice. But he was one of the lucky ones. These situations are growing increasingly common as USCIS sits on legal immigrants’ applications, not processing them and instead waiting for the chance to arrest them. Many immigrants are actually losing their legal status during these lengthy waits as their temporary status expires and they are unable to renew. As of July 2026 there were nearly 1.6 million pending green card applications, and wait times for some categories have grown to multiple years.

USCIS Director Joseph Edlow has emphasized his agency’s “great relationship with ICE.” As a result, USCIS has worked with ICE to arrest spouses of American military personnel, refugees resettled by the U.S. government, and crime victims applying for a visa for immigrants who help law enforcement investigations. Congress has created the U visa for the purpose of allowing some immigrants with temporary or no status to receive status in exchange for cooperation with the police, but ICE often arrests them before USCIS reviews their applications.

description:

text:
After federal immigration agents fatally shot two people in Minnesota, David Streever emailed Todd Lyons, then-Acting Director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), on January 26. He expressed his outrage over the shootings.

In June, immigration agents went to Streever’s home in New York while he was abroad. They left a “warning notice” stating that he may have “threatened” Lyons.

Streever’s case is part of a growing list of people who have faced government action after criticizing immigration enforcement. These actions include formal notices and administrative subpoenas.

Such actions threaten the right to freedom of expression. The US government must stop targeting and intimidating people who criticize immigration enforcement.

Here’s what you can do:

Write to the Secretary of Homeland Security urging him to:

Revoke the warning notice against David Streever and protect his right to freely express his opinions without interference.

Stop issuing warning notices and administrative subpoenas against people who peacefully exercise their right to freedom of expression. Revoke any such notices and subpoenas already issued.

Respect and protect everyone’s rights to privacy and freedom of expression.

Write to:

Secretary Markwayne Mullin

Department of Homeland Security

Email: dhssecretary@hq.dhs.gov

Salutation: Dear Secretary Mullin,

And copy:

His Excellency Peter Hoekstra

Ambassador

Embassy of the United States of America

490 Sussex Drive

Ottawa, ON K1N 1G8

Tel: (613) 238-5335 / 688-5335 (24h) Fax: (613) 688-3082

Operation Metro Surge

In December 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) launched “Operation Metro Surge” in Minnesota. The operation deployed more than 4,000 federal agents to the area. Agents targeted Minnesotans of Somali descent and other racialized immigrants.

President Trump had previously described people of Somali descent as “garbage” who were “completely taking over the once great State of Minnesota.”

The operation led to numerous human rights violations. These included widespread racial profiling, arbitrary detention, unlawful surveillance and the repression of protests. Agents also used excessive force, including lethal force against three people.

David Streever’s email

Outraged by the government’s actions, New York resident David Streever emailed Todd Lyons, then-Acting Director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), on January 26.

Streever titled his email “What’s next”. He compared Lyons to a Nazi war criminal. He also wrote that Lyons’ protection of those who killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti would bring him a sense of “shame” that would “torment” him until his “last day on Earth.”

Five months later, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents went to Streever’s home while he was outside the United States. They gave his wife a warning notice addressed to him. The notice stated that he “may be in violation of federal law” because of the email.

The notice described his email as threatening. It also stated that it is “unlawful” to “impede, intimidate, and/or interfere with a federal official…due to the performance of their duties.”

After Streever returned to the United States, federal agents tracked his movements to his hotel in New York City. He had arrived at the airport and stayed at the hotel for one night. An agent left a card at the hotel front desk and instructed Streever to call him.

Since receiving the warning notice, Streever has feared speaking out against the government. He fears further retaliation.

A wider pattern of targeting critics

Streever’s warning notice forms part of a wider pattern by DHS to silence dissenting voices. This includes issuing administrative subpoenas to technology companies. These companies include social media platforms and email service providers.

The subpoenas request background and biographical information about online users who criticize the government’s immigration enforcement actions and tactics.

Freedom of expression and privacy

The US government’s use of administrative subpoenas and warning notices raises serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy. These actions can intimidate people and discourage them from speaking out about human rights abuses.

The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects both rights. The United States has signed and ratified the Covenant.

Amnesty International is concerned that these formal notices aim to intimidate and silence people who exercise their right to freedom of expression. This includes people who speak out about human rights abuses during ICE enforcement operations.

text:
Johnson County resident Oscar Sanchez-Corona had prepared his two elementary school-aged kids for the possibility he would be detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

His daughter made a drawing with the words, “ICE, don’t take my daddy.”

But ICE took him.

On the morning of Aug. 18, masked ICE agents asked for Sanchez-Corona at his worksite in Lawrence. They transported him to Leavenworth, Kansas, and then detention centers in Louisiana and Texas.

Less than three weeks later, Sanchez-Corona was deported to Mexico, leaving behind his two children, four siblings and the Kansas community he called home.

Brought to the United States at age 1, Sanchez-Corona went to Shawnee Mission schools and has a tattoo of the Mexico and American flags intertwined. Skylar Roush, Sanchez-Corona’s brother-in-law, described him as “a regular American guy.”

The Star attempted to contact Sanchez-Corona in ICE detention and was unable to reach him. ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Roush’s account, along with advocate narratives, court records and government data illustrate Sanchez-Corona’s 18 days confined by ICE.

Family members believe Sanchez-Corona was targeted because of a previous deportation following a nonviolent misdemeanor and probation violations as a teen. They say a mistake 15 years ago shouldn’t separate a father from his kids.

Sanchez-Corona is one of the more than 150,000 people with nonviolent criminal convictions detained by ICE since the start of the second Trump administration, according to Department of Homeland Security data shared by the Deportation Data Project. These individuals make up over 30% of all those detained.

In Kansas, 2,609 people were arrested and detained by ICE from Aug. 2025 through July 2026, a 90% increase from the previous 12 months.

Recent increases in ICE arrests have come from people with nonviolent convictions or no criminal records, both Kansas and nation-wide data show, despite Trump officials saying they target the “worst of the worst.”

Roush said his brother-in-law paid the price for the misdemeanor more than a decade ago, and that the punishment of deportation is disproportionate compared to that faced by American citizens.

“He’s getting this second massive punishment 15 years after the fact, you know, even though he’s lived a peaceful life as a worker and father.”

A Johnson County father

Sanchez-Corona’s kids had just started their first week of classes in the Blue Valley school district when, Roush described, the two elementary schoolers came “home after school, and their father’s been detained.”

When Sanchez-Corona was a baby, his family left rural central Mexico looking for job opportunities. They settled in the Kansas City area, where Sanchez-Corona attended Shawnee Mission schools from elementary to high school.

At age 18, Sanchez-Corona was charged with a misdemeanor for damaging property worth less than $1,000, reported by the Overland Park Police Department, according to Kansas court records. The Star was unable to access the court filings to see details of the incident.

Sanchez-Corona violated his probation multiple times, records show, and was deported, Roush said. It is unclear what the violations were.

After six months in Mexico, Sanchez-Corona returned to the U.S., Roush said. His whole family — including siblings, parents and his parents’ extended family — lived in the states.

Since then, Roush said his brother-in-law turned his life around. Sanchez-Corona focused on his work in concrete construction and, later, his two children. He shares custody of the kids, born in the U.S., with his ex-partner.

Roush described Sanchez-Corona as a devoted father, taking his kids to the zoo and trampoline park. During the FIFA World Cup, the pair gathered with their kids to cheer on Mexico’s soccer team.

“He just loves the Chiefs, he loves the Royals,” Roush said. “He does all the same things like every 30-something-year-old man in Johnson County, Kansas.”

Day of the arrest

A Facebook post details the morning that changed the lives of Sanchez-Corona and his family.

Sanctuary Alliance Lawrence, an immigrant advocacy group, collected accounts and photos from witnesses and rapid response volunteers to share on their social media.

On the morning of Aug. 18, Sanchez-Corona was in Lawrence, pouring concrete at a construction site near Iowa Street and W. 29th Terrace. Around 6:30 a.m., ICE agents came to the site, calling for Sanchez-Corona specifically. No one else was taken, advocates wrote.

A photo from Sanchez-Corona’s boss shows three agents in tactical vests in front of Sanchez-Corona, who wore his long-sleeve safety-orange shirt and jeans. A Jeep blocks the street and the curb-pouring project sits abandoned.

Sanctuary Alliance Lawrence shared another photo with five agents, at least three of them wearing black face coverings.

Three black Jeeps, a silver Nissan and a white Ram truck were on the scene — Sanctuary Alliance said some of those vehicles had been spotted at other ICE raids in Lawrence and Olathe.

All the images were taken from a distance — on July 1, a Kansas law took effect, barring onlookers from coming within 25 feet of first responders, including ICE agents.

The Star attempted to contact Sanctuary Lawrence and Sanchez-Corona’s employer multiple times and did not receive responses.

Sanchez-Corona was brought to the Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, an immigration detention facility run by prison contractor CoreCivic. But no one from ICE told his family — they learned when Sanchez-Corona’s boss called one of his sisters.

But questions remained.

“We didn’t know where he was for the rest of that day,” Roush said.

‘Like a package’

Confusion and anger defined the time after Sanchez-Corona was detained, family members say.

At first, Sanchez-Corona’s family rushed to find an immigration lawyer with openings, but many didn’t have any for weeks.

Four days after the arrest, Roush drove out to Leavenworth to see his brother-in-law. There, he learned Sanchez-Corona was moved that morning to Winn Correctional Center in Louisiana, where two detainees had died in less than two months.

“It’s just almost like he’s a package from Amazon or something, as opposed to a human being.”

After less than a week in Louisiana, Sanchez-Corona was moved to El Paso Camp East Montana, the Texas facility where at least three people have died. He rode on a deportation flight, but because of a plane malfunction, the flight returned to Texas.

Sanchez-Corona was deported to Juarez, Mexico on Sept. 4. Three days later, he arrived at the home of his cousin, the one relative that lives in Mexico, according to Roush.

ICE “won’t return” Sanchez-Corona’s phone and Mexican passport.

The bar should be a lot higher, Roush said, to separate a father from his kids.

“This image of our tax dollars going to ICE agents rolling up to a job site in unmarked cars and just literally removing a worker while he’s pouring concrete,” Roush described. “How is that helping our country’s economy?”

“A few mistakes he made as a 19-year-old are now separating him from his kids.”
