text:
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration is proposing to stop counting immigrants without permanent residency status in the Census, which is conducted to determine state representation in Congress and the distribution of federal funds.

The Census, which is administered every 10 years and is next set for 2030, is also considering asking about each respondent’s citizenship, a departure from past practice, which could discourage the participation of immigrants.

The Census might also remove questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation from its short-form questionnaire. The stated purpose would be to encourage more people to fill out the forms without fear of having their privacy violated.

The Commerce Department, which oversees the Census, is seeking comment on the proposals for 30 days after publication, which is scheduled for Sept. 10.

The Supreme Court blocked the addition of a citizenship question during President Donald Trump's first term. The latest proposal cites legal decisions and policies to justify the various changes.

Census disputes have wide-ranging implications. The population count determines how many House seats each state gets in Congress, which carries huge influence. The count is also used to distribute many forms of federal funding.

The proposed changes are "disastrous," and could touch "all aspects of society," according to Rob Santos, the former director of the U.S. Census Bureau appointed by President Joe Biden.

"Taking away that race and ethnicity question is going to do considerable damage to the ability to do local community engagements or local community assessments of what the community needs are, economic explorations about where to put a factory in and what types of population," Santos told USA TODAY.

The Commerce Department didn't respond to a request for comment.

Census proposes to stop counting undocumented immigrants for House seats

The Census acknowledged it has long counted foreign citizens as part of determining how many House seats each state deserved. But the proposal noted numerous legal challenges and opposition within the first Trump administration to counting undocumented immigrants.

The Constitution's 14th Amendment calls for the Census to determine House seats by counting the "whole number of persons in each state," not including Native Americans who were not taxed. But the proposal echoed arguments from the Trump administration against a provision in the amendment granting citizenship to nearly all babies born in the United States. The Supreme Court ruled in June against a Trump executive order that aimed to restrict birthright citizenship.

The Census proposal argued that immigrants without green cards, or permanent residency status, have insufficient ties to the country to qualify as "true inhabitants" or having a "usual residence" to be counted in the Census. The proposal aimed to exclude undocumented immigrants "whose legal status is less durable and indefinite in length than lawful permanent residence status."

The effort could have "earth-shattering" effects, leaving cities and states that have relatively large immigrant populations with insufficient federal aid and political representation, said Meeta Anand, senior director of the census and data equity program at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights.

Census data "undergirds so much of our democracy and our society," Anand said. "So you'll start seeing a very inaccurate picture of our country, and then we're making political decisions, business decisions, investment decisions based on data that are flawed."

The Census seeks again to ask about citizenship, which the Supreme Court has rejected

Besides asking about citizenship, the Census is considering using its broad access to government records to help determine a person’s legal status.

The records include data from the Treasury Department, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Homeland Security, State Department, Defense Department, U.S. Postal Service and from third-party organizations.

“The Census Bureau is considering how best to distinguish between foreign citizens in the United States who are counted for apportionment and those who are not counted for apportionment,” the proposal states.

The Census could drop demographic questions about race and ethnicity

While seeking more information about nationality, the Census, which has asked about demographics since 1790, proposes to drop questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

The proposal cited Trump’s executive order seeking to end “diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility” programs and activities in the federal government, which he called “radical” and “wasteful.”

A 2023 opinion from Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, who is Black, cited in the proposal described race as a “social construct” based on “ephemeral, socially constructed categories” that “are little more than stereotypes.”

Asking such questions tends to reduce the number of responses. But dropping the questions could boost responses without risking privacy violations.

“Excluding such questions from the decennial census in this manner would reduce response burden as well as the risk of disclosure,” the proposal states.

But removing the question to increase responsiveness to the Census "doesn't make sense, given the simultaneous inclusion of a citizenship question which the Census Bureau's own researchers have shown would decrease participation," Santos said.

Santos warned that the proposals could have public health effects, complicating the tracking of "certain diseases by subgroup and you can better then attend to helping people."

Democrats on the House Oversight Committee argued that Trump is “trying to rig the Census” to prevent the collection of data critical to enforcing the Voting Rights Act.

“We will fight this,” the lawmakers said on social media.

text:
America has a runaway president, and no one on his team is willing to rein him in.

White House officials and elected Republicans have abandoned their attempts to sway Donald Trump’s opinion, finding it futile to push back on the president’s demands, Axios reported Wednesday.

Despite a growing distrust of the president’s instincts, Trump’s inner circle has found it increasingly difficult to change his mind once it’s made up, according to numerous aides, advisers, and donors that spoke with Axios.

“Why bother?” one longtime adviser told the outlet. “He’s the boss.”

The Republican Party has repeatedly caved to Trump’s whims since 2016, allowing him to meander through his second term without the threat of consequence or even a second opinion. As a result, Trump thrust America into war with Iran without any clear goals, aggravated some of America’s longest allies—notably Canada—by shitposting online, incensed the public by tearing down the White House in order to build a $600 million, gold-laden ballroom, and effectively made an already contentious midterm cycle a referendum on his popularity.

“He’s an 80-year-old man who did it his way,” a donor who recently met with the president told Axios. “What he wants, he gets.”

Part of the determination to stay in the president’s good graces stems from Trump’s enormous political clout—a reality that many in his orbit claim is unlikely to expire anytime soon.

“Discount Trump at your peril,” a top adviser told Axios. “He wields enormous power in the party, in politics and culturally.”

“Anyone who thinks he’s going to retreat into the shadows is either stupid or has bad political instincts,” they added.

Insiders are apparently planning to live and die by Trump, even if that means allowing him to run roughshod over the country’s better interests.

“He’s going to remain the dominant political figure even after his term ends,” the adviser told Axios. “And everybody knows it.”

President Trump is trying once again to skirt the Constitution and mess with the U.S. census.

The White House is proposing changes to the 2030 census that would exclude every non–U.S. citizen without permanent residency, flouting the Constitution’s Fourteenth Amendment, which states that the census must count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The proposal, released online Wednesday, also seeks to stop asking about race and ethnicity, which has been included in every census since 1790, and ban any future questions on sexual orientation.

If Trump’s current effort survives court challenges, it will affect congressional redistricting, which is already being manipulated by Republican-led states thanks to the Supreme Court gutting the Voting Rights Act earlier this year. It could also affect antidiscrimination efforts and laws by preventing the collection of relevant statistics.

During Trump’s previous term as president, his administration attempted to include a question about citizenship status, only to abandon the effort after being blocked by the Supreme Court. Trump also attempted to exclude all undocumented immigrants from the count with a July 2020 executive order. A federal court in California ruled against the order, and the census results weren’t completed before Trump left office, after which President Biden repealed those changes.

But Trump clearly didn’t give up on the plan. The administration is supposed to send a report to Congress, which has final approval over the census per the Constitution, by April 1, on its proposed questions for the survey. Trump’s Republican allies in Congress have proposed similar changes to the census themselves to support their gerrymandering efforts.

All of this could hurt participation in the census even if Trump’s changes don’t go through, as respondents would be suspicious of what the federal government plans to do with the data. That could lead to inaccurate results and hurt communities across the country. These days, the White House is trying to use every tool at its disposal to manipulate elections or serve its mass deportation agenda, regardless of what the Constitution or federal law says.

“When they come to me, and I ask them why you pulled me over, they say, ‘We are immigration, so give me your work permit,’” Abdullah, 31, said. “And I asked them, ‘Do you have a warrant, and what’s the reason to pull me over?’ And they say, ‘We don’t need a warrant; we are immigration, and we know you are Adam Abdullah.”

Abdullah was only given 10 minutes to speak to MPR on the phone, but managed to tell the station that the agents didn’t explain why he, an asylum-seeker with a work permit and Social Security number who regularly checked in with ICE, was targeted. The auto mechanic arrived in the U.S. in 2023. After being arrested by ICE last year, he was initially held at the Freeborn County Jail in Albert Lea, Minnesota, before being moved to detention centers in Kentucky and then Louisiana.

Eventually, immigration officers told Abdullah they would send him back to Somalia via Miami. But in Miami, he said he was told that his flight would stop in Cuba for refueling before stopping in other countries on the way to Somalia. But he never made it to Africa at all; the stop in Cuba was permanent. Abdullah also reported that his wrists and ankles were shackled through every flight.

Abdullah told MPR that he’s been at Guantánamo Bay’s Camp Six for about two weeks, with limits on phone calls and exercise time. He said he’s learned that he’s one of eight Somalis at the prison, several of whom were arrested in the Twin Cities.

“Calls are limited to five to 10 minutes, and we don’t even know if they’re confidential,” said his immigration attorney, Marc Prokosch, who noted that Abdullah is his first client to be held in Guantánamo. “And that’s the only way that we can communicate with our clients is through these phone calls that may or may not be under attorney-client confidentiality.”

Trump signed an executive order last year to send immigration detainees to Guantánamo Bay, and promised to send 30,000 immigrants there during his 2024 presidential campaign. As of May, reports indicated that there were only six immigrants detained there, all from Haiti, although Abdullah’s interview suggested that more have arrived in the last few months from different countries.

Canada is making sure Americans feel the consequences of President Trump’s trade war by focusing its tariffs on states where Republicans may lose a midterm election.

In Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted and former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown are locked in a tight battle, Canadian tariffs are particularly important, as Canada is the largest export market for the entire state—buying $17.5 billion in U.S. products, primarily automobiles and machinery (which are now sanctioned). And while Husted, like most Republicans, has attempted to justify his support for Trump’s initial tariffs, this recent escalation has made that stance much harder to take.

“It depends on how it ends,” Husted said. “If we get a good deal, both Canada and America can come out of this well, but it’s going to require both sides.”

Maine is bracing for impact just as hard, as Canada placed a 50 percent tariff on wood and agriculture products, a massive export from the border state. It’s also where Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are expected to have a close race. While both have criticized the trade war, Jackson is blaming Collins for not doing more to fight it.

“Retaliatory tariffs hitting today are going to drive up costs for everyday Mainers,” he wrote on Tuesday. “This trade war was entirely preventable, but Susan Collins chose to back Trump’s agenda instead of standing up for Maine’s working class. This November, we’ll put working families first and retire Susan Collins.”

In Kansas, things look a little different, with Trump directly putting his own party at risk. The president’s Labor Day threat to end sales of Canadian airplane manufacturer Bombardier will likely have a negative impact on Kansas, where the company’s U.S. headquarters are located. It employs over 1,000 Kansans, and has been defended by GOPers and Democrats alike. But that will be a harder sell for Republican gubernatorial and Senate candidates Ty Masterson and Senator Roger Marshall given that their party leader is responsible for creating the problem.

“Bombardier supports 1,500 Kansas families, providing good-paying jobs that put food on the table and keep a roof over their heads during a cost of living crisis caused by Washington. And now, the president is trying to take that away,” Democratic Senate candidate Adam Marshall wrote on Monday. “The decision to ban Bombardier from selling in the U.S. is a direct attack on Kansas workers and Kansas jobs—yet Roger Marshall is notably silent. We cannot allow this chaotic economic policy to continue to hurt Kansans; they deserve so much better. As your Senator, I will always stand up for Kansas workers.”

“I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Marshall wrote on Tuesday without naming Trump. “We agree on the mission: bring more good-paying manufacturing jobs back to Wichita. America buys more than half of what Bombardier sells. If that’s the market, more of those planes should be built here. Wichita has one of the nation’s top skilled manufacturing workforces and is a leader in aerospace manufacturing.”

Sherri Tenpenny, an anti-vax activist and “doctor,” circulated Kavanaugh’s headshot on X in the wake of his decision, declaring that “Brett Kavanaugh is a TRAITOR.”

Pro-Trump pundit Eric Daugherty referred to Kavanaugh’s decision as “SERIOUSLY disappointing,” claiming on X that this is “why states like Indiana should’ve redrawn.” SteveLovesAmmo, a self-described “Freedom Aficionado,” said that Kavanaugh’s description illustrated how “SCOTUS is severely compromised.”

The drama began last summer, when Donald Trump ordered several Republican-led states to redraw their congressional maps in a brazen attempt to create a GOP advantage in the House of Representatives come midterms.

Congressional maps are typically redrawn every 10 years, after new census data is released. Yet Trump’s order arrived in the middle of the decade, raising alarms that the nationwide effort was an attempt to undermine American democracy.

Republicans wasted no time implementing the directive in Missouri, where they cleaved portions off of the state’s Democratic stronghold around Kansas City to endanger Representative Emanuel Cleaver’s seat. The new map offered Republicans a 7–1 advantage, a one-seat gain over their current 6–2 delegation.

A group called People Not Politicians collected more than 300,000 signatures in opposition to the new map—more than double the amount required—to force a statewide referendum on the matter, which is due to take place on November 3 on the statewide ballot.

Nonetheless, Missouri opted to use the new maps during its August 4 primary. But this week, things got especially messy.

A federal judge decided on Tuesday that the state should not use the original maps during the November election, in light of its decision to move forward with the new maps last month. But the judge’s decision was in direct conflict with the U.S. Supreme Court, which had decided moments earlier that a previous decision from the Missouri Supreme Court should stand, ordering the old map to be used rather than the new ones.

text:
The ACLU of Connecticut filed a lawsuit Wednesday challenging Hartford Immigration Court's policy of withholding records related to individual cases from the public.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for Connecticut, argues that records like case numbers, case names and in absentia removal orders — which the immigration court issues when a person fails to appear for their hearing date — should be open to the public under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which the lawsuit says has traditionally granted access to judicial records.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The First Amendment guarantees that we the people have access to documents used to adjudicate cases like these,” Dan Barrett, the ACLU of Connecticut's legal director, said in a statement. “The Immigration Court’s judgments and dockets are no more secret than those of the Connecticut Superior Court two blocks across town."

A spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review said the office and the Department of Justice "declines to comment on litigation-related matters."

Unlike federal district and circuit courts and the U.S. Supreme Court, immigration courts are part of the U.S. Department of Justice. That means they fall under the Executive Branch, not the independent judiciary. In immigration court, unlike in most state and federal courts, case records are not accessible to the public. Some hearings are open, but some of the most consequential happen behind closed doors. And while the court itself records every hearing, even recordings of public hearings are considered confidential.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Last year, CT Insider filed a request under the federal Freedom of Information Act for recordings of Hartford immigration judges speaking during public hearings a reporter had attended in person. Those recordings did not identify individual defendants or include any details of individual cases. EOIR denied that request, citing an exemption to the public records law for records that "constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of the personal privacy of third parties."

EOIR also declined to tell CT Insider last year what immigration judges were hearing cases in Hartford. And while Hartford Immigration Court posts a daily list of people who have cases before in its lobby, EOIR has refused to provide information to CT Insider about upcoming hearings upon request.

“EOIR does not provide copies of immigration court records, including the posted daily docket,” spokesperson Kathryn Mattingly said in a statement last October. “Immigration courts are created by statute and regulation and are not Constitutional courts of public record.”

The new lawsuit comes after the ACLU of Connecticut sent a letter in July to Assistant Chief Immigration Judge Angela Munson, who oversees the Hartford Immigration Court, requesting docket numbers, case captions, the names of defendants and in absentia removal orders for May, June and July 2026, according to the complaint filed in federal court Wednesday. The ACLU made that request under the First Amendment, not under FOIA, it said. The ACLU followed up on that request via email in August, according to the complaint, which says Munson ignored those requests.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The suit names Munson and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as defendants. It asks the federal district court to order Hartford Immigration Court to produce the records and enjoin it from denying future requests.

The ACLU of Connecticut is being represented in the case by Alexa Talin Millinger of Hinckley Allen Snyder LLP, court records show. The case had not yet been assigned to a judge as of press time, nor have the defendants responded or have any hearing dates been set.

Wednesday's lawsuit marks the second time Hartford Immigration Court has come in for criticism this week. U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal sat in on about an hour of hearings in court Thursday, after which he held a press conference during which he accused the court of "intentional injustice."

More than 250 people were scheduled for hearings before one of three judges in the court on Tuesday, according to a list posted in its lobby. The sheer volume is a dramatic change from this time last year, when CT Insider observed between 20 and 40 cases at such a hearing. These new "mega master hearings," as they're called, along with staff turnover and the termination or retirement of judges, have dramatically remade the court since CT Insider spent a week there last year documenting its operations.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Blumenthal vowed Tuesday to return to the immigration court as part of what he called an "investigation" into its operations.

text:
On August 6, Matías Pourrain, an Argentine-born U.S. resident, was at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport with his Miami United teammates. The club is a perennial title contender in the semi-professional United Premier Soccer League. The players were in good spirits as they looked forward to a trip to Los Angeles for the Spring National semifinal against New York Renegades FC.

Pourrain, with his carry-on in one hand and his maté thermos in the other, walked over to a water fountain for a refill before the cross-country flight. He and his teammates had just cleared the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screening process when, Pourrain said, two men in civilian clothes, without any visible police insignia, approached him and asked to see his identification.

Pourrain, a 34-year-old creative midfielder who signed with Miami United in January, has lived in South Florida since 2019. He said he came to the U.S. legally on a tourist visa and then secured a work permit. In July, he renewed his Florida driver’s license. Pourrain said he does not have a criminal background, with public records revealing only traffic violations. In April he played in the first-ever U.S. Baller League, a six-a-side indoor soccer tournament. He had mingled with Brazilian great Ronaldinho, singer J Balvin, and Olympic sprinter Usain Bolt, among other well-known athletes and digital creators.

At first, Pourrain wasn’t too alarmed. He handed the two men his driver’s license.

“Where’s your passport?” Pourrain recalled one of them asking. “Do you have any other identification?” said the other.

Pourrain gave the man his U.S. work permit. “Come with us,” one of the men said, as they both lifted up their shirts slightly to reveal their ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) badges.

Pourrain said he was told that they needed to check something “on the computer” related to his pending immigration case. It shouldn’t take more than 10 minutes, one of the officers said, and that after a quick check, Pourrain would be able to rejoin his teammates at the departure gate. Pourrain texted his head coach Claudio Frean.

“I’ll be back in 10 minutes,” he wrote in Spanish.

Two more ICE officers arrived and told Pourrain he would be arrested and taken into custody. He said he was not told why. “What did I do?” Pourrain asked desperately. A person with his immigration status, Pourrain said, would not have been able to secure a renewed driver’s license or a work permit if they had committed a crime.

“You’re coming with us the easy way or the hard way,” an ICE officer said. Pourrain said he did not resist. He was handcuffed and quickly ushered out of the airport. He overheard one officer tell an ICE agent to use a specific airport exit to avoid being seen by a local news crew that was on site.

As Pourrain recalls, he was placed inside an unmarked van, with his hands and ankles handcuffed. He was told that information would be given to him once he had arrived at the makeshift detention center in Miramar, Fla., roughly 20 miles to the southwest of the airport. His teammates and the Miami United coaching staff had no idea what had happened. He believes that his driver’s license was flagged by TSA officials. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released a statement after his arrest:

“On August 6, 2026, ICE arrested Matias Alejandro Pourrain, an illegal alien from Argentina, at the Fort Lauderdale International Airport. On November 12, 2019, Pourrain was legally admitted into the country at the Atlanta Intercontinental Airport, with permission to stay for six months. He chose to stay beyond May 11, 2020, in violation of our nation’s laws. Pourrain will remain in ICE custody pending his removal proceedings and will receive full due process.”

Pourrain was not back in 10 minutes. He would not see any of his teammates for 26 days.

From his apartment in Miami, Pourrain, visibly exhausted and gaunt, and at times emotional, told The Athletic that when he submitted to the authorities that day, he did so hoping that it was all a misunderstanding.

“I was not going to fight,” he said. “But at no point did they explain anything to me. They just said it had to do with my pending case. When I got to Miramar they’d explain.”

“Miramar,” Pourrain said, his voice trembling, “was the worst thing that’s ever happened to me in my life.”

At the Miramar processing center, Pourrain was placed inside a holding cell with nearly 70 other men. The room, he said, was roughly 160 square feet. He remembers the two urinals that faced each other inside the room. A water fountain that hardly worked sat inches away. Pourrain said he sat shackled to a chair the first 24 hours he was there and spent nearly three days without eating. He struggled to eat the food that the detention center officials gave the inmates.

“Hunger is the worst thing there is,” he said. “Hunger really hurts. The food they gave us had mold. I could see little black circles on the bread. It was not edible.” But when the hunger became unbearable, Pourrain ate it.

Twenty-four hours after being detained, he said, authorities allowed Pourrain to make a phone call. He called his wife, an Argentine whom he met in Florida. She urged him to stay strong, and more importantly, to eat and to stay hydrated. We’ll get you out of there, she told him. But drinking water was just as unsanitary, he said. “The water fountain was close to where people urinated,” Pourrain said. “And the water trickled along the spout where the urine had just passed. It was impossible. I couldn’t do it.”

“Guys would sleep right next to the toilet,” he continued. “Someone’s head would be right next to the toilet, so when you urinate, it would splash and the urine would land on the people sleeping there. It was inhumane.”

After four days, he said, the stench inside the room became intolerable. Pourrain was then moved, along with a large group of inmates, to the Krome North Service Processing Center in Miami before arriving at the Glades Correctional Facility in Belle Glade. By then, Miami United ownership had contacted attorney Regina Borges de Moraes. Pourrain was charged with overstaying a U.S. visa. She took the case pro bono.

“What they have (on Pourrain) right now is just allegedly overstay, which I have an issue with,” Borges de Moraes told The Athletic. “He entered legally in November of 2019 with a tourist visa. So it gives him the right to go in front of an immigration judge if they attempt to remove him, which is a good thing.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Miami United FC (@miamiunitedfc)

According to Borges de Moraes, cases like Pourrain’s are increasing under the current administration.

“I would say beginning of June and of May, it became much more common,” Borges de Moraes said. “Usually for someone like Matías, if ICE encountered them, they would do what’s called catch and release, which is write them up for removal proceedings, but then let them go. Either have them pay a bond, put on an ankle monitor, or nothing, and just set them up for court.”

Borges de Moraes is also currently handling the case of Cuban national team midfielder Neisser Sandó, who defected to the U.S. while he played for Cuba at the 2023 Concacaf Gold Cup. Sandó has lived in Miami since and was recently detained at Miami International Airport on the same visa charge as Pourrain. Sandó is in the process of obtaining a U.S. green card through the Cuban Adjustment Act. Borges de Moraes said he is being detained at an ICE detention center in Rio Grande, Texas.

Pourrain’s description of his time in detention is not uncommon. Three days before Pourrain was detained, Venezuelan national Claudia Rodríguez, 28, was released from ICE custody after being held for 20 days. Rodríguez, like Pourrain, was detained at the Fort Lauderdale airport before boarding a domestic flight and taken to the same Miramar detention center. After her release on August 3, Rodríguez detailed the conditions she experienced.

“I (felt) like I was an animal in a zoo on the floor, dirty,” Rodriguez told reporters at a news conference on August 4, where she was joined by U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz. “So everyone is sleeping, eating, pooping, going to the bathroom in this small detention room, ” Wasserman Schultz said. “(DHS) told me they only keep people (at Miramar) for 72 hours. Claudia was there for eight days.” Rodríguez has been in the U.S. since 2017. She does not have a criminal record and has a pending political asylum case.

Also in August, five U.S. congress members visited the Stewart Detention Center in Columbus, Ga., following reports of poor living conditions inside the ICE detention facility. A detainee died in custody at the facility in April.

When approached for comment by The Athletic, DHS disputed Pourrain’s claims about the facility’s conditions.

“Claims that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention centers are FALSE,” DHS wrote. “ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens. All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, clean water, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries. Illegal aliens also have access to phones to communicate with their family members and lawyers. Certified dietitians evaluate meals.”

Borges de Moraes offered her own assessment.

“Detention centers do have higher standards and Matías was treated much better at the detention centers,” she said. “But not at Miramar processing. Not at a freaking building where they have cages basically in the basement and they have 68, 69 men handcuffed and leg-cuffed with chains from legs to hand, sleeping sitting up. The conditions that these individuals are in are horrendous. Horrendous.”

At Glades, Pourrain said, he was given an orange jumpsuit to wear. Orange was reserved for inmates that posed a medium risk, while anyone in a red jumpsuit was considered dangerous and high risk.

“Try to relax,” his wife would tell him over the phone. “You have a right to bail.”

Any hope that he would soon be released was extinguished after Pourrain was removed from the Glades facility and placed inside an unmarked van along with other inmates. He assumed he would be moved to another facility in South Florida, but unbeknownst to him, he was on his way to the airport.

“I managed to finally fall asleep inside the van,” Pourrain said. “I was calm because I knew I had an immigration appointment in Miami in September. As I’m falling asleep I overhear one of the (inmates) say “airport” and I jumped up from my seat. I was in handcuffs, my hands, ankles and waist. I tried to look out of a small window to see where we were going.”

Hours passed and the van arrived at an airport in Louisiana. Pourrain and the others were led onto an airplane. It was then, he said, that he was told that he would be sent to a detention center near Laredo, Texas. Pourrain had never heard of Laredo, but on the flight, an ICE agent told him it was near the U.S.-Mexico border.

Up until that moment, Pourrain had not feared that this situation would lead to him being sent to another country. But now panic had set in. “They could just throw me over the border and then what?” Pourrain remembered asking himself. “I wasn’t able to make any calls. I couldn’t contact anyone.

“I became desperate during that drive to the prison in Laredo. I was scared.”

Pourrain didn’t know it at the time, but his family and attorney were unaware of his location. Borges de Moraes could not find his name in the ICE immigration system.

“He didn’t show up on the ICE locator,” Borges da Moraes said. “It took almost 24 hours for him to get to Laredo. Rio Grande is the detention facility. But Laredo Court has jurisdiction for Rio Grande. I had to refile my bond motion.”

Pourrain said he felt a sense of relief when he saw the facility and realized that he was still in the U.S. At Rio Grande, he swapped his orange jumpsuit for a blue one, a color that identifies inmates as having a pending immigration case. He was given outdoor recreational time once a day. There was a flat soccer ball that inmates would use to play pick-up.

When Pourrain joined in one day, he subtly flashed his talent, which he said earned him some respect.

“I wanted to stay to the side,” he said. “I didn’t feel comfortable getting close to the people who’d been there a long time, because you don’t know, you know? You don’t want problems with anyone.”

He was released from the Rio Grande detention center on August 28 after his family paid a $20,000 bond. Just days ago, as he sat on his apartment balcony with his wife, sharing a maté and eating a piece of toast, he felt that he was eating the best meal of his life. And while he was in ICE custody, Pourrain’s story had spread in Argentina and the U.S. He believes that soccer saved him.

“Soccer helped me outside as well, in that this went viral,” he said. “So many people supported me and thank God I got to leave. If it hadn’t been for soccer, maybe I wouldn’t even have gotten out, no one would’ve known about my story. I don’t know what would have happened.

“There are people who don’t have that luck, who are locked up today, who were denied bail,” he said. “They have to wait inside because a lot of people choose to wait inside rather than go back to their country. My message to them is have faith and fight to the end.

Pourrain described his ordeal bluntly. “It was torture,” he said. “Mentally, it was pure terror.” Pourrain’s idea of life in America took a turn that will stay with him forever. But, he said, he loves this country, and he plans to continue to pursue his immigration case legally.

“Unfortunately something happened that’s also the worst thing I’ve ever gone through in my life,” he said as he fought back tears. “I’ve also gone through beautiful moments here. I don’t know, it’s mixed. It’s strange. I just went back to the academy in Key Biscayne where I coach, and the support I received from the parents, from the community — from so many American citizens, was overwhelming.”

text:
Ask José Palma what brought him to the United States three decades ago and he’ll gently correct you. It’s not what brought him. It’s what shoved him here.

“Lo que me sacó fue la guerra,” he told an editorial board member, his voice measured. The war drove me out.

The Cold War-era conflict, a dozen years of scorched-earth struggle between left-wing guerrillas and the military-led government, displaced roughly a fifth of El Salvador’s population between 1980 and 1992. Both sides viewed innocent civilians as fair game. Only one was armed to the teeth with American weapons and billions of U.S. taxpayer dollars.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

What spat Palma out of his native country was, in no small part, the United States itself.

Now, the country where Palma found refuge — where he raised four U.S.-born children, bought a home and built a career as a paralegal and as a voice for other immigrants like him — is threatening to expel him again.

Houston Chronicle Logo

Want more Houston Chronicle?

Make us a Preferred Source on Google to see more of us when you search.

Add Preferred Source

Palma is one of an estimated 200,000 Salvadorans whose Temporary Protected Status is set to expire today. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson shared the following statement: “An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.” Should the government refuse to extend that status, he'll join over a million other TPS holders stripped of legal protections under the Trump administration’s widening delegalization push. Out of 17 countries that held TPS status at the beginning of Trump’s second term, now only three remain.

Salvadorans are the original TPS holders, the first to receive the status after George H.W. Bush cemented it in 1990. Losing it will unravel a life in the U.S. measured in decades — in mortgages paid off, in businesses built from the ground up and in an estimated 150,000 American children now forced to contemplate a future severed from their parents.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

That crisis is born of our own history.

The origins of TPS

In 1981, an elite unit of Salvadoran soldiers — funded and trained by the U.S. military — rounded up the villagers of a town called El Mozote for a limpieza. A cleansing. More than 1,000 people, half of them children, were killed. Their severed limbs were dumped in a pit.

When news reached Washington, President Ronald Reagan denied it, certifying to Congress that the Salvadoran military met human rights standards. It was the only way to keep U.S. funding flowing — eventually soaring to over $1 million per day.

The massacres didn’t end with El Mozote. Eventually, they arrived in Palma's hometown. His family fled to an encampment for war refugees and later to the city, but the bloodletting only worsened.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

At 22, Palma set out alone for the United States. It was 1990 and, like so many expelled by the war, he figured he had an open-and-shut case for political asylum. He didn’t know Salvadorans were being systematically rejected at a staggering rate of 98%.

As Palma explained, in his even-keeled way, “granting asylum to people fleeing the civil war would mean accepting that the funding being provided to El Salvador was destabilizing an entire country.”

In other words, it would mean admitting guilt.

Everyday Americans, including Houstonians working through the Rothko Chapel and Casa Juan Diego and the First Unitarian Church, demanded change. A coalition of 80 church groups and grassroots activists sued the government for discrimination, and indignant members of Congress crafted a solution: liminal legality for people fleeing unstable, “extraordinary” country conditions, renewed every six to eighteen months at the executive branch’s discretion.

The bitter compromise? A work permit, but no path to a green card.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Permanent uncertainty

The 1990 act that created TPS was the last major immigration reform package Congress would pass.

Since then, Democrats and Republicans have found it easier to extend TPS than to do the hard work of legislating lasting solutions for people whose status has been provisional in name only. Pressured by the demands of another regional exodus, this time from Venezuela, President Joe Biden frantically used TPS like a Band-Aid — bringing in millions with no long-term plan.

Immigrants who’d waited years for legal status felt deeply betrayed.

But letting TPS fizzle out is another kind of betrayal.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Every 18 months for 28 years, Palma has done what the American government has demanded. Diligently, he has paid the fees, filled out the paperwork, submitted fingerprints, and cleared background check after background check.

Each time, he has wondered whether it would be the last. Still, the enduring uncertainty — itself a kind of stability — allowed him to build a life here, first in Boston and then in Houston. The soupy climate here reminds him of his coastal Salvadoran hometown.

In Katy, he found a community of fellow “tepesianos,” or TPS holders like him. He now fights for them as the national coordinator of the TPS Alliance, leading delegations to meet with Congress and helping families cope. But Palma dreams of the day when he won’t have to strive so hard just to stay here; when he can focus on law school or spend his time coaching youth soccer.

The suburban sports complex where he plays pickup soccer is a snapshot of our city: a “mini Houston,” as Palma puts it, of rich and poor, immigrants and native-born Americans, all playing together.

A path forward

Today, that community is gripped by terror. As U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia warned us recently, Katy and other parts of southwest Houston could be the next targets for roving immigration round-ups.

Palma’s adult American children are sponsoring him for residency. But without TPS, he only has “adjustment of status,” a fragile administrative reprieve that ostensibly protects applicants from deportation while a green card is pending. Even that temporary safety net is under assault.

“What we’re living through isn’t a normal application of the law,” Palma said. It’s cruelty wielded as policy — bald-faced and unrelenting — to drive honest people to despair.

That cruelty is deadly. This summer, a 20-year-old Haitian honors student was fitted with a GPS ankle monitor after losing TPS. His father said the former varsity soccer player and Wright State University student was ruthlessly bullied and barred from playing his favorite sport. Unable to bear being branded a criminal, he walked into highway traffic in Ohio.

Like the war in El Salvador, the battle we’re waging against our own neighbors will leave lasting, jagged wounds.

Our Salvadoran community is about 219,000 strong, one of the nation’s largest. They contribute $590 million annually to Houston alone. To let fear hollow out the soul of this city — to watch pupuserias shuttered, homes abandoned mid-construction and soccer pitches emptied out — is a profound erosion of our own humanity and a self-inflicted wound to our economy.

Congress must find the spine to push for reform. In July, Rep. Garcia launched a discharge petition to force a House vote on the American Dream and Promise Act, which would secure permanent protections and a pathway to citizenship for certain TPS holders, among other immigrants.

Three Republicans have signed. The petition needs only one more name.

One Republican with moral courage can move this bill forward. One Republican should. We owe our neighbors — and our own conscience — at least that much.

text:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld an injunction blocking the Internal Revenue Service from sharing personal information such as the addresses of taxpayers with immigration authorities, ruling the Trump administration's policy was unlawful.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found that the IRS unlawfully disclosed taxpayer information in response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement's request for the last known addresses of 1.28 million suspected illegal migrants. The court said the IRS failed to ensure that ICE's requests met the "stringent conditions" required under a federal tax-confidentiality law adopted in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal, which generally bars the IRS from sharing tax-return information with other federal agencies.

Last year, the IRS shared roughly 47,000 taxpayer addresses with ICE under a policy that aims to assist President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. The IRS had adopted a policy that allowed ICE to collect taxpayer information, sparking lawsuits over allegations that the practice was unlawful.

A lower-court judge sided with the plaintiffs and blocked the policy, although by that time the IRS had already shared 47,289 taxpayer records with ICE.

IRS ERRONEOUSLY SHARED CONFIDENTIAL IMMIGRANT TAXPAYER DATA WITH DHS: COURT FILING

The administration appealed, arguing the ruling hindered federal law enforcement.

"But that's a gripe with Congress, not the court," U.S. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard said in the appeals court's ruling on Tuesday.

Pillard said the IRS procedures violated federal law in several ways, including "most egregiously" by not requiring ICE to provide an actual taxpayer address, as the law requires.

"The IRS failed to require ICE to provide a 'specific reason' why the requested return information 'is or may be relevant to [a qualifying] proceeding or investigation,' as the statute demands," Pillard wrote.

"It entirely fails to ensure that ICE lists a federal employee, let alone one ‘personally and directly engaged’ in a qualifying investigation of a particular taxpayer," Pillard continued. "That failure has serious consequences. When ICE requested information on 1.28 million taxpayers in the summer of 2025, ICE identified the same person as the point of contact for every single request."

The practice "automates the review of millions of records without any individual review or any other means of ensuring compliance with the legal prerequisites to releasing each individual taxpayer's information," the judge added.

The three-judge panel also ruled that information sharing would violate privacy laws.

"The Data-Exchange Procedure reduces noncitizens’ privacy rights in their tax returns. By providing a distinct, automated pathway for ICE to request noncitizens’ information, the Data-Exchange Procedure deprives noncitizens of the protections that section 6103 guarantees to all taxpayers," the court found.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement to Reuters that it disagrees with the ruling and "will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal."

text:
The town of Hudson has refused for months to take any steps to review and enforce its zoning code as it applies to a planned immigration detention center there, say the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to block the facility — and three Hudson residents are now joining them.

Wendy Homstad, Caden Grosshans and Emily Shanks, all residents of Hudson, were added as plaintiffs alongside Weld County resident Janet Carlson and the nonprofit Together Colorado, in an amended complaint filed Tuesday in state court, the group said. Carlson is a neighbor of the dormant prison known as the Big Horn Correctional Facility, which operated as a private prison for the Alaska Department of Corrections from 2009 until 2013, but her property is not within town limits.

The GEO Group, a private prison company, has announced a five-year contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen the facility as a 1,200-bed immigration detention center. But the lawsuit, filed in July against the town of Hudson, its town council, its planning commission and Planning Director Jennifer Woods, alleges that a conditional use permit for the site, approved by voters in 2008, is now void after more than 12 years of vacancy.

“I’ve gone to meeting after meeting, and I’ve watched my neighbors do the same, and every time the answer is the same: it’s not our problem,” Shanks said in a statement Wednesday. “I’m not asking Hudson to take a side in a national debate. I’m asking Hudson to follow its own rules, the same rules it would make anybody else follow.”

Hudson officials have maintained that the town “does not have authority to approve or deny federal use of this private facility.”

Faith group, Weld County resident sue Hudson over ICE detention center zoning issue

Attorneys for the town filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit last month, arguing the plaintiffs lack standing to bring the case. Together Colorado “lacks any connection to the Town,” they argued, while Carlson “lacks a direct connection to the Town,” and the injuries both plaintiffs claimed in the initial complaint were “presently speculative and cannot be determined until a remote time in the future.”

The amended complaint, however, points to Hudson’s own estimates, in its Water Supply Master Plan, that the reopened facility’s water consumption could reach 230 acre-feet annually, nearly doubling the town’s average water use over the last 20 years.

“The reopening of the (Big Horn Correctional Facility) will reintroduce demands that the Town has not anticipated for some time,” the plan says.

“Once the (facility) reopens, Hudson no longer can use the (Colorado-Big Thompson Project water) dedicated for the prison to meet other water demands within Town,” it continues. “This drives the need for Hudson to immediately shift its approach to use other water resources to meet its water demands.”

Other concerns cited by town residents in the new complaint relate to a projected increase in 911 calls, a trend observed in other rural ICE detention centers run by GEO, and the risk of public health emergencies like the tuberculosis case state officials have been barred from investigating at GEO’s facility in Aurora.

“After hearing about deaths and disease outbreaks in other detention centers, including a tuberculosis outbreak at the GEO-operated facility in Aurora, Plaintiffs Homstad and Grosshans have also grown concerned about the public health risks posed by the Facility, which could spread to the community through Facility staff and visitors, and the strain on the Town’s limited emergency services infrastructure,” the complaint reads.

Despite months of residents raising concerns about the facility through public comment periods and other official channels, town officials have declined to formally explain their position, review the alleged violation, “adopt an official code revision, or issue a conditional use permit” for the facility, the suit alleges.

“Hudson has had every opportunity to sit down, answer questions, and follow the process laid out in its own code,” said David Seligman, executive director of Towards Justice, the progressive legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs. “Instead it has chosen silence, and now litigation.”

Immigration advocates and Colorado Democrats have been staunchly opposed to the Hudson facility’s potential use as an ICE detention center since last year. The Aurora facility, which has long been the target of criticism from activists over allegations of inhumane conditions and dehumanizing treatment, is Colorado’s only currently operational ICE detention center.

GEO seeks to intervene

In his second term, President Donald Trump has pledged to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” aiming to remove all of the estimated 12 million immigrants in the country without permanent legal status, regardless of how long they have been in the country, the legal status of their family members or whether they have criminal records.

Together with CoreCivic, another large private-prison company, The GEO Group is expected to be the prime beneficiary of a multibillion-dollar windfall for expanded immigration detention services authorized by Republicans’ 2025 spending and tax cut law. Last year, GEO chairman George Zoley spoke during an earnings call about the “attractive opportunity for investors” presented by “the unprecedented growth opportunities we anticipate will materialize over the balance of this year and next year.”

Attorneys for GEO moved to intervene in the case last month so that the company “can seek dismissal of this lawsuit and, if necessary, defend its substantial interest in performing its contracts with the property owner and ICE.”

The plaintiffs say their case only concerns the town of Hudson’s application of its zoning laws. They’re seeking a court order requiring town officials to comply with the “relevant procedures for amending the Land Development Code and/or granting or amending a conditional use permit.”

“This case concerns only the Town’s own authority and duties under the LDC — not the validity, meaning, or performance of any contract to which GEO is a party,” the plaintiffs in an Aug. 31 filing said. “GEO’s efforts to intervene in this matter will do nothing other than needlessly complicate this litigation.”

Despite months of residents raising concerns about the facility through public comment periods and other official channels, town officials have declined to formally explain their position, review the alleged violation, “adopt an official code revision, or issue a conditional use permit” for the facility, the suit alleges.

“Hudson has had every opportunity to sit down, answer questions, and follow the process laid out in its own code,” said David Seligman, executive director of Towards Justice, the progressive legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs. “Instead it has chosen silence, and now litigation.”

Immigration advocates and Colorado Democrats have been staunchly opposed to the Hudson facility’s potential use as an ICE detention center since last year. The Aurora facility, which has long been the target of criticism from activists over allegations of inhumane conditions and dehumanizing treatment, is Colorado’s only currently operational ICE detention center.

GEO seeks to intervene

In his second term, President Donald Trump has pledged to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” aiming to remove all of the estimated 12 million immigrants in the country without permanent legal status, regardless of how long they have been in the country, the legal status of their family members or whether they have criminal records.

Together with CoreCivic, another large private-prison company, The GEO Group is expected to be the prime beneficiary of a multibillion-dollar windfall for expanded immigration detention services authorized by Republicans’ 2025 spending and tax cut law. Last year, GEO chairman George Zoley spoke during an earnings call about the “attractive opportunity for investors” presented by “the unprecedented growth opportunities we anticipate will materialize over the balance of this year and next year.”

Attorneys for GEO moved to intervene in the case last month so that the company “can seek dismissal of this lawsuit and, if necessary, defend its substantial interest in performing its contracts with the property owner and ICE.”

The plaintiffs say their case only concerns the town of Hudson’s application of its zoning laws. They’re seeking a court order requiring town officials to comply with the “relevant procedures for amending the Land Development Code and/or granting or amending a conditional use permit.”

“This case concerns only the Town’s own authority and duties under the LDC — not the validity, meaning, or performance of any contract to which GEO is a party,” the plaintiffs in an Aug. 31 filing said. “GEO’s efforts to intervene in this matter will do nothing other than needlessly complicate this litigation.”

text:
LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen is facing pushback from the challengers to his reelection bid over his immigration stance as a new Flatwater Free Press investigation states his family ag operation has long hired undocumented laborers.

The Flatwater report, released Wednesday in partnership with The New York Times, states Pillen’s hog business has employed migrant workers for more than a decade, some of whom are in the country legally and others who are not. The Flatwater story says it confirmed the reporting with state and federal court records and interviews with more than 40 current and former employees, prosecutors, immigration lawyers and community organizers.

The challengers to Pillen’s reelection each argued Wednesday that the investigation shows Pillen plays by “his own set of rules.”

Hours after the investigation was released, Pillen’s campaign released “Pillen Playbook 2.0,” an updated policy wishlist. It’s a play on Pillen’s having been a defensive back for the Huskers in the 1970s.

The memo mentions immigration once, with no specifics: “Eliminate state taxpayer benefits for illegals.”

Pillen and family company respond

According to Flatwater, Pillen Family Farms and an official spokesperson for Pillen said neither the company nor the governor “knowingly hired an illegal immigrant.”

Laura Strimple, Pillen’s spokesperson, told Flatwater the governor “went above and beyond the legal requirements to verify the immigration status of his employees” and that he “has the strongest immigration record in Nebraska history.”

Nearly one year ago, at Pillen’s direction, the director of the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services signed a contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to convert a state prison in McCook into a new ICE holding facility. Pillen and federal officials dubbed the rebranded Work Ethic Camp the “Cornhusker Clink.”

“We want President Trump to know that Nebraska is supportive and grateful for his ongoing, critical work with Secretary (Kristi) Noem to arrest and deport criminal, illegal aliens,” Pillen said in an Aug. 19, 2025, statement when he announced the Nebraska-ICE partnership.

Pillen and Corrections Director Rob Jeffreys also fought back against a lawsuit, mostly from McCook residents, challenging their authority to convert the prison without legislative approval. A judge upheld Pillen’s discretion. Advocates are appealing to the Nebraska Court of Appeals.

At a campaign event in late August in Lincoln, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, a longtime prosecutor who is Pillen’s homeland security adviser, did not reference the McCook facility but did praise Pillen for twice deploying Nebraska National Guard soldiers to the U.S.-Mexico border

“We found some great Nebraska soldiers who were willing to do that, and it was very helpful to that overall effort to do and give us what we’ve got today: a border where people aren’t climbing over those fences every five minutes like they were years ago,” Kelly said at the time.

Pillen’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday on the Flatwater-NYT investigation.

‘His own set of rules’

Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, Pillen’s Democratic opponent this fall, said the Flatwater investigation outlines Pillen’s “latest con.” She asserted, as she has before, that Pillen has been “enriching himself and his friends since day one, and this falls right into the pattern.”

“When the cameras are off, the rules don’t seem to apply to him,” Walz said in a statement. “He’s built a career holding other people to standards he won’t keep himself. When it’s his farm, his business, his bottom line — suddenly the rules have a lot more flexibility.”

Walz said she would be a governor “who actually is what they say they are.”

Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, who is running for governor as the America First Party nominee, said in a social media post Wednesday that he read the “disturbing” story but is “not at all surprised. This is exactly who Governor Jim Pillen is.”

“He plays by his own set of rules while holding the rest of the state to a different standard. If this is how he has run his business for decades, how has he been running the state the last 3.5 years?” Lindstrom wrote.

Lindstrom ran against Pillen for the GOP nomination in 2022. He later switched to nonpartisan earlier this year before switching to the America First Party to revive his gubernatorial bid.

Rick Beard, who is the gubernatorial nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, said that if people are “actually serious” about border control, then corporate owners and leadership need to be held criminally accountable for their illegal practices.

“Making them accountable removes the engine creating unauthorized workforces in the first place,” Beard said in an email to the Nebraska Examiner. “Our culture of excusing corporate crimes while calling those crimes a necessity to do business has to end. No one is above the law in the state of Nebraska.”

‘Pillen Playbook 2.0’

Walz and Lindstrom have each released their own platforms. Walz’s is “Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans,” and Lindstrom’s is the “Nebraska Doctrine.” Beard, while he does not have a set policy document, has called for a state-run medical cannabis program, among other priorities.

Among the new items in Pillen’s “Playbook 2.0” released Wednesday:

Lower property insurance rates.

Stop hedge funds from buying up Nebraska homes.

Eliminate toxins in food and water.

Protect the Ogallala aquifer.

Protect the integrity of elections and reform the “broken ballot petition process.”

Counter aggression from the Chinese Communist Party and other foreign adversaries.

Ensure all third graders can read at grade level.

Reform K-12 funding to have the state take on more of the burden of educating children.

Expand trade opportunities for agricultural products.

As with policy platforms released by other gubernatorial candidates this year, Pillen’s campaign does not state exactly how he would achieve or fund the ideas in his “playbook.”

Said Pillen: “The new Pillen Playbook is about my commitment to the people of our state: making Nebraska more affordable, defending the values that make our state extraordinary, investing in our kids and workforce and protecting the land, water and communities we are proud to call home.”

Beard, responding to Pillen’s policy platform, described the updated Pillen platform as “all hat and no cattle.” Beard said his proposals, to grow Nebraska’s own food and produce new revenue with cannabis and industrial hemp, would clean Nebraska’s soil and provide new rural opportunities.

Lindstrom said in a text that “what’s most striking” about the document “is what’s missing.”

“There’s no mention of Nebraska’s budget crisis, the hundreds of millions of dollars in shortfalls or any accountability for the decisions made over the last three and a half years that helped put us here,” Lindstrom said. “Nebraskans don’t need a recycled playbook of promises. They deserve an honest assessment of where we are today and a real plan to fix it.”

Walz had no immediate comment on the “Pillen Playbook 2.0.”

The general election is Nov. 3.

text:
Thirty-one-year-old Daysi González is among around 170,000 people originally from El Salvador who are legally living in the U.S. through Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.

On Tuesday, when she spoke with Spectrum News, she was uncertain whether she would still be a legal resident after Wednesday.

“I’ve been telling people that it feels like the rug is being pulled out from under me constantly,” she said. “ … It’s never felt this final. Like, it’s never gotten this close to the expiration date without any news.”

Earlier this year, the Trump administration announced it is ending TPS for Salvadorans effective Wednesday. But Gonzalez said that she has heard nothing since that announcement and has been planning for the worst-case scenario.

“The plan is to sell my house, everything that I can’t take with me and go back to El Salvador, a place I haven’t been to since I was 5,” Gonzalez explained.

Late Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security offered Gonzalez and others like her some answers on the future of her legal status. Gonzalez was worried that on Thursday she would lose her ability to continue working in the U.S. or risk being deported.

“An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson told Spectrum News in a statement. “Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”

The information from DHS is not what Gonzalez had hoped for, which was that TPS would be extended again. Thd designation for Salvadorans has been extended many times since it was first put into place in December 2000. The news does, however, allow Salvadoran TPS holders to continue working for now. Not knowing how long those protections will last keeps Gonzalez and others like her in limbo.

USC Gould School of Law professor Jean Reisz says that TPS holders generally don’t have a legal pathway toward citizenship.

“TPS doesn’t provide a pathway to permanent resident status, and one has to be a permanent resident before they can become a citizen,” she said. “The only way to become a permanent resident is through a close family member, through employment, with special skills and through asylum or as a refugee.”

Reisz added that a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision also gives the Trump administration a lot of power in deciding when it wants to end TPS protections.

“The problem is the Supreme Court decision, Mullin vs. Doe, really took a lot of rights away to challenge a decision not to extend TPS or the decision to terminate it,” Reisz said. “It made a lot of those challenges go away because the Supreme Court says we can’t really review that decision.”

A bipartisan group of lawmakers has previously lobbied the Trump administration to extend TPS for other groups but has been unsuccessful. Immigration advocates, however, say that deporting Salvadoran TPS holders will have a unique impact on the U.S. economy.

According to the American Immigration Council, Maryland, Virginia, California, Texas and New York have the largest numbers of Salvadoran TPS holders. There are also significant numbers living in North Carolina, Massachusetts and Georgia. Many of them work in construction, food service and landscaping.

“It’s going to create a lot of hiccups in the economy, and a lot of businesses can’t survive because they can’t hire such workers,” said Ernesto Castaneda, director at the Center for Latin American and Latino Studies. “If they don’t have enough workers and they cannot fulfill the contracts, they’re going to have to close. So a lot of American citizens stand to lose money and probably lose their jobs because there won’t be enough workers for those businesses that hire them.”

Castaneda believes that even President Donald Trump could be impacted by a decision to end Salvadoran TPS. He said he believes the deportation of these TPS recipients could lead to delays with some of Trump’s own construction projects in the D.C. area.

“Right now, there’s a heliport that is being finished, being built in front of the White House, as well as the ballroom,” Castaneda said. “Some of those workers are likely Salvadorans. Some of them will have been working legally here through TPS.”

While living in their communities and working, TPS holders have also been paying taxes and spending money at local businesses. Some have started their own businesses which employ U.S. citizens. Others have started families and risk separation from children who are U.S. citizens.

text:
MIAMI — Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador expire Wednesday, but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens.

On Wednesday a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News, “An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”

The Trump administration has ended protections for hundreds of thousands of TPS recipients from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries.

If DHS takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days.

About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of Homeland Security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits.

During President Donald Trump’s second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 14 countries, including El Salvador, Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. Only about 103,000 from three countries remain protected with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon.

The Trump administration obtained a major victory when the Supreme Court ruled in June that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS.

Congress created temporary protections in 1990

TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026.

The vast majority of Salvadoran TPS holders have children born in the U.S. Many have lost their jobs and fear being detained, separated from their American family members, and deported to a country they barely know.

El Salvador has been a Trump ally

El Salvador, once one of the most violent places in the world, has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador’s travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders.

Bukele has been an ally of Trump’s policy of mass deportations and was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison in El Salvador also known as CECOT.

Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture, and disappearances in the Central American nation’s prison system.

Trump received Bukele at the White House in April of 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Less than a year later, in July of 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington, the Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits.

Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of country’s gross domestic product, according to El Salvador’s central bank.

title: New report shows the economic toll of ICE raids - NPR
description:
Now, new research quantifies how much these ICE arrest operations are costing local economies, and not just in immigrant neighborhoods.
Rumors were running wild that this city was going to be the first to see ICE raids.
A new study out today shows just how big an economic impact that panic and the ICE raids that followed had.
The report by the University of Illinois Chicago used anonymous GPS data from cellphones to unpack the economic toll of ICE operations in 2025 throughout Chicago.
GARSD: Several other studies have confirmed that ICE raids have sent economic shock waves throughout local economies in and well beyond immigrant neighborhoods.
text:
Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

The Trump administration's nationwide immigration crackdown is well into its second year. Federal immigration agents have arrested hundreds of thousands of people since Inauguration Day. On any given day, about 65,000 people are sitting in immigration detention. That's a record. And about 70% of them have no criminal conviction. Now, new research quantifies how much these ICE arrest operations are costing local economies, and not just in immigrant neighborhoods. Here's NPR's Jasmine Garsd.

JASMINE GARSD, BYLINE: In the days after President Donald Trump took office on January 20, 2025, the mood in Chicago's Latino neighborhoods was tense. Rumors were running wild that this city was going to be the first to see ICE raids. A waitress NPR spoke to back then, named Caridad, requested that we not use her last name for fear of being targeted.

CARIDAD: (Speaking Spanish).

GARSD: "I have to go grocery shopping," she said, "but I haven't because what if ICE is there? People are more than afraid. They're panicking." A new study out today shows just how big an economic impact that panic and the ICE raids that followed had. The report by the University of Illinois Chicago used anonymous GPS data from cellphones to unpack the economic toll of ICE operations in 2025 throughout Chicago. The study tracked movement between immigrant neighborhoods and nonimmigrant neighborhoods in Chicago's Cook County. Professor Matt Wilson, a study co-author, says the usual back-and-forth between the two areas stopped almost immediately.

MATT WILSON: The flows from the high Latin American-born areas to the low Latin American-born areas collapsed after January 20.

GARSD: Wilson says it's remarkable how strongly the economic impact was felt outside those immigrant communities. Now, the report estimates that the raids cost retail and restaurants in nonimmigrant neighborhoods in the county about $1.26 billion, and it cost the state around $107 million in tax revenue.

WILSON: We see that 9% drop in retail and 10% drop in restaurant visits, and it persists for about a year. People's behavior systematically changed after January 20, 2025, and it never recovered.

GARSD: For a small business, a 10% drop over the course of a year can be a financial hit. In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, quote, "If there was any correlation between rampant illegal immigration and a good economy, Biden would have had a booming economy. Removing these criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers." Wilson, the researcher, says the report underscores that no community is an island.

WILSON: I think a lot of people treat Latino and some immigrant communities as if they're insular and they're isolated. But it's really that these communities are much more integrated into the broader economy and they're making trips to faraway places in the county routinely.

GARSD: Several other studies have confirmed that ICE raids have sent economic shock waves throughout local economies in and well beyond immigrant neighborhoods. Jasmine Garsd, NPR News, New York.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Customs and Border Protection has launched a new Trusted Traveler App mobile app to continue its mission to improve and innovate the traveler experience.

“The new Trusted Traveler mobile app brings application and membership management features together with our popular Global Entry arrival confirmation feature,” said Executive Assistant Commissioner Diane J. Sabatino, of CBP’s Office of Field Operations. “Having one official app to support all of our services makes every step of the journey less complicated for travelers.”

The Trusted Traveler App brings the capabilities of two previously available apps into one official app. The free app, available in both the Apple App Store and Google Play, helps travelers manage their applications to Global Entry, NEXUS, SENTRI, or FAST. It supports membership updates, enrollment interview scheduling, and the ability to renew memberships. The app also allows Global Entry members to confirm their international arrivals with CBP when arriving at a U.S. airport.

Currently, 85 airports and multiple CBP Preclearance locations support the new Trusted Traveler App. Travelers who have used the previous Global Entry Mobile App and/or Trusted Traveler Programs App can download the new app and sign in using their existing credentials, and their profile and membership information will transfer over. The previously available apps have been discontinued.

Global Entry, one of the Department of Homeland Security’s Trusted Traveler Programs, provides expedited clearance for prescreened, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States. All applicants undergo rigorous background checks and in-person interviews before enrollment.

Global Entry has millions of members worldwide benefiting from expedited entry services each year. Through these partnerships, CBP continues to promote secure and efficient travel while fostering stronger multilateral relationships.
