text:
Current and former Members of Congress mobilized in a court filing challenging the legality of President Donald Trump’s Executive Order seeking to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The effort was led by House Administration Ranking Member Joe Morelle; Assistant House Minority Leader Joe Neguse, who leads the House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force; and Task Force Co-Chairs Oversight Ranking Member Robert Garcia and Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin. In the Senate, the brief was championed by Rules Committee Ranking Member Alex Padilla; Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer; Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin; and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gary Peters.

The group, made up of a bipartisan, bicameral coalition of 261 lawmakers, filed an amicus brief to the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al., a lawsuit brought by a coalition of State Attorneys General against the U.S. Postal Service. The court case challenges a Final Rule issued by the USPS pursuant to Trump’s directive that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

One-third of Americans are expected to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections—a voting practice Donald Trump himself used as recently as August 2026, when the president voted in Florida’s Republican primary.

In the court filing, the amici curiae argue that Trump’s Executive Order 14399, “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” violates the separation of powers and usurps congressional authorities outlined in Article I of the U.S. Constitution, which gives the states and Congress exclusive authority over election administration.

“As current and former legislators, amici took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States—including its guarantee of the separation of powers. Amici have a particular interest in defending the institutional role of the Legislative Branch under Article I of the Constitution and in vindicating the long-settled principle that the Constitution commits ultimate regulatory authority over federal elections to Congress. The Constitution does not contemplate the Executive Branch acting unilaterally to assert power over federal elections. Yet that is what the Order and Final Rule do,” wrote the lawmakers.

The amici also pointed to a recent federal court ruling blocking the USPS from implementing its newly finalized mail ballot rule for the midterm elections, saying the agency lacked the authority to implement the rule and that its actions are “substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law.”

“The district court correctly concluded that Appellees are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims that USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule, that the Final Rule unconstitutionally imposes mail-ballot requirements on the States, and that the Final Rule unconstitutionally bars non-compliant State and local election officials from using the USPS to mail ballots at all.”

The group concluded by asserting States’ power to administer elections and Congress’s power to make or alter rules regulating elections, which the Supreme Court itself has described as an “override” authority. The president’s illegal incursion on this authority is an attempt to disenfranchise people who depend on mail-in ballots to vote.

The lawmakers concluded: “The integrity of our constitutional system depends on each branch keeping to its assigned role. The Framers set up a two-part system that gave the States default authority to regulate federal elections subject to Congress’s authority to override the States. The Framers did not provide the President with any authority to interfere in that system, nor has Congress imbued the Executive Branch with any such authority by statute.”

Click HERE to view the full brief.

Keep scrolling to see what leading lawmakers had to say about the matter.

“The Constitution is clear that the states and Congress make the rules for federal elections, not the President. Yet, in utter defiance of the Constitution, President Trump is attempting to use the Postal Service to decide who can and cannot receive a ballot just days before mail-in voting begins in some of the states. This is a naked power grab by a historically unpopular President—who himself regularly votes by mail—to inject confusion and chaos into our elections in a last-ditch effort to keep his party in power. It will not work. I’m proud to stand with a strong bipartisan, bicameral group of current and former colleagues in urging the court to continue rejecting this lawless election interference,” said Ranking Member Jamie Raskin.

“Presidents do not control our elections—the American people do. Today, in a bipartisan agreement, Members defended the constitutional authority of Congress and deliberately chose to protect our elections from executive overreach. Our elections are safe and secure, and we intend to keep them that way. We will not allow USPS to put Americans’ ballots at risk,” said Ranking Member Joe Morelle.

“The law is clear: states and Congress have authority over our elections — not the President and certainly not the Postal Service. Protecting the right to vote-by-mail is critical to ensure every eligible voter can make their voices heard in the November midterm elections and in future elections,” said Senator Alex Padilla. “Despite the Trump Administration’s attempts to eliminate vote by mail and suppress voter participation, voting by mail remains one of the most safe and secure ways to vote, especially for service members, rural voters, and Americans living abroad. I urge the courts to uphold our Constitution and reject Trump’s attacks on our fundamental right to vote.”

“Donald Trump is trying to unconstitutionally rig the midterm elections because he knows that's the only way he can hold on to power. This scheme could potentially stop millions of American citizens from receiving their ballots and having their vote counted. We are fighting this in court and defending the Constitution,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.

“Donald Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting are in direct contravention of the U.S. Constitution. His executive order and the USPS actions to implement it would disenfranchise millions of Americans, silencing an untold number of citizens that rely on mail ballots to make their voices heard. But the right to vote is sacrosanct, and we’ll do whatever it takes to protect it,” said House Assistant Minority Leader Joe Neguse. “I’m proud to see the outpouring of support from current and former Members of Congress—across the political spectrum—to assert the rule of law in this matter and to stand up for the right of every eligible voter to fairly cast their ballot.”

“Donald Trump is once again asking the highest court in the land to silence voters and destroy the precious integrity of the American electoral process,” said Leader Schumer. “Mail-in voting is proven safe and secure, and Trump’s continued efforts to obstruct America’s free and fair elections are blatant, unconstitutional attempts at interfering with the November midterms. Trump’s message to the American people is clear: he isn’t worried about voter fraud, he’s afraid of voter accountability. I urge the court to uphold the Constitution and reject Trump’s baseless attempt at poisoning our democracy.”

Background

The Litigation Task Force launched in the first month that followed President Donald Trump’s chaotic return to office. We immediately set out to push back against an administration showing no respect for the Constitution or rule of law—and we haven’t stopped since. Our first amicus brief, filed in February 2025, defended American consumers from predatory lenders and other bad actors and helped persuade a federal judge to block efforts to dismantle the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).

Since then, the Task Force has directly responded to a myriad of other unlawful directives issued by the Trump administration, including simultaneously filing a court motion challenging the legitimacy of the president’s corrupt attempt to “settle” his lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — an agency he oversees — in exchange for the creation of a $1.7 billion slush fund for political allies.

text:
A new study shows that the widespread fear and isolation caused by the immigration crackdowns that began in early 2025 had a significant economic toll on Chicago commerce, draining over $1.26 billion from local businesses.

The report, published by the University of Illinois Chicago, used anonymous cellphone GPS data to track movement between immigrant and non-immigrant neighborhoods throughout Chicago's Cook County. Researchers found that the routine back-and-forth between these areas collapsed almost immediately after President Donald Trump took office on Jan. 20, 2025, amid rampant rumors and the subsequent sweeps that Chicago would be targeted for immediate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids.

Professor Matt Wilson, a co-author of the study, noted how strongly the economic ripples were felt outside of immigrant communities in the area. The report estimates that decreased consumer mobility cost retail shops and restaurants in non-immigrant neighborhoods roughly $1.26 billion, while costing the state of Illinois an estimated $107 million in lost tax revenue.

"We see a 9% drop in retail and a 10% drop in restaurant visits, and it persisted for about a year," Wilson told NPR. "And it's not that it recovered after a year. People's behavior systematically changed after January 20, 2025." He says the city has yet to recover.

For small businesses, a sustained 10% drop in foot traffic business over the course of a year can be a serious financial hit. The new study challenges assumptions about immigrant community isolation, Wilson added. "I think a lot of people treat Latino and some immigrant communities as if they're insular and isolated," Wilson said. "But it's really that these communities are much more integrated into the broader economy, and they are making trips to faraway places in the county, routinely."

The intense fear that triggered these behavior shifts was palpable in the days surrounding the 2025 inauguration.

"I have to go grocery shopping, but I haven't. What if ICE is there?" a Chicago waitress named Caridad told NPR at the time, requesting that her last name be withheld, for fear of being targeted. "People are more than afraid, they're panicking."

Since then, the administration's immigration crackdowns have resulted in hundreds of thousands of arrests nationwide. Today, the immigration detention population sits at a record high of approximately 65,000 people.

The White House defended the aggressive enforcement strategy. In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "Removing these criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S."

However, ICE's own agency statistics show that roughly 70% of those currently detained have no criminal convictions.

The new report is part of a growing body of research confirming that large-scale immigration enforcement operations send severe economic shockwaves through broader local economies. A Brookings Institution report estimates estimates a roughly 1.7 percentage point decline in aggregate consumer spending in high-enforcement states

In Minneapolis, the city estimates total economic damage from ICE enforcement sweeps there at nearly $700 million, with small businesses in the city losing more than $81 million in revenue in January alone.

text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — A former Nicaraguan paramilitary detained by U.S. immigration authorities could soon be deported to the country where he said he was imprisoned and tortured — or sent to another country where he would be rendered stateless.

Marlon Gerardo Sáenz Cruz, 65, who defected from the ruling Sandinista party, was among 222 prisoners stripped of their Nicaraguan citizenship and brought to D.C. through a U.S. State Department initiative in February 2023. Now, after being detained during his check-in with immigration authorities in Los Angeles on Aug. 17, he must make his case before an immigration judge to remain in the U.S.

His immigration court date on Sept. 8 comes as asylum denial rates have spiked under the Trump administration and as people granted lesser protections from deportation are increasingly being sent to third countries in Latin America and Africa where they have no ties.

“Even if he manages to get protection from a U.S. immigration judge, it’s not ensured safety,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Sáenz’s detention followed a letter sent to the U.S. State Department last year by a group of Nicaraguan exiles, mainly in Miami. They allege that he and dozens of other former government officials maintain their ties to the government of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo.

The exiles also accused Sáenz of harassing other government opponents while in the U.S. A legal representative for Sáenz said he was simply responding to attacks against him.

“We are asking the State Department to investigate all these people because it’s unacceptable that they are washing the blood off their hands and covering up the actions of a criminal who shouldn’t be in the United States and who is a threat to national security,” said Aida Carrion-Vanegas, president of the advocacy organization Nicaraguan Americans United for the Republic.

In October 2025, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau responded to Carrion-Vanegas on X, saying he would look into the allegations. She has not heard from him since. The U.S. State Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Sáenz’s potential deportation to Nicaragua would send a message that “discourages future defections and reinforces the regime’s narrative that there is no safe exit,” said accredited court representative Muriel Sáenz, who has been assisting with his asylum application and is not related to him.

From Sandinista to prisoner to ICE detainee

Sáenz, known in Nicaragua as El Chino Enoc, became a guerrilla fighter as a teenager in the 1970s and remained close to high-level Sandinista figures for decades. He later spoke to Nicaraguan press about his involvement in a government-aligned paramilitary group that repressed protesters following mass anti-government marches demanding Ortega’s resignation in 2018. Hundreds were killed.

Ortega has claimed the 2018 protests were a U.S.-backed coup to overthrow him and that those imprisoned were involved in the plot.

Sáenz’s accredited representative denied that he had killed anyone or committed any crime in Nicaragua.

Sáenz broke with the government in 2019, and began using his popular YouTube channel to denounce corruption within the Ortega-Murillo government, which has maintained its grip on power for nearly two decades while stifling dissent through the imprisonment and torture of opponents.

He was imprisoned in Nicaragua in May 2022 on drug and weapons trafficking charges that he has called politically motivated.

He now has a leg ulcer, glaucoma and other health issues, some stemming from being tortured and held in solitary confinement, according to Muriel Sáenz, who said she fears for his health. She said complications from having polio as a child have worsened in ICE detention and he now uses a wheelchair.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment, but its online locator shows Sáenz is being held at Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center.

A complicated immigration case

Sáenz’s immigration case presents a legal dilemma because an immigration judge will have to weigh his alleged involvement in human rights abuses against the principle of not sending someone to danger, explained Heather Hogan, a lawyer and policy and practice counsel for the American Immigration Lawyer Association.

Sáenz and the other Nicaraguan prisoners entered the U.S. on humanitarian parole, a temporary status granted in emergencies that does not guarantee a pathway to citizenship. He then opened an asylum case within a year of entering the country as required.

Under U.S. immigration law, perpetrators of human rights abuses, including torture, enforced disappearances or extrajudicial killings, are barred from receiving asylum, and a judge would have to determine if Sáenz’s past involvement with the Sandinista government makes him ineligible.

But a judge could also grant Sáenz deportation deferral under the Convention Against Torture, CAT, an international human rights treaty that the U.S. is party to, if he is found likely to face torture in Nicaragua.

That protection would prevent Sáenz from being deported to Nicaragua, but would not grant him permanent immigration status or prevent the U.S. from sending him to a third country, as has become common under the Trump administration.

“In some cases like this, people do get granted deferral,” said Hogan, who previously decided cases of people implicated in possible human rights abuses as an asylum officer for the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

“Because our analysis is more about following our laws and international obligations … not carrying out a trial and imposing a punishment for their past actions.”

But the Trump administration has broken with the precedent of allowing people with CAT protections to remain in the U.S., instead sending them to third countries, said Arvey of Human Rights First.

“It’s a bleak situation because never before has this population been targeted in this way,” she said.

Raising questions on accountability for human rights abuses in Nicaragua

Nicaraguan exiles are split on how Saénz’s case should be handled.

Miguel Mora, a former prisoner who arrived in the U.S. in the same group as Sáenz and also has a pending asylum case, said Sáenz’s involvement in the 2018 repression made the case “complicated,” but he said “it corresponds exclusively to U.S. authorities to determine, based on the law and the evidence in the case, if he does or does not have the right to asylum.”

Danny Ramírez-Ayérdiz, a Nicaraguan lawyer and founder of the Interamerican Center for Legal Assistance in Human Rights that investigates abuses of the Ortega-Murillo government, said that Sáenz should be held accountable for his alleged crimes — but only after a political transition in Nicaragua, when he could be extradited there to face justice.

“But if they send him to Nicaragua now, he’s at a risk of dying,” Ramírez-Ayérdiz said. “Just like other former Sandinistas, the government would be particularly cruel with him.”

Manuel Prado, vice president of the Miskitu American Organization, which advocates for the rights of Nicaraguan Indigenous groups, said the outcome of Sáenz’s case will send a message about how Nicaragua will move forward “to heal the nation.”

Four years of my career was working out of Houlton on the Maine/Canada border with the U.S. Border Patrol, the U.S. Immigration Agency and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. These officers on the border earned the trust of the people they serve.

text:
The Arlington County Board has set aside $50,000 for grants to support families whose primary wage earner has been detained by immigration enforcement.

Grants distributed by Arlington Thrive will provide up to $2,000 per affected family over the coming 10 months. Funds will support basic needs such as housing, food and utilities.

The 4-0 vote, with Board member Susan Cunningham absent, was taken at a special Board meeting on Sept. 2 in response to a recent immigration enforcement surge in the D.C. area.

“We stand with our immigrant families, and we will not stop doing so,” Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said. “We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed.”

The grant agreement allows for Arlington Thrive to provide funding in the form of checks or debit cards to meet individual circumstances of individual families.

If neither format works well, the organization and county will work with the families on an alternate option.

“A lot of these families are unbanked,” County Manager Mark Schwartz said.

Elizabeth Matlock, a staff member in the county manager’s office who is coordinating the effort, said the funding will be available shortly.

“Thrive is eager to get started with this project,” she said.

The County Board’s action follows an Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation that resulted in roughly 1,300 arrests across the D.C. area during two weeks in August. It is unclear how many of these arrests took place in Arlington.

Federal law prohibits local governments and their law-enforcement agencies from interfering with federal immigration operations, de Ferranti acknowledged in August. However, he said that Arlington leaders “will do everything we can within the law to provide support and to protect the safety of all our residents, documented and undocumented.”

One arrest during the recent ICE operation, that of Jose Mejia Hernandez, has prompted an investigation by the Arlington County Police Department. Mejia Hernandez has alleged that he suffered a brain bleed and other injuries after ICE reportedly chased him and shot him with a stun gun in a parking lot on Columbia Pike on Aug. 11.

As the Supreme Court has acknowledged, presidents have no authority to remove officers or employees whom they do not appoint.
text:
Congress created the office of the Register of Copyrights over a hundred years ago to, among other things, provide advice to Congress on the nation’s copyright program. Congress also specified that the Librarian of Congress had the exclusive authority to appoint, supervise, and remove the Registrar. Notwithstanding this, President Trump attempted to unilaterally remove Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter, after firing the Librarian of Congress who had appointed her. The administration was seemingly punishing Register Perlmutter for her report on the use of copyrighted material to train generative AI.

In September 2026, the Constitutional Accountability Center filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of two Members of Congress who are deeply familiar with the Register’s work, Ranking Member of the Committee on House Administration Joseph Morelle and Ranking Member of the House Committee on the Judiciary Jamie Raskin. Their brief in support of Registrar Perlmutter makes three principal points.

First, Congress exercised its broad authority over federal offices when creating the Register of Copyrights as a legislative officer under the control of the Librarian of Congress. The Constitution gives Congress the authority to determine how to shape the federal government, and Congress chose to place the Register of Copyrights within the legislative branch, under the exclusive control of the Librarian of Congress. In doing this, Congress exercised its authority to regulate the appointment and removal of “inferior” officers like the Register of Copyrights. And nowhere in the legislation creating the Register of Copyrights did lawmakers grant the President any authority over her.

Second, presidents have no inherent authority to remove the Register of Copyrights. As the Supreme Court has acknowledged, presidents have no authority to remove officers or employees whom they do not appoint. This holding is consistent with the Framers’ understanding at the Founding, confirmed by decades of subsequent practice. And though the Supreme Court recently invalidated removal restrictions applicable to certain presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed heads of independent agencies exercising “vast” regulatory powers, their decision provides no basis for extending the President’s removal power to inferior officers who are not appointed by the President.

Finally, the administration has argued that the Take Care Clause gives presidents inherent constitutional authority to designate acting officers, but no court has ever endorsed that theory. And with good reason: it is at odds with constitutional text and historical practice. Even the executive branch had not previously licensed such a broad contravention of the Appointments Clause.

Immigration fines are authorized under several different provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Broader Constitutional Challenges Beyond individual defenses, immigration advocates are challenging the expanded use of immigration fines in federal court.

Final Thoughts Civil immigration fines have become one of the federal government's most aggressive immigration enforcement tools.
text:
For years, immigration enforcement in the United States was measured largely by arrests, detention, and deportations. Today, however, another enforcement strategy has emerged—one that can have devastating financial consequences for immigrants and employers alike.

Federal immigration agencies are increasingly relying on civil monetary penalties as a powerful enforcement tool. Through Notices of Intent to Fine (NIFs) and, more recently, Notices of Violation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) are seeking to impose significant financial penalties on individuals and businesses for alleged immigration violations.

For many recipients, these fines come as a surprise. Even more concerning, some notices seek penalties totaling more than a million dollars for an individual.

The good news is that receiving one of these notices does not mean the government automatically wins. Many fines can be challenged, reduced, or even rescinded if addressed promptly.

What Is a Notice of Intent to Fine?

A Notice of Intent to Fine (NIF) is a formal notice issued by DHS or ICE advising an individual or employer that the government intends to assess civil monetary penalties for alleged violations of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

Historically, these notices were relatively uncommon. Recently, the Trump Administration has begun sending them widely, part of its efforts to drive people out of the country.

More recently, ICE has also begun issuing Notices of Violation in certain cases. Unlike a Notice of Intent to Fine, which provides advance notice before a penalty is imposed, a Notice of Violation immediately assesses the civil penalty and generally provides only a limited period in which to contest it.

Who Can Receive Immigration Fines?

Immigration fines are authorized under several different provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Individuals can receive notices based on:

Failure to Depart After a Final Removal Order: Willfully failing to depart after a final removal order, with fines potentially accruing daily

Failure to Comply with Voluntary Departure failing to leave after agreeing to voluntary departure

Improper Entry entering or attempting to enter the United States at locations other than a designated port of entry

Employers are increasingly targeted through Notices of Intent to Fine following Form I-9 inspections. ICE is seeking civil penalties against businesses, and those fines can escalate quickly depending on the number of alleged violations and whether ICE believes the violations were repeated or intentional.

How Do These Fines Become So Large?

I know, the term “more than a million dollars” was thrown around earlier, which can sound shocking but this is really what people are experiencing. While some immigration fines begin at relatively modest amounts—such as civil penalties for improper entry—the most financially devastating assessments generally involve alleged failures to comply with removal orders, nearly a thousand dollars a day in certain failure-to-depart cases.

Because these penalties may accrue daily and be calculated retroactively, the total amount can increase rapidly. Using the applicable statute of limitations, the government has sought penalties approaching $1.9 million in some cases.

Adding to the concern, many recipients report that the notices provide little explanation of how the government calculated the total amount demanded, making it difficult to verify whether the assessment complies with the law.

If This Seems to Be Happening Really Fast, You’re Right

Recent regulatory changes have significantly altered how immigration fines are issued and collected. Among the most important developments are:

shorter advance notice periods before penalties become final

authorization for service of notices by regular mail rather than requiring personal service in some circumstances

expanded use of Notices of Violation that immediately impose penalties rather than merely announcing the government's intent to fine

compressed deadlines for filing administrative challenges

Because these deadlines may be very short, recipients should never ignore a notice or assume there will be additional opportunities to respond later. Acting promptly can be essential to protecting the recipient's rights and ensuring a meaningful opportunity to challenge the government's claims before significant financial penalties become final.

Don’t Panic: Legal Defenses May Be Available

Every case is different, but immigration fines are often subject to legal and factual challenges. This is where I encourage you to speak to qualified legal counsel as each case is different.

Possible defenses include challenging the alleged willfulness of failing to depart, such as if a person was detained by immigration authorities, incarcerated, hospitalized, or otherwise unable to depart, the government may be unable to establish the required element of willfulness.

Attorneys may also be able to challenge whether a voluntary departure agreement was valid, whether the individual remained eligible for relief, or whether equitable circumstances warrant reducing or eliminating the penalty.

In certain circumstances, individuals may qualify for statutory protections or exceptions, including protections available under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA). It may also be worth looking into whether the government has complied with applicable statutes of limitation and other procedural requirements.

Broader Constitutional Challenges

Beyond individual defenses, immigration advocates are challenging the expanded use of immigration fines in federal court.

Among the issues being raised are:

Due Process: Whether notices that fail to explain how penalties were calculated violate the Fifth Amendment.

Excessive Fines: Whether penalties reaching hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of dollars violate the Eighth Amendment.

Administrative Procedure Act (APA): Whether recent procedural changes were lawfully adopted.

Institutional Fairness: Whether allowing DHS both to impose fines and adjudicate administrative appeals provides meaningful due process.

These challenges could significantly influence how immigration fines are imposed in the future.

The Importance of Acting Quickly

Perhaps the most important thing recipients should understand is this: an immigration fine is not necessarily final.

Failing to respond, however, can have serious consequences. Missing the applicable deadline may result in the assessment becoming a final order with limited or no opportunity for further administrative review.

Attorneys across the country have successfully challenged immigration fines through timely administrative responses and legal advocacy. In many cases, fines have been reduced substantially or withdrawn altogether.

And, please keep in mind that contesting an immigration fine doesn’t by itself determine a person's underlying immigration status or eligibility for immigration benefits.

Ongoing Federal Litigation

The legality of these expanded enforcement practices is currently being challenged in Maria L. v. Noem, a class action brought by the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) and Public Justice. The lawsuit challenges both the legality of the government's civil fine program and the procedural rules governing how those penalties are imposed and reviewed. Because the litigation remains ongoing, practitioners should monitor developments that may affect pending and future cases.

Final Thoughts

Civil immigration fines have become one of the federal government's most aggressive immigration enforcement tools. Whether directed at noncitizens accused of failing to depart, individuals alleged to have entered improperly, or employers facing Form I-9 penalties, these assessments can carry enormous financial consequences.

It is vital that anyone (individual or business) receiving this type of notice recognizes that essentially these notices are legal proceedings—not simply bills. You need to respond in a timely manner or important rights could be lost.

But those are just blips in the broader landscape of immigration detention.
As the Trump administration plans to pour up to $45 billion in the next few years into locking up immigrants, we’ll dive into the immigration detention ecosystem in the Bay Area and nationwide.

text:
The federal government has been scrambling to find places to send immigrants that have been arrested at record levels – close to 50,000 in July alone. Trump’s rush to detain immigrants has led to inadequate and overcrowded facilities and out-of-state transfers. Some immigrants have been held for days in unsanitary conditions at San Francisco International Airport. Meanwhile, Gilroy residents have been fighting a proposed field office for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. But those are just blips in the broader landscape of immigration detention. As the Trump administration plans to pour up to $45 billion in the next few years into locking up immigrants, we’ll dive into the immigration detention ecosystem in the Bay Area and nationwide.

Guests:

Tyche Hendricks, senior editor covering immigration, KQED

Doug MacMillan, Reporter covering corporate accountability, The Washington Post

Sara DiNatale, reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California, San Francisco Chronicle

This is a computer-generated transcript. While our team has reviewed it, there may be errors.

Alexis Madrigal: Welcome to Forum, I’m Alexis Madrigal. The Trump administration came into office promising to transform immigration in America, and they have endeavored to do so, arresting and deporting entirely different groups of people than previous administrations. Immigration agents arrested close to 50,000 people in July alone. So where do all those people go?

In Northern California, it’s not a simple situation. We don’t have a big ICE facility nearby. In fact, the closest one is a converted prison in California City, out in the Mojave Desert. We’re gonna talk about the network of facilities that exist now, and that may get built with the surge of money that the Trump administration is plowing into ICE.

Joining us first, we’ve got Tyche Hendricks, senior editor covering immigration here at KQED. Welcome, Tyche.

Tyche Hendricks: Glad to be here.

Alexis Madrigal: And we’ve got Sara DiNatale, who is a reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California at the San Francisco Chronicle. Hey. So, Tyche, just kind of give us an overview here. Like, how is immigration detention supposed to work? How did it, generally speaking, work in the past, and sort of what’s different now?

Tyche Hendricks: Sure. Well, I mean, I think at the get-go we should say immigration detention is civil detention. It’s not punishment for a crime. It’s not supposed to be punitive. It is primarily aimed at people who are a flight risk or a danger, who, you know, the government feels should be held in custody until they go through their immigration court proceeding, deportation proceeding.

There are some people subject to mandatory detention, people, for example, who have certain criminal convictions. And this administration and this Republican Congress have vastly expanded, you know, who they think should be mandatorily detained, which is part of why we’re seeing this huge increase in people in detention facilities.

But, yeah, arrests are coming up to record numbers, and detention also is near a record high. And one thing we should say, even though in California there are some really high numbers, we’re the third highest in arrests after Florida, and Texas is number one. And in those places, it’s ramped up significantly.

So partly because we have these sanctuary laws that mean that when you have a traffic stop with a police officer, you’re not necessarily gonna be handed over to ICE as you would be in those other states, right?

Alexis Madrigal: Yeah. You know, what about the, you know, we’ve seen many of these arrests, either the viral ones and the many more that occur out of the public eye. Where do people actually go? Like, if you got detained — there was someone detained on Telegraph Avenue, you know, a few weeks ago or a month ago. What are the kind of pathways that someone might go through there?

Tyche Hendricks: Sure. I mean, typically, you would go to an ICE office where there are sort of short-term hold rooms in San Francisco. It’s at the ICE sort of field headquarters at 630 Sansome Street, where we’ve seen a lot of protests. And those are hold rooms meant for like a 12-hour processing, you know, short-term, not for overnight.

And then you would be taken on to a long-term detention facility. As you say, there are none currently in Northern California. So the closest are down in Southern Kern County.

But I will say that there was kind of a bottleneck with the short-term hold rooms. And people were being held there for days and days without proper medical care, medical screening, without bedding, without proper food and hygiene. And a court order has now said, that’s no good. And so ICE has sort of fallen back and tried to regroup.

Alexis Madrigal: Sara, you were reporting on what’s been happening at SFO, which seems like exactly an example of one of these situations, right? Where it’s supposed to be short-term detention, but as you discovered talking to people who were actually held there, it has not been.

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, exactly. So what’s happening at SFO, one, I mean, I think people have seen the viral videos of domestic terminal arrests. So what we’re talking about with people actually being held at the airport is happening in the international terminal.

So these are a lot less typically a lot more visible because it’s happening when an immigrant is reentering the country through customs, where they often would be — it’s not abnormal to have a secondary inspection interview. Those happen behind closed doors, you don’t have your cell phone, you’re kind of going over your particulars with a federal agent.

But what’s happening is folks, and a lot of green card holders included, are being flagged, going through that secondary inspection interview, being told like, hey, you have an old arrest on your record and we need to investigate it further. And rather than releasing them on something called parole, which essentially is like, hey, come back for a follow-up appointment, they’re holding them at the airport.

And they’re keeping them in a — they call it a lounge, to be clear. That is their language. They call it an in-transit lounge, and it is by Customs and Border Protection policy only supposed to be used for 72 hours. I would say from the people I’ve spoken to have been held there, they would say like 72 hours is still way too long.

There’s not beds. They’re mainly chairs. They renovated recently, and now they have couch-like benches, which is a step up from before, when people told me they were sleeping upright for up to eight days.

So these holds are really long. Essentially, agents are deciding what to do with them based on their arrest history and following Trump’s executive order about detaining people if they’re deemed potentially inadmissible. And eventually, after that process at the airport, they’re transferred to California City, which is that big holding facility in the Mojave Desert.

Alexis Madrigal: So talk to me, Sara, about Gilroy and what’s been happening down there. There’s this proposed facility that’s just outside the city limit, as I understand it, right? So it’s in Santa Clara County. What is that supposed to be? Is that gonna be a California City-type thing, or is it something, some intermediate kind of facility?

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, the details are not like super specific. Shout-outs to San Jose Spotlight for unearthing some of these internal documents and things that found that they had plans to house up to 150 people. So it’s kind of like not quite as large as California City, but it is still not — it would be more than something like we’re seeing at Sansome.

Alexis Madrigal: More than a lounge, private prison.

Sara DiNatale: Um, the current status right now is that construction is on hold. There’s actually a court hearing today where a judge will decide potentially what the future of that site could be.

But essentially, because it’s in Santa Clara County and not the city of Gilroy, Santa Clara County is the one that’s actually suing the federal government, arguing that the land that’s being used is zoned agriculturally and shouldn’t be used for — whether it’s a holding center or a detention facility, whatever verbiage you want to use. It would be a nice facility, and they are against that. Yeah.

Alexis Madrigal: Tyche, the one that I had heard about and saw protests around was out there in the East Bay, right? In Dublin, former women’s prison, right? What’s been going on with that?

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, that’s been a little quiet recently. This was the, right, this former women’s prison that was closed down for, like, horrible rape abuses and sexual violence against the inmates. ICE did take a tour, I think, at one point. And the city council and a lot of elected officials really raised a hue and cry and said, no ICE facility here.

ICE told me some months ago that they were not looking at it, so it’s kind of quiet at this point. But that is a federally owned prison in the Bay Area. And, you know, Homeland Security officials have said that they’re looking for something that’s closer into San Francisco, which is a big ICE headquarters in California.

Alexis Madrigal: I mean, do we feel like detention is actually a bottleneck? Like, is the fact that we don’t, you know, if California City was actually in Dublin, Pleasanton, do you think we’d see more arrests? Like, what do we know about the relationship between those two things?

Tyche Hendricks: You — I mean, I think there is an argument that advocates are making that the more detention space there is in the area, the easier it is for people to be locked up there.

Certainly this administration — well, this Republican Congress — has been sort of throwing money at ICE and immigration enforcement more broadly. And so there is, you’re seeing around the country a vast ramp-up in detention, and people are also flown, you know, from here to there to here to there, channeled into detention facilities in Texas and other places.

Alexis Madrigal: I mean, Sara, I think this is kind of my question on this. I mean, it has seemed to many people in the Bay Area like it’s odd that we’ve had less immigration enforcement action here than in other parts of the country, given the way that the Trump administration has tended to operate and that this is like a stronghold of anti-Trump sentiment.

Do you think it’s sanctuary city policy? Do you think it’s a lack of detention centers? I mean, do you have any sense of the role that these various factors are playing?

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, I would say it’s probably somewhere in the middle. Like, there’s probably — like, both things, I think, can be true.

I know lawmakers especially have said that they think part of the reason we have had less enforcement efforts is because we don’t have a place to put people easily. It requires more coordination. That has come up in response to the center outside of Gilroy.

Now, some cities and counties in Northern California have proactively been creating ordinances that would make it more difficult for ICE to open new facilities in their areas, just by amplifying existing land-use laws and environmental impact requirements. Things that would just make it, like, more annoying to open a new facility. And they are very candid about that’s why they’re creating these new local laws.

And when you talk to those local city leaders, like the mayor of San Jose, they’re pretty explicit and like, yeah, we think that this is part of why we haven’t had as big of a nice crackdown in our community, because we don’t have that infrastructure.

So it’s definitely a belief that people carry. I mean, in my reporting, I haven’t found a definitive answer, but I think there are logical conclusions that are easy to reach between both those things.

Alexis Madrigal: We’re talking about the network of immigration detention facilities in the Bay Area. In our next segment, we’re gonna kind of take it nationwide and look at what’s happening everywhere else.

We’re joined this morning by Tyche Hendricks, a senior editor covering immigration. We also have Sara DiNatale, who you just heard, a reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California for the San Francisco Chronicle. And, of course, we would love to hear from you.

Maybe you live near Gilroy or Dublin or another community where a detention center has been proposed. Tell us what you’ve seen on the ground. Tell us you’ve heard from your neighbors. What do you think about how your local and state leaders are responding?

And give us a call now. The number is 866-733-6786. You can email Forum at kqed.org. You can find us on Bluesky, Instagram, Discord, or KQED Forum and all those places.

I’m Alexis Madrigal. Stay tuned for more.

Bangkok, Thailand – September 08, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

Siam Legal International, a leading law firm in Thailand, is reporting that a United States federal court has struck down a policy that paused immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries, including Thailand, since January 2026. The ruling, issued August 21, 2026, by Judge Jeannette Vargas of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in the case CLINIC v. Rubio, directly affects Thai nationals pursuing CR-1 and IR-1 spousal visas to join American citizen spouses in the United States.

The US Department of State announced the pause in January 2026, directing consular officers to withhold approval of immigrant visa applications from nationals of the affected countries under Section 221(g) of US immigration law, citing concerns about public charge risk. Consular officers were instructed to apply this outcome regardless of whether an individual applicant had already demonstrated eligibility during the interview, according to court filings. Thailand was among roughly forty percent of countries worldwide included on the list, while nonimmigrant categories such as tourist, student, and K-1 fiancé visas remained unaffected throughout the pause.

Judge Vargas found that the policy conflicted with US immigration law by removing final decision-making authority from individual consular officers and imposing a predetermined refusal based solely on an applicant’s nationality. The court rejected the government’s reliance on a 2018 Supreme Court decision upholding an earlier travel ban, ruling that the earlier case addressed presidential authority over entry into the country rather than the government’s ability to direct officers to refuse applicants already found individually eligible. The ruling vacated the policy in its entirety rather than limiting relief to the plaintiffs, extending its effect to applicants from all 75 affected countries.

The decision differs from a separate July 2026 ruling in De Moura Gomes v. Rubio, in which a federal court in Washington also found the policy unlawful but limited relief to the family that filed the case. Under the August ruling, any CR-1 or IR-1 refusal issued on or after January 21, 2026, that relied solely on the policy is set aside, and affected cases are expected to be returned for individual review. Siam Legal International notes that this does not guarantee approval, as applicants must still satisfy standard requirements, including a public charge assessment conducted on an individual basis rather than a blanket rule.

“Thai nationals who received a hold on their spousal visa case earlier this year now have grounds to have that case reconsidered on its own facts, not as part of a blanket policy,” said Rex Baay, Senior Immigration Consultant and Operations Manager at Siam Legal International. “Applicants should not assume this ruling means automatic approval, and strengthening documentation around financial support and the sponsor’s background remains an important step while embassies work through the practical process of applying the decision.”

Applicants with a pending case may check status through the Consular Electronic Application Center to confirm whether a prior refusal has been updated since the ruling, and should confirm that medical examinations and police clearance certificates have not expired during the delay. The ruling has not resolved every claim raised in the underlying litigation, with remaining issues due before the court by September 11, 2026, and the government has not confirmed whether it intends to appeal. Siam Legal International’s US visa team continues to track the practical rollout of the decision at the US Embassy in Bangkok and other posts processing Thai applicants.

Siam Legal International first outlined the scope of the original pause and its effect on Thai applicants in a Siam Legal US from Thailand visa advisory, published earlier in 2026, and the firm continues to update its guidance as the litigation progresses.
